mustNotClaim: that the gap did not happen

touches.purpose: Say plainly that this is not a renewal and that the conditions have to be met again, listing them.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Explain that the old one stays expired and a new one is issued in its place, and what differs between them.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

mustNotClaim: that the old one is revived

touches.purpose: Say there is no way back to this one and name what exists instead, if anything does.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Confirm what is valid now and, where a replacement was issued, that it is a new one rather than the old one revived.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

guardrails: complaint
message_after_success
unsubscribe

useCases: someone acting on something that expired, told the one route that restores it
a replacement issued and kept distinct from the expired entity

requires: an authoritative expiry recorded against the entity
an attempt by the holder to use, renew or ask about it after that expiry
the holder being the party the entity belonged to
insufficientAlone: an expiry with no attempt against it
a scheduled win-back date with no action from the holder

nodes.does: Establish what the expiry actually did to this entity - suspended it, invalidated it, or ended the relationship behind it - before naming any route back. Reading every lapse as the same lapse is how somebody is sent to renew something that can only be replaced

nodes.asks: Which mechanism restores validity here?

branches.label: Renewal
branches.when: the governing rules let the same entity be carried forward from where it stopped

branches.label: Requalification
branches.when: validity depends on evidence or a check that has to be satisfied again

branches.label: Replacement only
branches.when: the expired entity cannot become valid again and a new one has to be issued in its place

branches.label: No route back
branches.when: nothing restores validity - the basis for it has gone

nodes.does: Name renewal as the route, what it costs, and what carries across the gap. Somebody who came back on their own does not need persuading, only telling exactly what to do next

Say plainly that this is not a renewal and that the conditions have to be met again, listing them. Letting somebody believe a click will fix it, and then asking for evidence halfway through, is how an intent that arrived willing leaves annoyed

Explain that the old one stays expired and a new one is issued in its place, and what differs between them. The replacement is a different object, and the holder will be asked later about a period when they held neither

Say there is no way back to this one and name what exists instead, if anything does. A dead end stated clearly ends the attempt once; a dead end left vague produces three more attempts and a support contact

after.rule: The named route is left open for a bounded response window from the moment it was named; an untaken route closes as still expired.

timeout.reason: re-entry routes are bounded by the rules that created them, and an offer that outlives its own window is one nobody can honour

nodes.recheck: the the expired entity and the holder's attempt to act on it re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.asks: Did validity come back?

branches.label: Valid again
branches.when: the route completed and something valid now exists for the holder

branches.label: Abandoned
branches.when: the holder stopped partway or explicitly declined the route

nodes.does: Confirm what is valid now and, where a replacement was issued, that it is a new one rather than the old one revived. The gap during which nothing was valid is a fact the holder will need later, and hiding it here is what makes that conversation go wrong

nodes.state: valid again by the route that was named
nodes.reEntry: the restored or replacement entity has its own expiry, and a later lapse enters here again

nodes.state: still expired; the route was offered and not taken
nodes.reEntry: a further attempt by the holder starts a new instance with the route re-evaluated from current rules

nodes.state: expired with no route back
nodes.reEntry: nothing re-enters here - a new entitlement of this kind is a different object and starts at its own issuance

guardrails: The route is worked out before anything is said. One wrong route spends an intent that arrived willing.
An expiry is never undone by editing its date. The gap during which nothing was valid stays on the record.
The replacement and the expired entity stay separately addressable, and the holder is told which one they now have.
A dead end is said once, clearly, with whatever alternative exists - not softened into a route that does not work.
journeys.reusableRule: Somebody returning to something expired has already done the hard part, and the only way to waste that is to name the wrong way back.

journeys.name: Entitlement qualification → grant, deny or pending
journeys.purpose: Establish whether a right actually exists, as a state distinct from being eligible for one or having paid toward one.

entity.scope: the person or account plus the specific entitlement, at its own scope and validity
entity.note: One entitlement per right per scope. A second grant for the same right produces two expiries and two revocations, which is why an existing one is reconciled rather than duplicated.

distinctFrom.because: Eligibility asks whether the rules would permit this. Entitlement asks whether it has been granted. ACQ-06's own guardrail names the difference; this journey is the state on the other side of it.

journeys.objective: Establish whether a right actually exists, as a state distinct from being eligible for one or having paid toward one.
eligibility: an authoritative basis for a right: a completed purchase, an activated plan, an assigned role, an earned benefit, an effective contract, or a satisfied policy condition
no instance of this journey is already open for the the person or account plus the specific entitlement
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Eligibility is not entitlement. Being permitted to have something is not having it.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A payment attempt is not an entitlement. Authorised is not settled, and settled is what establishes the right.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A marketing promise is not a granted right unless an authoritative business state confirms it.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: An existing entitlement is reconciled, never duplicated.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Qualified but capacity-blocked is pending rather than denied. Somebody who met every requirement and arrived when the allocation was full has not been refused, and recording it as a denial closes a case that policy may reopen with a waitlist or a later grant.

guardrails: state_written_on_stale_entity

useCases: a completed purchase or activated plan turned into a right with a scope and validity
a right already held, reconciled instead of granted twice

requires: an authoritative basis for a right: a completed purchase, an activated plan, an assigned role, an earned benefit, an effective contract, or a satisfied policy condition
insufficientAlone: a payment authorised but not settled
eligibility for a plan nobody has bought
a marketing promise, which describes what we offer rather than what has been granted

nodes.does: Evaluate the authoritative basis - the record that establishes the right, not the process that led toward it. What matters is whether the business state confirms the grant, not how close it came

nodes.asks: Does an entitlement already exist for this right at this scope?

branches.label: Already held
branches.when: a prior grant covers the same right and scope

branches.label: New
branches.when: no existing grant covers it

nodes.does: Reconcile scope and validity against the existing grant rather than issuing a second one. Two grants for one right produce two expiries, two revocations and a state nobody can read

nodes.state: existing entitlement reconciled; no duplicate grant issued
nodes.reEntry: a further change to the basis re-opens this against the reconciled grant

nodes.asks: Are the requirements for this right satisfied?

branches.label: Satisfied
branches.when: the authoritative basis establishes the right

branches.label: A named requirement is outstanding
branches.when: the right is available in principle and something specific has not been met yet

branches.label: Not available
branches.when: the requirements cannot be met for this account - a structural exclusion rather than a missing step

nodes.state: PENDING_REQUIREMENT; the right is reachable and not yet held
nodes.reEntry: satisfying the named requirement re-opens this. Pending and denied are kept apart because the route back differs - one needs a step completed, the other needs the rules to change

nodes.state: DENIED; the right is not available on this basis
nodes.reEntry: a different basis - a purchase, a role, a contract - is evaluated on its own terms

nodes.does: Record GRANTED with the basis that established it, the scope it covers and its validity. Granting is idempotent - the same basis arriving twice grants once

nodes.on: a right being established
carries: the entitlement, its scope and its validity
the explicit fact that nothing has been provisioned yet, so nothing downstream reads the grant as working access

guardrails: Eligibility is not entitlement. Being permitted to have something is not having it.
A payment attempt is not an entitlement. Authorised is not settled, and settled is what establishes the right.
A marketing promise is not a granted right unless an authoritative business state confirms it.
An existing entitlement is reconciled, never duplicated.

Qualified but capacity-blocked is pending rather than denied. Somebody who met every requirement and arrived when the allocation was full has not been refused, and recording it as a denial closes a case that policy may reopen with a waitlist or a later grant.
journeys.reusableRule: Entitlement represents an established right to a defined capability or benefit, not merely eligibility to receive it.

journeys.name: Entitlement grant → provision → verify availability
journeys.purpose: Hold the distance between a right being granted and the thing behind it actually working.

entity.scope: the entitlement plus the resource or capability being provisioned for it
entity.note: One provisioning run per entitlement, keyed idempotently. Retries and redeliveries are expected, and none of them may provision a second copy.

requires: an entitlement recorded as GRANTED with a scope that implies a resource

nodes.does: Create the provisioning action and record the state as PROVISIONING, keyed so that a redelivered event provisions once. A granted entitlement in PROVISIONING is not yet usable, and nothing downstream may present it as though it were

timeout.reason: a provisioning run that has neither succeeded nor failed within its SLA is a failure that has not reported itself, and treating silence as success is how a customer finds the gap first

nodes.asks: How did provisioning end?

branches.label: Succeeded
branches.when: the provisioning system reports success

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the provisioning system reports failure

nodes.asks: Does actual availability need to be verified?

branches.label: Verification matters
branches.when: the holder's ability to reach the capability is what the entitlement is for, and a reported success is not proof of it

branches.label: The provisioning record is authoritative
branches.when: the provisioning system is itself the source of truth for availability

nodes.does: Check that the capability is genuinely reachable by its holder. A provisioning API returning success is a statement about the API - whether anyone can use the thing is a separate question with its own answer

nodes.asks: Is it actually available?

branches.label: Available
branches.when: the capability is reachable

branches.label: Provisioned but unreachable
branches.when: the resource exists and the holder still cannot use it

nodes.state: ACTIVE; the right is granted, provisioned and usable
nodes.reEntry: a scope change re-opens provisioning for the delta rather than for the whole entitlement

nodes.on: a provisioned resource the holder cannot reach
carries: the entitlement, the provisioning result and what verification actually found
the fact that the grant is valid, so this is an access fault rather than an entitlement question

nodes.asks: What class of failure is this?

branches.label: Transient and retry-safe
branches.when: the failure is expected to clear and the retry budget has room

branches.label: Permanent, or the budget is spent
branches.when: retrying will not help, or has already been tried as often as the budget allows

nodes.does: Retry against a budget fixed at the first failure. The budget does not renew - that is the difference between a retry policy and a loop that provisions forever

nodes.on: provisioning that cannot be completed automatically
carries: the entitlement and what has been attempted
the fact that the customer holds a valid right they currently cannot use

guardrails: A granted entitlement is not a provisioned one. The grant is a business record; provisioning is a distributed operation that can fail on its own.
Provisioning success is not availability. Where the difference matters, availability is checked rather than assumed.
Provisioning is idempotent. Redelivery provisions once.
Retries are bounded by a budget fixed at the first failure.
journeys.reusableRule: A granted right becomes usable only after the required resource or capability is successfully provisioned and available.

journeys.name: Entitlement change → recalculate scope → expand, reduce or preserve
journeys.purpose: Apply only the difference between the old and new rights, rather than re-applying a whole scope over a working one.

entity.scope: the entitlement whose basis changed, and the delta between its previous and new scope
entity.note: The delta is the unit of work. Re-applying the full new scope reprovisions what already worked and revokes what should have survived, and the holder sees both as an outage.

requires: an authoritative change to the basis of an existing entitlement: a plan change, a role change, a contract amendment, a benefit or quantity or coverage change

nodes.does: Compare the previous scope, the new scope and the effective time, and derive the delta. What gets applied is the difference - a capability present in both scopes is not touched at all

nodes.asks: Which way did the scope move?

branches.label: Expanded only
branches.when: capabilities were added and none removed

branches.label: Reduced, or mixed
branches.when: at least one capability is no longer covered, whether or not others were added

nodes.does: Provision the newly granted capabilities, idempotently, and leave everything already working untouched

Apply any expansion, and identify precisely which capabilities are no longer covered. Historical data and resources created under the previous scope are not destroyed by a scope change - a reduction removes a right, not a record

nodes.asks: Do existing commitments or in-flight usage depend on what is being removed?

branches.label: Something depends on it
branches.when: a confirmed reservation, an in-progress service, a purchased benefit or an open transaction rests on the capability being removed

branches.label: Nothing depends on it
branches.when: the reduction affects only future use

nodes.on: a scope reduction with live commitments underneath it
carries: the capabilities being removed and their effective time
the commitments that depend on them, which are reconciled separately rather than cancelled by the scope change

nodes.does: Apply the reduction to future access only, idempotently. Future access loss and cancelling an existing obligation are two different decisions, and this one makes only the first

nodes.state: delta applied; unchanged capabilities untouched
nodes.reEntry: a further basis change is compared against the new scope

guardrails: A reduction in entitlement does not destroy historical data or resources created while the right was held.
Future access loss and cancelling an existing obligation are separate decisions made by separate journeys.
The delta is applied idempotently, so a redelivered change does not reprovision or re-revoke.
journeys.reusableRule: Entitlement changes should apply the difference between old and new rights without rewriting the history of what was previously valid.

journeys.name: Entitlement loss → revoke future capability → reconcile existing obligations
journeys.purpose: Stop future use of a right that has ended without cancelling what was validly created while it was held.

entity.scope: the entitlement that ended, plus the resources and commitments that depended on it
entity.note: Revocation stays scoped to this entitlement. A right held on another basis is untouched, and the record that this one existed remains.

distinctFrom.because: Suspension restricts a right that still exists and is designed to come back. This is the right ending, which is why it reconciles obligations rather than holding them.

requires: an authoritative end to a right: a plan downgrade, a contract termination, a role removal, a benefit expiry, an eligibility-linked revocation, or a policy decision

nodes.does: Determine when the loss actually takes effect - immediately, at period end, or on a future date. Assuming immediate is how someone loses what they have already paid for, and everything downstream depends on getting this right
Identify the capabilities affected, scoped to this entitlement alone. A lost role does not revoke rights the same person holds on a different basis

Prevent future use of the affected capabilities from the effective time, idempotently. The record that the entitlement existed and what was done under it is untouched - losing a right does not mean it was never held

nodes.asks: Do valid commitments exist that were created while the right was held?

branches.label: Commitments outstanding
branches.when: a confirmed reservation, an in-progress service, an already purchased benefit or an open transaction exists

branches.label: Nothing outstanding
branches.when: the right governed only future use

nodes.on: an entitlement ending with commitments still live under it
carries: each commitment and when it was created relative to the loss
the explicit fact that nothing has been cancelled - the reconciliation decides that on its own terms

nodes.asks: Does a provisioned resource need removing?

branches.label: Resource provisioned
branches.when: something was provisioned for this entitlement and is no longer authorised

branches.label: Nothing provisioned
branches.when: the right had no provisioned resource behind it

nodes.on: a provisioned resource whose entitlement has ended
carries: the resource and the effective loss time
the fact that removal is a capability question and not a data-deletion authorisation

nodes.state: future use revoked; history and commitments intact
nodes.reEntry: the right may be granted again on a new basis, which is a new entitlement rather than a revival of this one

guardrails: Losing an entitlement does not mean the entitlement never existed. The historical record stands.
Existing commitments are reconciled separately and are never cancelled automatically by the loss.
Revocation stays scoped to the affected entitlement.
Stopping future use is idempotent.
journeys.reusableRule: Losing a right prevents future unauthorized use but does not automatically erase commitments created while the right was valid.

journeys.name: Access request → authorization check → allow, deny or step up
journeys.purpose: Decide at the moment of the attempt whether this actor may take this action on this resource.

entity.scope: the individual access request - one actor, one action, one resource
entity.note: The decision belongs to the request. Allowing one action says nothing about the next, and a cached decision is re-checked against critical state that may have moved since.

distinctFrom.because: Approval is a business decision taken in advance about a subject. Authorization is a runtime decision taken at the moment of the attempt, and being approved for something does not authorise every action within it.

requires: an actor attempting a protected action on an identified resource
insufficientAlone: a successful authentication, which establishes who is asking and nothing about what they may do
holding an entitlement to the product the resource belongs to

nodes.does: Evaluate at execution time: the identity, the entitlement, the role and permission, the resource's own scope, the current security state, and the policy requirements for this specific action. A cached decision is re-checked against critical state, because the states that matter most are the ones that change fastest

nodes.asks: What does the current state permit?

branches.label: Fully authorized
branches.when: every required condition is satisfied for this actor, action and resource

branches.label: Authorized subject to stronger verification
branches.when: the conditions are met except for an assurance level this action requires

branches.label: Not authorized
branches.when: at least one required condition fails

nodes.state: ALLOW; this action on this resource, now
nodes.reEntry: the next attempt is decided again. Allowing one action never authorises the following one, however similar it looks

nodes.on: an action requiring an assurance level the current session does not hold
carries: the pending request, so it can resume rather than be retyped
the assurance level required and why this action requires it

nodes.does: Record the denial with its reason category - entitlement missing, permission missing, resource out of scope, security state blocking, or policy prohibition. A bare denial cannot be appealed, debugged, or distinguished from an outage

nodes.state: DENY, with a recorded reason category
nodes.reEntry: a change to any of the evaluated states makes the next attempt a new decision

guardrails: Entitlement to a product is not permission for every action within it.
Authentication success is not authorization. The two answer different questions.
A cached authorization respects current critical state changes rather than the state at the time it was cached.
Every denial carries a reason category.
journeys.reusableRule: Access should be granted only when the current actor, resource and action satisfy the required authorization conditions at execution time.

journeys.name: Credential issued → activate → use, expire or revoke
journeys.purpose: Run an access artifact through its own validity lifecycle, separately from the right it represents.

entity.scope: the individual credential - its id, owner, scope and validity
entity.note: A credential's validity is its own. It can be valid while the entitlement behind it has lapsed, and revoked while that entitlement is perfectly live.

distinctFrom.because: The entitlement is the right. The credential is an artifact that presents it. Treating the artifact as the right means revoking a token looks like removing a benefit.

requires: a credential issued with an owner, a scope and a validity

nodes.does: Store the credential id, owner, scope, issue time, validity, whether activation is required, and its status as ISSUED. Issued is not active, and nothing may present it as usable until it is

nodes.asks: Does this credential require activation before use?

branches.label: Activation required
branches.when: policy requires the holder to activate it

branches.label: Active on issue
branches.when: policy makes it usable as issued

until: the credential is revoked before activation

timeout.reason: an unactivated credential does not become active by waiting, and leaving it ISSUED indefinitely keeps a usable artifact alive that nobody ever claimed

nodes.asks: What happened during the activation window?

branches.label: Activated
branches.when: the holder activated it

branches.label: Revoked first
branches.when: a revocation arrived before activation

nodes.does: Expire the credential unactivated, recording that it was never claimed. An expired-unactivated credential and an expired-active one are different facts about how the artifact was used

nodes.state: EXPIRED, never activated
nodes.reEntry: a replacement credential is issued as a new artifact with its own id and lifecycle

nodes.does: Record the credential as ACTIVE for its scope and validity

timeout.reason: validity ending is the ordinary path; the wait is watching for the two things that can end it sooner

nodes.asks: What ended the credential's active life?

branches.label: Revoked
branches.when: an authoritative revocation arrived

branches.label: Replaced
branches.when: a replacement credential was issued for the same purpose

nodes.state: REPLACED; this artifact is no longer usable
nodes.reEntry: the replacement runs its own lifecycle. This one is never reactivated, whatever happens to the replacement

nodes.on: a credential being revoked
carries: the credential, its scope and its owner
the revocation reason

nodes.does: Re-read the credential's current version before expiring it. An extension or a replacement may have moved its validity since this timer was written, and expiring on the remembered value would undo a later decision

nodes.asks: Does the current version still expire now?

branches.label: Still expiring
branches.when: the current validity ends at this moment

branches.label: Validity moved
branches.when: an extension or replacement changed it

nodes.does: Record the credential as EXPIRED. Expired is not revoked - the artifact reached the end of its validity rather than being withdrawn, and the two mean different things to anyone investigating later

nodes.state: EXPIRED after active use
nodes.reEntry: the entitlement behind it may still be perfectly valid; a new credential is issued for it rather than this one being revived

nodes.state: expiry superseded by an extension or replacement
nodes.reEntry: the current validity governs, and its own end executes when it arrives

guardrails: A credential issued is not a credential active.
Credential validity is not entitlement validity. Either can end while the other holds.
A revoked credential is never restored by a stale activation or refresh event.
Expiry re-reads the current version before applying, so an extension is not undone by an older timer.
journeys.reusableRule: Credentials are access artifacts with their own validity lifecycle and should not be treated as the entitlement they represent.

journeys.name: Credential compromise or revocation → disable → replace or re-authenticate
journeys.purpose: Take a credential out of use immediately, and let any replacement come through its own authorised path.

entity.scope: the specific credentials affected, and their owner
entity.note: Scope is the whole question. One compromised artifact does not implicate unrelated ones unless policy says the compromise reaches them.

requires: a requirement to revoke: suspected or confirmed compromise, a manual revoke, a password or security reset, a device removed, access terminated, or a token invalidation

nodes.does: Determine which credentials are actually affected. One compromised artifact does not revoke unrelated ones unless policy says the compromise implies them - over-revoking on a suspicion locks people out of things that were never at risk, and the lockout becomes the incident

Revoke the affected credentials immediately, ahead of everything else in this journey. Security revocation takes precedence over queued access actions - an artifact invalidated at ten o'clock must not still authorise a request queued at one minute to
Invalidate the refresh and activation operations tied to the revoked credentials, so nothing in flight can bring one back after it has been withdrawn

nodes.asks: Is a replacement allowed?

branches.label: Replacement permitted
branches.when: the owner remains entitled and policy allows re-issuing

branches.label: No replacement
branches.when: access is being removed, or the owner is no longer entitled

nodes.state: revoked; no replacement issued
nodes.reEntry: a new credential requires the entitlement and the authorisation to be established again, which is a different journey and not a continuation of this one

nodes.asks: Does issuing a replacement require verification first?

branches.label: Verification required
branches.when: the revocation reason means the requester's identity or control has to be re-established

branches.label: No verification needed
branches.when: the revocation was routine and the owner's identity is not in question

nodes.on: a replacement requiring identity or control to be re-established
carries: the revocation reason, which sets how strong the verification has to be
the fact that the old credential is already revoked and stays revoked whatever the verification concludes

nodes.does: Issue a replacement as a new credential with its own id and its own lifecycle. The revoked artifact is never reactivated - a replacement replaces, and reusing the old identifier would make the revocation unverifiable

nodes.on: a replacement credential being issued
carries: the new credential and the credential it replaces
the revocation reason, which is part of the new artifact's history

guardrails: One credential compromise does not automatically revoke unrelated credentials unless policy requires it.
A replacement never reactivates the revoked credential. It is a new artifact.
Security revocation takes precedence over queued access actions, including refresh and activation already in flight.
journeys.reusableRule: Credential revocation should immediately invalidate the affected access artifact while replacement follows an independently authorized path.

journeys.name: Access suspension → restricted state → restore or terminate
journeys.purpose: Restrict defined capabilities for a reason, in the smallest scope that addresses it, while keeping restoration genuinely possible.

entity.scope: the account or person plus the specific capability scope being restricted
entity.note: The scope is recorded rather than implied. Anything reading the account has to be able to tell which capabilities are blocked and which still work.

distinctFrom.because: Grace continues a right whose validity has ended. Suspension restricts a right that is still valid. One is continuity after an ending; the other is a hold before one.

competition.precedence: lower than a suspected-compromise investigation (IDN-90) on the same account - an active security incident is the more urgent, safety-critical question, and a business-reason suspension defers to it rather than resolving independently while it is open

journeys.objective: Restrict defined capabilities for a reason, in the smallest scope that addresses it, while keeping restoration genuinely possible.
eligibility: a decision to suspend for a stated reason: a payment state, a security review, a policy review, a temporary operational restriction, or an administrative hold
no instance of this journey is already open for the the account or person plus the specific capability scope being restricted
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Suspended is not terminated. Suspension is designed to be reversible and its record says so.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: The suspension uses the smallest scope that addresses its reason.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Restoration does not blindly return every previous capability - it hands to a journey whose job is revalidating first.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A suspension without a review point is a termination nobody authorised.

guardrails: state_written_on_stale_entity

useCases: a suspension for a stated reason in the smallest scope that addresses it
a review point reached with nothing resolved: extend, lift or escalate

requires: a decision to suspend for a stated reason: a payment state, a security review, a policy review, a temporary operational restriction, or an administrative hold
insufficientAlone: an outage, which removes access without anyone deciding to

nodes.does: Record the reason, the scope, when it takes effect, which capabilities are blocked, which continue, and what would end it. The scope is the smallest that addresses the reason - a payment problem does not justify blocking a security setting, and over-broad restriction makes the restriction itself the incident

nodes.asks: Does anything remain accessible?

branches.label: Partial
branches.when: capabilities outside the reason's scope are unaffected

branches.label: Full
branches.when: the reason justifies blocking everything in scope

nodes.does: Leave the unaffected capabilities working, so the state is legible as a suspension rather than as an outage - and so the holder can still do the thing that would resolve it
Record a full suspension within the affected scope, with the same review condition. Full is still not terminal, and the record says so

after.rule: The review point or the recorded expiry.

timeout.reason: a suspension with no review is a termination that nobody had to authorise, and the review is what keeps the two apart

nodes.recheck: the the account or person plus the specific capability scope being restricted re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.asks: How was it resolved?

branches.label: Reason resolved
branches.when: what justified the suspension has been dealt with

branches.label: Terminal decision
branches.when: the review concluded that the right should end rather than resume

nodes.asks: At the review point with nothing resolved, what now?

branches.label: Extend with a new end
branches.when: the reason still holds and policy allows a further period

branches.label: Lift it
branches.when: the reason has lapsed even though nothing formally resolved it

branches.label: Nobody decided
branches.when: the review point arrived with no decision made at all

nodes.does: Record the extension as its own suspension instance with a new review point, so the number of times someone has been suspended without a decision stays countable rather than hidden inside one long record

nodes.state: suspension extended; a new instance carries the new review point
nodes.reEntry: the extension runs as its own instance with its own end

nodes.on: a suspension ending without a terminal decision
carries: which capabilities were blocked and why
the explicit instruction that restoration revalidates rather than replays - the previous capability set is history, not a target

a restoration_case_id minted at this handoff, deterministically derived from account_id + capability_scope + this suspension's own review outcome, so ACC-79 can construct its own instance without inventing one

nodes.on: a review concluding that the right should end
carries: the suspension history and the terminal decision
the entitlement now ending

nodes.on: a suspension review point reached with no decision
carries: how long access has been restricted and on what reason
the fact that an undecided suspension is costing the holder access every day it continues

guardrails: Suspended is not terminated. Suspension is designed to be reversible and its record says so.
The suspension uses the smallest scope that addresses its reason.

nodes.asks: How much of the previous capability set is currently valid?

branches.label: All of it

branches.label: Some of it
branches.when: part of the set is currently valid and part is not

branches.label: None of it

Restore only the subset that is currently valid, and invalidate the obsolete restriction actions for it. Expired credentials, withdrawn permissions, lapsed entitlements, deleted resources and roles that no longer exist are not resurrected - each ended for its own reason, and restoring access never addressed any of them. What is not restored is named, so the holder can ask about it rather than discover it

nodes.state: capabilities restored against current valid state
nodes.reEntry: a further restriction and restoration is its own cycle

nodes.state: partially restored; what did not return is named
nodes.reEntry: each capability not restored re-enters when its own requirement is met - the subset that is missing is a list rather than a vague sense that something is wrong

journeys.name: Deprovision request → dependency check → remove, retain or escalate
journeys.purpose: Remove a capability that is no longer authorised, after establishing that nothing still depends on the thing being removed.

entity.scope: the provisioned resource or capability, and the entitlement whose end triggered its removal
entity.note: The resource is the entity, not the entitlement. A shared resource outlives any single right to it, which is why dependency is checked before anything is removed.

distinctFrom.because: ACC-74 ends a right and stops future use. This removes the technical resource behind it, which is a separate operation with its own failure modes and its own reasons to wait.

requires: a valid requirement to deprovision: an entitlement ended, an account closed, a role removed, a contract terminated, or a resource explicitly removed
insufficientAlone: a period of non-use, which is not an authorisation to remove anything

nodes.does: Identify the provisioned resources affected, and which of them are shared with anything still entitled

nodes.asks: What still depends on these resources?

branches.label: Shared with a live entitlement
branches.when: another holder is still entitled to the same resource

branches.label: A commitment must complete first
branches.when: an in-progress service or open transaction needs the resource until it finishes

branches.label: Data transfer or a special process applies
branches.when: an export, a handover or a defined termination process has to run before removal

branches.label: Nothing depends on it
branches.when: the resource serves only the entitlement that ended

nodes.state: retained; another entitlement still depends on it
nodes.reEntry: when the last entitlement to the shared resource ends, removal is evaluated again. Removing it now would take it from everyone else who is still entitled

timeout.after: the horizon appropriate to the dependent commitment
timeout.reason: a dependency that never clears leaves an unauthorised capability alive indefinitely, which is the failure deprovisioning exists to prevent

timeout.reason: silence is not success, and an unauthorised capability that may still be live is worth escalating rather than assuming away

nodes.asks: How did it end?

branches.label: Succeeded
branches.when: the system reports the resource removed

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the system reports a failure

nodes.asks: Does the access consequence matter enough to verify?

branches.label: Verify it
branches.when: continued access would be a real problem, which is the usual case for anything security-relevant

branches.label: The removal record is sufficient
branches.when: the deprovisioning system is authoritative for whether the capability exists

nodes.does: Confirm the capability is genuinely no longer available. A deprovisioning API returning success is a statement about the API, and the question here is whether anyone can still get in

nodes.state: capability removed; records and audit data untouched
nodes.reEntry: re-provisioning follows a new entitlement rather than an undo. Deleting the retained data is a separate lifecycle with its own authorisation

nodes.asks: Is this failure retry-safe within the budget?

branches.label: Retry
branches.when: the failure is transient and the budget fixed at the first attempt has room

branches.label: Escalate
branches.when: the failure is permanent, or the budget is spent

nodes.does: Retry against the budget fixed at the first failure, idempotently, so a partially completed removal is completed rather than restarted

nodes.on: a capability that could not be removed
carries: the resource, what was attempted, and how long it has been unauthorised
whether the capability is believed to still be reachable, which is what makes this urgent rather than administrative

guardrails: An entitlement ending is not an authorisation for destructive deletion.
Deprovisioning does not delete historical or audit data. That is a separate lifecycle with separate authorisation.
Shared resource dependencies are checked before removal.
Where the access consequence matters, technical success is verified rather than assumed.
Deprovisioning is idempotent, so a retry completes a partial removal rather than restarting it.
journeys.reusableRule: Deprovisioning removes no-longer-authorized capability only after active dependencies and retention obligations have been reconciled.

nodes.asks: Can the holder do anything about this?

branches.label: Resolvable by them
branches.when: the release condition is something the account holder can satisfy - a payment, a document, a correction, a re-verification

branches.label: Not theirs to resolve

branches.label: Placed by a security response

nodes.state: informed, resolution not theirs

nodes.state: restriction announced by the security response; no separate notice sent

branches.label: Unreachable

nodes.recheck: the person or account plus the specific restriction or end date placed on it re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

branches.label: Restored

branches.label: Still restricted

nodes.state: restored and confirmed

journeys.name: Entitlement or credential issued → activation window → activated or lapsed unclaimed
journeys.purpose: Get somebody to actually use what they have been granted, before the window in which they can claim it closes - because an unredeemed entitlement is indistinguishable from one that was never granted.

ACC-76 tracks the credential's own issue/expire/revoke lifecycle. Here the only question is first use inside the window.

eligibility: an entitlement or credential authoritatively granted to a named holder
confirmation that it is provisioned and reachable by that holder
an activation window or expiry
no instance of this journey is already open for the the issued entitlement or credential and its activation window

journeys.purpose: Establish confidence in one specific identity claim, bound to the evidence that established it.

entity.note: Verification belongs to a claim, not to a person. Two claims about the same person are two verifications, and neither carries the other.

distinctFrom.because: Verification asks whether a claim is true. Authentication asks whether whoever is present right now controls it. A verified claim from last year says nothing about who is at the keyboard.

journeys.objective: Establish confidence in one specific identity claim, bound to the evidence that established it.
