requires: a document submitted against an identified requirement
insufficientAlone: a file uploaded, which is a transfer rather than a submission against anything

nodes.does: Record the document as SUBMITTED against the specific requirement it is offered for. Uploaded is not validated, and nothing may treat the submission as satisfying the requirement while it sits here

Validate the properties this requirement actually cares about: the document type, whether it belongs to the person offering it, readability, completeness, validity dates, the required fields, and integrity or authenticity where the requirement demands them

nodes.asks: What did validation find?

branches.label: Valid
branches.when: the document satisfies this requirement's acceptance rules

branches.label: Correctable
branches.when: something specific is wrong that a better submission would fix - unreadable, cropped, an expired copy of a current document

branches.label: Invalid
branches.when: the document cannot satisfy this requirement whatever is resubmitted

nodes.does: Record ACCEPTED for this specific requirement, with what was checked. Accepted here is not universally valid - the same document offered against a different requirement is assessed again on that requirement's rules

nodes.state: ACCEPTED for the stated requirement
nodes.reEntry: the same document offered against another requirement enters as a new submission, because acceptance travels with the requirement rather than with the file

nodes.does: Record REJECTED with the reason. A rejection that does not say what was wrong produces the same submission again

nodes.state: REJECTED for this requirement, with a recorded reason
nodes.reEntry: a different document may be submitted; this one is not reassessed unchanged

nodes.does: Record CORRECTION_REQUIRED, stating specifically what is wrong and what would fix it

timeout.after: the requirement's deadline, or this document's own validity end
timeout.reason: a correction request with no end leaves the requirement permanently half-satisfied, and the process behind it permanently waiting

nodes.state: correction window closed; the requirement remains unsatisfied
nodes.reEntry: a new submission opens its own instance with the full history attached

nodes.does: Link the replacement to the original and keep the original submission and its validation result readable. A replaced document is superseded rather than deleted - what was offered and why it was not accepted is part of the record

nodes.asks: Is another correction round allowed?

branches.label: Round available
branches.when: the number of attempts against this requirement is within the policy limit

branches.label: Limit reached
branches.when: repeated corrections have not produced an acceptable document

nodes.on: repeated corrections failing to satisfy a requirement
carries: every submission and why each was not accepted
the requirement itself, which may be the thing that is wrong rather than the documents

guardrails: Uploaded is not validated.
Accepted for one requirement is not universally valid.
The original submission and its validation history stay auditable after a replacement.
Correction rounds are bounded, and the limit routes to a person rather than to a rejection.
journeys.reusableRule: A submitted document satisfies a requirement only after validation against that requirement's current acceptance rules.

journeys.name: Verification failure → reason → retry, remediate, review or exit
journeys.purpose: Route a failed verification by why it failed, and keep our own failures out of the customer's verification record.

entity.scope: the verification instance that failed
entity.note: The failure belongs to the attempt. A technical failure and a mismatch are different facts about different things, and only one of them is about the person.

journeys.objective: Route a failed verification by why it failed, and keep our own failures out of the customer's verification record.
eligibility: a verification attempt that did not establish its claim
no instance of this journey is already open for the the verification instance that failed
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Retry limits are policy-defined and bounded, and the bound is tighter where the claim is security-sensitive.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A technical failure is never recorded as an identity rejection.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Repeated retries do not bypass security controls. Exhausting the budget routes to a person, not to an acceptance.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: The failure reason is preserved, because the route out depends on it.

value.rule: Every touch runs against a budget fixed when the instance opened; the budget is the plan's own length, and no touch is repeated because nothing could tell whether it arrived.

default.applicableWhen: GLB-24; the graph's own touch count

cooldown.rule: This journey is per the verification instance that failed; a later instance concerns a different the verification instance that failed and no cooldown applies between them.

default.applicableWhen: the entity note: one instance per entity

roles.when: the person is active in the product and the action is taken there
the message has to be kept and survive until the person can act on it

touches.purpose: Explain exactly what needs correcting and offer the bounded retry.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Say that this claim cannot be verified on this basis, and name what basis would be accepted if any is.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

guardrails: complaint
message_after_success
unsubscribe

useCases: a failed check explained with exactly what to correct and a bounded retry
our own technical failure kept out of the person's verification record

requires: a verification attempt that did not establish its claim
insufficientAlone: a verification that expired with no attempt made, which is IDN-81's expiry
a policy change invalidating an existing verification without anyone having attempted one

nodes.does: Classify the failure as INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, MISMATCH, UNREADABLE, EXPIRED_EVIDENCE, TECHNICAL_FAILURE, POLICY_FAILURE, REVIEW_REQUIRED or UNKNOWN. The class decides the route, and it decides something else: recording our own outage as an identity rejection marks someone as having failed a check they never got to attempt

nodes.asks: What kind of failure was it?

branches.label: The person can correct it
branches.when: insufficient evidence, unreadable evidence, or evidence that has expired

branches.label: Ours, and transient
branches.when: a technical failure on our side or a provider's

branches.label: Needs a person
branches.when: a mismatch, an explicit review requirement, or a failure nobody could classify

branches.label: Terminal by policy
branches.when: policy forbids verifying this claim on this basis at all

nodes.asks: Does the retry budget for this claim have room?

branches.label: Room to retry
branches.when: attempts against this claim are within the policy limit for its security sensitivity

branches.label: Budget spent
branches.when: the limit is reached - and repeated failure is also what a genuine person struggling looks like

nodes.does: Explain exactly what needs correcting and offer the bounded retry. A retry offered without an explanation produces the same attempt again, which spends the budget without improving anything

nodes.asks: Is a safe retry available within the backoff budget?

branches.label: Retry
branches.when: the failure is transient and the budget has room

branches.label: Persistent
branches.when: the technical failure is not clearing

nodes.does: Retry with backoff, recording nothing against the person's verification history. Our failure is not their rejection, and the distinction has to survive into whatever reads that history later

Say that this claim cannot be verified on this basis, and name what basis would be accepted if any is. Somebody who attempted verification and hears nothing will attempt it again, and each attempt writes a failure against a person who was never going to be able to pass

nodes.state: bounded retry available; the verification instance stays open
nodes.reEntry: the retry runs as part of the same verification instance, against the same budget - a new instance would reset the count, which is how a bounded retry becomes an unbounded one

nodes.on: a technical failure that is not clearing
carries: the failure class and how often it has recurred
the people currently unable to verify because of it, which is what makes this operational rather than administrative

nodes.on: a failure requiring human judgement, or a budget reached
carries: the failure class and every attempt made
the claim being verified, so the reviewer assesses the claim rather than the attempts

nodes.state: verification not possible on this basis
nodes.reEntry: a different basis or a different claim is assessed on its own terms; what would have to change here is the policy rather than the evidence

guardrails: Retry limits are policy-defined and bounded, and the bound is tighter where the claim is security-sensitive.
A technical failure is never recorded as an identity rejection.
Repeated retries do not bypass security controls. Exhausting the budget routes to a person, not to an acceptance.
The failure reason is preserved, because the route out depends on it.
journeys.reusableRule: Verification recovery should follow the reason verification failed rather than treating every failure as equivalent.

journeys.name: Authentication challenge → authenticate, step up or deny
journeys.purpose: Establish that whoever is present controls the required identity, at the assurance the context demands.

entity.scope: the authentication session, bound to an actor and an account
entity.note: An authenticated session carries an explicit validity. A session with no stated lifetime is one that nothing can decide has expired.

distinctFrom.because: This establishes who is present. ACC-75 decides what they may do. A successful authentication is an input to that decision and never a substitute for it.

journeys.objective: Establish that whoever is present controls the required identity, at the assurance the context demands.
eligibility: a context requiring the actor's control of an identity to be established
no instance of this journey is already open for the the authentication session
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Authentication is not authorization.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A successful login does not prove entitlement to any particular resource.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: An authenticated session carries an explicit assurance level and an explicit validity.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: An unanswered challenge is not recorded as a failed authentication.

value.rule: The challenge is the authentication itself and is mandatory; nothing discretionary exists to cap.

default.applicableWhen: GLB-24; the graph's own touch count

cooldown.rule: This journey is per the authentication session; a later instance concerns a different the authentication session and no cooldown applies between them.

default.applicableWhen: the entity note: one instance per entity

roles.when: an asserted time bound lies inside the urgent horizon and permission for messages on this channel is recorded
a valid token or app session exists and the message is a single step from the notification
the message has to be kept and survive until the person can act on it

touches.purpose: Issue the challenge appropriate to the required assurance level
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

guardrails: complaint
message_after_success
unsubscribe

useCases: a challenge issued at the assurance the context demands
a session already at the required level, challenged for nothing

requires: a context requiring the actor's control of an identity to be established
insufficientAlone: a session that already holds the required assurance
an authorization question about what an authenticated actor may do

nodes.does: Determine the assurance level this context requires. Assurance is a property of what is being done rather than of who is doing it - setting it per user produces an over-challenged ordinary session and an under-challenged sensitive one at the same time

nodes.asks: Does the existing authentication already meet the required level?

branches.label: Sufficient
branches.when: a current session holds the required assurance and has not expired

branches.label: Not sufficient
branches.when: no session, an expired one, or one at a lower assurance than this context needs

nodes.state: already authenticated at the required level
nodes.reEntry: a context requiring higher assurance re-opens this. Being authenticated says who the actor is and nothing about what they may do

nodes.does: Issue the challenge appropriate to the required assurance level

after.rule: The challenge window.

timeout.reason: an unanswered challenge is not a failure to authenticate and is not recorded as one; the attempt simply ends

nodes.recheck: the the authentication session re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.state: challenge unanswered; nothing authenticated and nothing recorded against the actor
nodes.reEntry: a new attempt issues a new challenge

nodes.asks: What was established?

branches.label: Authenticated at the required level
branches.when: the challenge succeeded at the assurance this context needs

branches.label: Authenticated below the required level
branches.when: control was established, at a lower assurance than the context requires

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the challenge was not satisfied

nodes.does: Issue or update the authenticated session with an explicit assurance level and an explicit validity. Both are needed downstream: without the level nothing can require a step-up, and without the validity nothing can decide the session has aged out

nodes.state: authenticated, at a stated assurance and for a stated validity
nodes.reEntry: authorization for any particular action is decided separately, every time - a successful login proves control of an account and entitlement to nothing

nodes.on: control established below the assurance the context requires
carries: the session and the assurance it currently holds
the level the context requires

nodes.on: an authentication failure
carries: the attempt and its context
the explicit fact that one failure is a signal rather than a finding

guardrails: Authentication is not authorization.
A successful login does not prove entitlement to any particular resource.
An authenticated session carries an explicit assurance level and an explicit validity.
An unanswered challenge is not recorded as a failed authentication.
journeys.reusableRule: Authentication establishes that an actor currently controls the required identity/account at a defined assurance level.

journeys.name: Step-up requirement → stronger authentication → resume or deny
journeys.purpose: Raise identity assurance for a sensitive action, then check the action is still authorised before it runs.

entity.scope: the actor, the specific protected action and the authentication context around it
entity.note: The step-up is scoped to the action that required it. Raising assurance once does not open every sensitive action for the rest of the session.

requires: a protected action whose required assurance exceeds what the current session holds - a sensitive account change, a high-risk transaction, a credential change, a privileged action, or an unusual security context

nodes.does: Preserve the requested action's full context, so it can resume rather than be reconstructed by the person from memory
Initiate the stronger authentication or verification this action requires, scoped to it rather than to the session as a whole

timeout.reason: a step-up that is not completed leaves the action blocked, which is the safe outcome and needs no further decision

nodes.asks: Was the higher assurance established?

branches.label: Established
branches.when: the step-up succeeded

branches.label: Not established
branches.when: the step-up failed

nodes.state: protected action remains blocked; assurance not established
nodes.reEntry: a fresh attempt at the action issues a fresh step-up. Nothing is queued to execute if assurance is established later

nodes.does: Revalidate the requested action against current authorization before anything runs. Passing a challenge raises identity assurance and authorises nothing - the entitlement, the resource or the policy can all have moved while the challenge was in front of the person

nodes.asks: Is the requested action still authorised?

branches.label: Still authorised
branches.when: the action's authorization conditions hold at the raised assurance

branches.label: No longer authorised
branches.when: something the action depended on changed during the challenge

nodes.on: a step-up completed with the action still authorised
carries: the preserved action context and the raised assurance level
the fact that authorization is being decided now rather than inherited from before the challenge

nodes.state: assurance raised; the action is no longer authorised and does not run
nodes.reEntry: the raised assurance stands for its own window; the action is attempted again on its own terms and decided again

guardrails: Step-up success does not automatically execute the stale action.
The requested action is revalidated after the challenge, not before it.
The step-up is scoped to an appropriate assurance window and to the action that required it.
journeys.reusableRule: Step-up authentication raises identity assurance for a sensitive action without replacing the need to revalidate that action's authorization.

journeys.name: Authentication failure pattern → security check → recover or restrict
journeys.purpose: Tell an ordinary forgotten password apart from an account under attack, without converting the first into the second.

entity.scope: the account plus the authentication activity observed against it
entity.note: The pattern belongs to the account. A shared IP producing failures across many accounts is a different signal, assessed at a different scope.

distinctFrom.because: This weighs whether failures mean anything. IDN-90 starts from a material compromise signal and contains first. The route between them exists, and it is deliberately a decision rather than a default.

journeys.objective: Tell an ordinary forgotten password apart from an account under attack, without converting the first into the second.
eligibility: authentication failures crossing a meaningful threshold, or matching a pattern the detection considers notable
no instance of this journey is already open for the the account plus the authentication activity observed against it
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: One failed password attempt is not a compromise.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A risk model's output is not a confirmed attacker. It orders investigation and concludes nothing.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Any security response uses the smallest necessary scope.

guardrails: state_written_on_stale_entity

useCases: repeated failed logins told apart from an attack
a legitimate-looking actor with no way through, routed to recovery

requires: authentication failures crossing a meaningful threshold, or matching a pattern the detection considers notable
insufficientAlone: one failed password attempt, which is the most common event in this category
a single failure from an unfamiliar device

nodes.does: Evaluate the context around the failures: how fast they arrived, from what device and context, whether a credential reset is in play, whether the shape matches a known attack, and whether any session succeeded. A model's score orders the work and concludes nothing - what it produces is a case to look at, not an attacker

nodes.asks: What does the evidence actually support?

branches.label: Ordinary user error
branches.when: the pattern looks like someone who has forgotten a password - human pacing, a familiar device, no other signal

branches.label: The person cannot get in and needs a route back
branches.when: repeated legitimate-looking failures with no way forward through normal authentication

branches.label: Material security risk
branches.when: velocity, context change or attack-shaped behaviour that ordinary error does not explain

nodes.state: ordinary failure pattern; nothing security-specific applied
nodes.reEntry: the usual recovery routes remain open to them, unchanged. Treating this as an attack would lock out mostly legitimate people, which is the failure mode this branch exists to hold open

nodes.on: a legitimate-looking actor with no way through normal authentication
carries: the failure history, which is context for the recovery rather than evidence against the requester
the fact that no compromise has been established

nodes.does: Apply the smallest restriction the evidence justifies, and record what justified it. Most signals in this category are false positives, and for those the restriction is the entire customer-visible incident

nodes.on: a failure pattern that ordinary error does not explain
carries: the evidence and the restriction already applied
the explicit fact that nothing is confirmed - this is a suspicion with a scope, not a finding

guardrails: One failed password attempt is not a compromise.
A risk model's output is not a confirmed attacker. It orders investigation and concludes nothing.
Any security response uses the smallest necessary scope.
journeys.reusableRule: Authentication failure patterns should trigger proportionate security evaluation rather than converting ordinary mistakes into confirmed compromise.

journeys.name: Account recovery request → prove control → restore secure access
journeys.purpose: Give someone a way back into an account they can no longer authenticate to, without that route being weaker than the one it replaces.

entity.scope: the account plus this recovery case
entity.note: Recovery restores control of one existing account. It never merges identities, and it never creates a second account for the same person as a shortcut.

distinctFrom.because: Verification establishes that a claim is true. Recovery establishes that this requester is entitled to regain control of a specific account, which a true claim about their identity does not by itself demonstrate.

journeys.objective: Give someone a way back into an account they can no longer authenticate to, without that route being weaker than the one it replaces.
eligibility: a valid recovery request against an identified account
no instance of this journey is already open for the the account plus this recovery case
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Recovery does not weaken normal security controls. It is a different route to the same assurance, not a lower one.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Unsafe credentials and sessions are invalidated before replacement access is established, not after.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Account recovery is not identity merge.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: The recovery window is not restarted by repeated attempts.

guardrails: state_written_on_stale_entity

useCases: a recovery route no weaker than the login it replaces
insufficient proof routed to more evidence, a person, or denial

requires: a valid recovery request against an identified account
insufficientAlone: a failed authentication with no recovery request behind it
a support conversation about being locked out that names no identified account
a destination supplied inside the request itself

nodes.does: Determine the recovery basis available and read the account's current security state. What is happening on the account changes what recovery is allowed to do

nodes.asks: Is there an active compromise or security incident on this account?

branches.label: Incident open
branches.when: a compromise is suspected or confirmed and containment is in force

branches.label: No incident
branches.when: the account is simply unreachable by its owner

nodes.on: a recovery request arriving during an open security incident
carries: the recovery request and what the requester has offered
the fact that recovery is coordinated by the incident rather than run alongside it - a parallel recovery is exactly the path an attacker would take
the incident_id of the account's already-open IDN-90 instance, resolved via account_id - this handoff joins that existing incident rather than opening a new one

nodes.does: Collect only the evidence this recovery basis requires. Recovery is not an opportunity to gather more than normal authentication would, and it must not be an easier route to the same access than the one it replaces - it exists for the case where normal authentication has already failed, which makes it the door an attacker reaches for first

after.rule: Proof is waited for until the recovery window closes; the window is never restarted by repeated attempts.

timeout.reason: an open recovery case is a standing invitation to keep trying, and closing it is part of not being a weaker route

nodes.recheck: the the account plus this recovery case re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.state: recovery window closed without sufficient proof
nodes.reEntry: a new recovery request opens its own case, with this one in the history

nodes.asks: Is the proof sufficient for the assurance this account requires?

branches.label: Sufficient
branches.when: the requester has demonstrated control or entitlement at the required level

branches.label: Insufficient
branches.when: the evidence does not reach the required level

nodes.does: Invalidate the credentials and sessions that are no longer safe, before establishing anything new. An old credential left active after a recovery is precisely the thing the recovery existed to remove, and the order matters - new access first would leave both live at once
Establish secure replacement access at the assurance this account requires
Verify the recovered state: that the intended access works, and that the invalidated credentials genuinely no longer do. The second half is the one that gets skipped

nodes.state: secure control of the existing account restored
nodes.reEntry: this recovered one account and merged nothing. Two identities that turn out to be one person is a different problem with different evidence

nodes.asks: With insufficient proof, what does policy allow?

branches.label: Further evidence
branches.when: the recovery basis allows another route to proof within the window

branches.label: Manual review
branches.when: a person should weigh what has been offered

branches.label: Deny
branches.when: no route to sufficient proof remains

nodes.state: further evidence may be provided within the recovery window
nodes.reEntry: the same case continues; the window is not restarted by another attempt

nodes.on: recovery evidence that needs a person to weigh it
carries: everything offered and the assurance level required
the account's current security state, so the reviewer knows what is at stake

nodes.state: recovery denied; account access unchanged
nodes.reEntry: a new request with genuinely new evidence may be assessed; repeating the same evidence is not new evidence

guardrails: Recovery does not weaken normal security controls. It is a different route to the same assurance, not a lower one.
Unsafe credentials and sessions are invalidated before replacement access is established, not after.
Account recovery is not identity merge.
The recovery window is not restarted by repeated attempts.
journeys.reusableRule: Account recovery restores secure control of an existing account only after sufficient evidence that the requester is entitled to regain control.

journeys.name: Identity attribute change → verify if required → update → propagate
journeys.purpose: Change an identity attribute safely, and reconcile everything that depended on the old value independently rather than by inheritance.

entity.scope: the person or account plus the specific attribute changing
entity.note: Each dependent - a credential, a contact point, a permission - is reconciled on its own terms. None of them travels with the attribute automatically.

journeys.objective: Change an identity attribute safely, and reconcile everything that depended on the old value independently rather than by inheritance.
eligibility: a change to an identity attribute, requested by the holder or received from an authoritative source
no instance of this journey is already open for the the person or account plus the specific attribute changing
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Changing an email does not transfer the old address's contactability or its consent to the new one.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Identity history is not silently overwritten where auditability is required.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A stale update never restores a previous value - propagation carries origin and version so a late arrival is discarded.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A sensitive change is not applied on the strength of an existing session alone.

guardrails: state_written_on_stale_entity

useCases: an identity attribute changed with verification where policy requires it
credentials, contactability and permissions re-evaluated independently after the change

requires: a change to an identity attribute, requested by the holder or received from an authoritative source
insufficientAlone: a contact point change, which contact verification (CON-264) owns
a display-name edit with nothing depending on it
a propagation of an old value arriving after a newer change

nodes.does: Determine the attribute's sensitivity and what verification the change requires. Changing a display name and changing a legal name are not the same operation, and neither is changing a recovery address

nodes.asks: Does this change require additional verification?

branches.label: Verification required
branches.when: the attribute is sensitive, or is itself a route back into the account

branches.label: Not required
branches.when: the attribute carries no security or legal weight

nodes.does: Verify current control of the account and, where policy requires it, the new attribute itself. An attacker holding a live session must not be able to move the recovery address on the strength of that session alone

after.rule: The verification window for this change.

timeout.reason: an unverified sensitive change is not applied by default, so an unanswered verification simply leaves the attribute as it was

nodes.recheck: the the person or account plus the specific attribute changing re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.asks: Was the required control established?

branches.label: Verified
branches.when: control and, where required, the new attribute are established

branches.label: Not verified
branches.when: verification did not succeed

nodes.state: change not applied; the attribute stands as it was
nodes.reEntry: a new request is verified on its own terms. Nothing partial was written, so no downstream system holds a value that was never confirmed

nodes.asks: Is the change itself valid?

branches.label: Valid
branches.when: the new value is well-formed, permitted and not in conflict with another record

branches.label: Invalid
branches.when: the value cannot be accepted - malformed, prohibited, or already held elsewhere

nodes.state: change rejected as invalid
nodes.reEntry: a corrected value may be submitted

nodes.does: Update the authoritative identity record, preserving the previous value where policy permits, the new value, when it took effect, the source, and the verification evidence and status. Identity history is not silently overwritten where auditability is required - what someone was called, and when that changed, is often the whole question later
Propagate to dependent systems carrying change_origin and change_version, so a stale update arriving late cannot restore the previous value

nodes.asks: Does this change affect credentials, contactability or permissions?

branches.label: Dependents affected
branches.when: the attribute is used as a credential, as a contact point, or as the basis of a permission

branches.label: Nothing depends on it
branches.when: the attribute is descriptive only

nodes.does: Re-evaluate each dependent independently. A new email address inherits neither the old one's deliverability nor its consent - the new address starts with its own contactability state and its own permission, both empty unless policy explicitly says otherwise. Credentials tied to the old value are assessed on their own terms, and so are permissions that rested on it

nodes.state: identity updated; each dependent re-evaluated on its own terms
nodes.reEntry: each dependent's own journey owns what happens next - contactability, permission and credential lifecycles are separately triggered, because they have different owners and different rules

nodes.state: identity updated; nothing depended on the previous value
nodes.reEntry: a further change to the same attribute is assessed on its own sensitivity

guardrails: Changing an email does not transfer the old address's contactability or its consent to the new one.
Identity history is not silently overwritten where auditability is required.
A stale update never restores a previous value - propagation carries origin and version so a late arrival is discarded.
A sensitive change is not applied on the strength of an existing session alone.
journeys.reusableRule: Identity attribute changes should update the authoritative identity while independently reconciling any permissions, credentials or contact points that depend on that attribute.

journeys.name: Suspected account compromise → contain → verify → recover or clear
journeys.purpose: Limit the damage a possible compromise could do while the question is still open, and reach a conclusion that can go either way.

entity.scope: the account plus this security incident and the scope it affects
entity.note: The incident is its own record with its own history. Containment attaches to it, and both survive whichever way the investigation concludes.

distinctFrom.because: Suspension restricts for a stated business reason and expects to be resolved by that reason going away. This restricts on incomplete evidence about an adversary, which is why it opens an investigation rather than a review.

competition.precedence: highest in the group - a suspected compromise is the more urgent, safety-critical question, and a concurrent business-reason suspension (ACC-78) on the same account pauses rather than resolving independently while this investigation is open

journeys.objective: Limit the damage a possible compromise could do while the question is still open, and reach a conclusion that can go either way.
eligibility: a material signal: a credential-theft indication, an unauthorised sensitive change, a credible report from the owner, a high-confidence detection, or a suspicious session combined with a consequential action
no instance of this journey is already open for the the account plus this security incident and the scope it affects
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Suspected is not confirmed. The two are separate states and containment belongs to the first.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Containment does not erase forensic or audit history.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Restoration never blindly reactivates old credentials, sessions or permissions - it rebuilds from current valid state.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Unauthorised financial or business actions are corrected through their own dispute lifecycles, not from inside the incident.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE

nodes.does: Retain according to the applicable policy, marked as retained under an ended relationship rather than left looking like a live one

nodes.state: relationship ended; history intact, obligations reconciled separately
nodes.reEntry: a new relationship between the same entities is created on its own basis, and is a different relationship rather than a revival of this one

guardrails: Ending a relationship does not delete the historical relationship.
Ending a relationship does not automatically cancel commitments created while it existed.
Unrelated relationships between the same entities remain unaffected.

Ending a structural link does not terminate an agreement that ran through it. A contract, subscription, policy or membership reaches its own end on its own terms, and inferring one from the other cancels things nobody cancelled.
journeys.reusableRule: Ending a relationship removes future relationship-dependent behavior without erasing obligations legitimately created while the relationship existed.

journeys.name: Role change → authority and capability delta → apply
journeys.purpose: Move what someone may do next, by the difference between two roles, without disturbing what they did under the old one.

entity.scope: the person or member, the role, and the account or organisation the role is held in
entity.note: A role belongs to a link between a person and an organisation. The same person holds different roles in different places, and changing one changes nothing about the others.

distinctFrom.because: A role change alters what someone may do. An identity attribute change alters who they are on record. Treating a role change as an identity change rebuilds the person and loses their history.

journeys.objective: Move what someone may do next, by the difference between two roles, without disturbing what they did under the old one.
eligibility: an authoritative role change with an effective time
no instance of this journey is already open for the the person or member
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A role change is not an identity change.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A role downgrade does not invalidate actions historically performed under the previous role.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Pending decisions are revalidated against current authority before the delta is applied.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: The delta is scoped - capabilities common to both roles are left alone.

guardrails: state_written_on_stale_entity

useCases: a role change applied as the difference between two roles
pending approvals revalidated against the new authority

requires: an authoritative role change with an effective time
insufficientAlone: a permission edit that changes no role
an organisational change with no effective time recorded
a role change requested but not yet authorised

nodes.does: Compare the previous and new role and calculate the capability and authority delta. What gets applied is the difference - a capability present in both roles is not revoked and re-granted, which the holder would experience as an outage in the middle of an administrative change

nodes.asks: Does pending work or an open approval rest on the authority the previous role carried?

branches.label: Pending decisions under the old authority
branches.when: an approval, a decision or an assignment is open and was valid under the role being replaced

branches.label: Nothing pending
branches.when: no open decision depends on the previous role

nodes.on: a role change with decisions pending under the authority it replaces
carries: the capability and authority delta, which is applied once the pending decisions are settled
the pending decisions themselves, whose original requests and deadlines the role change does not reset

nodes.asks: Which way does the delta move?

branches.label: Grants only
branches.when: the new role adds capabilities and removes none

branches.label: Removes, or mixed
branches.when: at least one capability is no longer carried, whether or not others were added

nodes.on: a role change that only adds capabilities
carries: the delta and its effective time
the role as the new entitlement basis

nodes.does: Apply the delta: grant what the new role adds, and revoke or restrict what it removes, according to each capability's own dependency rules. Actions validly performed under the previous role are not invalidated - a downgrade changes what someone may do next, never what they already did

nodes.state: authority and capability delta applied; prior actions intact
nodes.reEntry: a further role change is compared against the current role

guardrails: A role change is not an identity change.
A role downgrade does not invalidate actions historically performed under the previous role.
Pending decisions are revalidated against current authority before the delta is applied.
The delta is scoped - capabilities common to both roles are left alone.
journeys.reusableRule: Role changes should modify current authority through scoped deltas while preserving the history of actions validly performed under prior authority.

journeys.name: Parent state change → determine child impact → propagate selectively
journeys.purpose: Let a parent's state reach only the children that genuinely depend on it, through a rule someone actually wrote.

entity.scope: the parent whose state changed, and each child evaluated individually against the dependency model
entity.note: Children are classified individually. A single verdict for the whole collection is the assumption this journey exists to prevent.

distinctFrom.because: This propagates downward through defined dependencies. REL-96 derives upward through an aggregation policy. They are opposite directions with different rules, and neither is the inverse of the other.

requires: a material state change on a parent entity - an organisation suspended, a master account closed, a contract state changed, a parent resource disabled

nodes.asks: Is a dependency model defined for this parent-child relationship?

branches.label: Defined
branches.when: a rule states which child states depend on which parent states, and how

branches.label: Not defined
branches.when: nothing states what this parent change should do to its children

nodes.on: a parent state change with no defined dependency model
carries: the parent change and the children that would be affected under a naive inheritance
the explicit fact that nothing was propagated, because inheritance was not assumed
suppresses: any automatic propagation to children while the model is undefined

nodes.does: Classify each child individually against the model: which are directly dependent on the parent's state, which are independently valid, and which carry open obligations. One verdict for the whole collection is the assumption that turns a suspended organisation into eleven deleted subsidiaries

nodes.asks: How does each class resolve?

branches.label: Directly dependent
branches.when: the model says this child's state follows the parent's

branches.label: Independently valid
branches.when: the child stands on its own basis and the model does not make it follow

nodes.state: child state preserved; the parent change does not reach it
nodes.reEntry: a parent change that the model does make this child follow is evaluated when it happens. A parent going inactive does not delete a child that stands on its own

nodes.asks: Do the dependent children carry open obligations?

branches.label: Obligations open
branches.when: a dependent child holds a commitment that would be destroyed by propagation

branches.label: Nothing open
branches.when: the dependent children hold nothing that outlives the propagation

nodes.on: propagation that would reach a child holding an open obligation
carries: the obligation and the propagation being held for it
the explicit fact that nothing destructive has been applied to that child yet

nodes.does: Apply the defined consequence to the dependent children only, recording what propagated, to which children, and under which rule. Propagation that cannot say which rule produced it cannot be reviewed, reversed or explained

nodes.state: consequence applied to dependent children, scoped and recorded
nodes.reEntry: a further parent change is classified again against the model

guardrails: A parent going inactive does not delete every child.
A parent restriction does not restrict every child globally unless the model defines it.
Propagation stays scoped and auditable - what went where, under which rule.
Where no dependency model exists, nothing propagates.
journeys.reusableRule: Parent state changes should propagate only through explicitly defined dependencies rather than through assumed inheritance.

journeys.name: Child state change → recalculate aggregate parent state
journeys.purpose: Derive a parent's state from its children through an explicit aggregation policy, recomputed from source rather than nudged by whichever child reported last.

entity.scope: the parent and the full collection of children the policy reads
entity.note: The aggregate is recomputed from the authoritative children, not incremented from the event that arrived. That is what keeps it rebuildable and stops it drifting.

requires: a change to a child state that the parent's aggregation policy reads
insufficientAlone: any child change, where no policy makes the parent depend on it

nodes.asks: Is an aggregation policy defined for this parent state?

branches.label: Defined
branches.when: a policy states how child states combine into the parent's, and what transitions it

branches.label: Not defined
branches.when: no policy states how these children combine

nodes.on: a child change with no aggregation policy to combine it
carries: the parent, the children and the change that arrived
the explicit fact that no ANY, ALL, majority or threshold rule was assumed in order to produce a parent state

nodes.does: Recompute the parent's derived state from the authoritative children using the defined policy, rather than adjusting it from the single child event that arrived. Recomputing from source means the aggregate can be rebuilt at any moment and cannot drift away from what the children actually say

nodes.asks: Does the recomputed aggregate meet the parent's transition criteria?

branches.label: Criteria met
branches.when: the policy's condition for moving the parent's state is satisfied

branches.label: Not met
branches.when: the aggregate moved and the parent's state does not

nodes.does: Update the derived parent state, recording which children and which policy produced it, so the transition can be explained without recomputing it by hand

nodes.state: derived parent state updated from the aggregation policy
nodes.reEntry: the next relevant child change recomputes it again from source

nodes.state: aggregate recomputed; parent state unchanged
nodes.reEntry: this is the ordinary outcome. One child changing is not the parent changing, and most child events correctly end here

guardrails: One child's state does not automatically become the parent's state.
Aggregation semantics come from policy. ANY, ALL, majority and percentage thresholds are never inferred.
The aggregate is recomputable from the authoritative children rather than accumulated from events.
journeys.reusableRule: Parent state derived from children must follow an explicit aggregation policy rather than simple state copying.

journeys.name: Duplicate entity detected → assess → keep separate, link or merge
journeys.purpose: Assess whether two records are the same entity, and route the answer - without consolidating anything.

entity.scope: the candidate set of records suspected of representing one entity
entity.note: The set is the unit. Three records suspected of being one person are assessed together, because a pairwise answer can be internally inconsistent.

distinctFrom.because: Linking is one of the outcomes this assessment can reach. It is a separate journey because a link has its own semantics and its own sharing rules, which the assessment does not decide.

requires: a match between records strong enough to be worth assessing
insufficientAlone: the same name
the same postcode or address
a similar spelling, which is what matching produces most of

nodes.does: Collect the matching evidence and record its strength: verified identifiers, authoritative external IDs, declared ownership, verified contact points, business identifiers and relationship history. A match score is a reason to look and never a conclusion - the same email may be a shared family address, and the same phone number may be a workplace

nodes.asks: What does the evidence actually support?

branches.label: Not the same entity
branches.when: the evidence is explained by something other than identity - a shared household, a shared workplace, a common name

branches.label: Related but distinct
branches.when: the records genuinely represent different entities that have a real relationship

branches.label: Same entity, consolidation looks safe
branches.when: verified identifiers or authoritative external IDs establish it, and nothing about the records makes merging risky

branches.label: Ambiguous or high-risk
branches.when: the evidence is suggestive and incomplete, or the records carry state that would be dangerous to consolidate wrongly

nodes.state: KEEP_SEPARATE; the records represent different entities
nodes.reEntry: stronger evidence later re-opens the assessment. Keeping two records apart is reversible; merging them usually is not, which is why this is the default when the evidence does not carry

nodes.on: records that are related and genuinely distinct
carries: both records and the evidence of the relationship between them
the explicit finding that they are not the same entity, so the link does not drift toward being treated as one

nodes.on: a candidate set the evidence supports consolidating
carries: the full evidence set and the confidence it establishes

the explicit fact that this journey has assessed and not authorised - detecting a duplicate is not permission to merge it, and the merge mechanism applies its own evidence requirements before consolidating anything

nodes.on: an assessment the evidence cannot settle, or one whose consequences are too large to settle automatically
carries: the candidate set, the evidence and what specifically is ambiguous about it
what each record currently holds, which is what makes a wrong merge expensive

guardrails: The same name is not the same person.
A shared email or phone number may not prove the same entity - it depends on the model, and households and workplaces share both routinely.
Duplicate detection is not merge authorization. This journey assesses and routes; consolidating records is a separate mechanism with its own evidence requirements.
journeys.reusableRule: Duplicate detection identifies a reconciliation candidate; merge requires separate evidence that consolidation is safe.

journeys.name: Entity link → shared context → preserve independent identity
journeys.purpose: Record that two entities are related and let defined context cross between them, while both remain two entities.

entity.scope: the link itself, plus the two entities it connects
entity.note: Each entity keeps its own lifecycle state and history. The link is a third record about them, not a step toward becoming one.

requires: a valid relationship or link between two distinct entities
insufficientAlone: a duplicate match, which is a question about whether they are one entity rather than evidence that they are two related ones

nodes.does: Define what this link actually means - the same household, related accounts, linked profiles, a business relationship, a cross-product connection. The semantics decide what may be shared, and a link whose semantics are undefined shares nothing at all

nodes.asks: What context do these link semantics explicitly permit sharing?

branches.label: Defined shared context
branches.when: the link's semantics name specific context that may cross between the entities

branches.label: Nothing shared
branches.when: the link records a relationship and permits no context to cross - which is the common case

nodes.does: Share only the context the semantics explicitly permit. Anything not named is not shared, including things that would obviously be convenient

Confirm each entity keeps its own lifecycle state and history. Consent does not cross the link, and neither does entitlement or access, unless the relationship rules explicitly permit it - a household link is not permission to email everyone in the household

nodes.asks: Is anything attempting to carry consent, entitlement, credentials or access across the link?

branches.label: Something is propagating
branches.when: a downstream process is treating the link as though the entities were one

branches.label: Nothing is
branches.when: only the permitted context crosses

nodes.does: Block the propagation and record it. This is the specific failure a link becomes when it is quietly treated as a merge, and catching it here is cheaper than discovering it as a consent complaint

nodes.state: linked; two entities, two lifecycles, defined shared context
nodes.reEntry: the link's semantics may be changed, and the link may be ended, but neither turns it into a merge. Consolidating the records is a separate decision with separate evidence

guardrails: Linked is not merged.
Consent does not automatically propagate across linked identities.
Entitlement and access do not propagate unless the relationship rules explicitly permit it.
A link whose semantics are undefined shares nothing.
journeys.reusableRule: Entity linking enables defined cross-entity context while preserving independent identity and lifecycle state.

journeys.name: Entity split required → create separate records → allocate history and state safely
journeys.purpose: Separate what should never have been one record, or what must now be managed apart, without copying the things that do not divide.

entity.scope: the source entity and the entities that result from the split
entity.note: The source entity's history remains the source entity's history. The resulting records inherit allocations, not a rewritten past.

distinctFrom.because: A link connects two records that already exist separately. A split creates that separation where it did not exist, which means deciding what each side gets - and what neither side may simply be given a copy of.

requires: an authoritative requirement to separate state currently held under one entity

nodes.does: Determine the split basis - what actually distinguishes the resulting entities from one another. Without it, allocation becomes a series of individual guesses

Classify every piece of existing information as entity-specific, shared, ambiguous, historical or non-transferable. The last category is the one that gets missed: consent, entitlements, credentials and financial obligations do not divide by being copied, and duplicating one creates an obligation nobody incurred or a permission nobody gave

nodes.asks: How does each classified item resolve?

branches.label: Clearly one entity's
branches.when: the item belongs unambiguously to one of the resulting entities

branches.label: Genuinely shared
branches.when: the item belongs to the relationship between them rather than to either

branches.label: Non-transferable
branches.when: consent, an entitlement, a credential or a financial obligation, none of which divides

branches.label: Ambiguous
branches.when: the item cannot be attributed on the split basis

nodes.does: Allocate the item to the entity it belongs to
Preserve the item through a relationship or reference model rather than duplicating it into both records. Two copies of one shared history diverge the first time either is edited
Leave it with the entity that holds it and record that it did not divide. A new record existing is not a reason for it to receive a copy of a consent, an entitlement or a debt

nodes.on: state that cannot be attributed to either resulting entity
carries: the item, the split basis, and why attribution failed
the fact that it is held unresolved rather than assigned to whichever record was created first

nodes.does: Recalculate each resulting entity's rights, permissions, entitlements, obligations and active journeys from what it now actually holds, rather than from what the source entity held

Record that the split occurred, when, and on what basis. History is not rewritten as though the records had always been separate - events that happened to the combined entity happened to the combined entity, and pretending otherwise makes every past event unattributable

nodes.state: entities separated; current state reconstructed, prior history preserved as it happened
nodes.reEntry: each resulting entity now has its own lifecycle. A further split is assessed against whichever of them requires it

guardrails: Consent, entitlements, credentials and financial obligations are never blindly duplicated across a split.
The audit trail preserves that a split occurred, when, and on what basis.
History is not rewritten as though the records had always been separate.
Ambiguous state is held unresolved rather than assigned by default.
journeys.reusableRule: Entity splitting reconstructs independent current states while preserving the historical fact that the records were previously represented together.

journeys.name: Required relationship missing → orphan state → resolve or reassign
journeys.purpose: Make a missing required relationship an explicit, findable state rather than a null field that active work quietly runs against.

entity.scope: the entity missing its required relationship, and the relationship type that is absent
entity.note: One orphan state per missing relationship. An entity missing two required links is in two unresolved states, each resolvable independently.

distinctFrom.because: OWN-51 routes work that has never had an owner. This handles an entity that had a required relationship and lost it, which means inherited deadlines and obligations are already running against it.

journeys.objective: Make a missing required relationship an explicit, findable state rather than a null field that active work quietly runs against.
eligibility: a relationship the entity requires to function being absent, invalid or removed - a work item without a required owner, a resource without a valid parent, a case without an account link, a dependent without a primary
no instance of this journey is already open for the the entity missing its required relationship
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A missing relationship never silently becomes a null field while active work continues.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A parent or owner is not guessed from weak evidence. Several candidates route to a person.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Inherited deadlines and obligations stay intact while the entity is orphaned.

guardrails: state_written_on_stale_entity

useCases: an entity whose required parent or owner is missing, made an explicit state
a deterministic replacement applied, or a holding scope while a person decides

requires: a relationship the entity requires to function being absent, invalid or removed - a work item without a required owner, a resource without a valid parent, a case without an account link, a dependent without a primary
insufficientAlone: an empty relationship field on an entity that does not require that relationship
a transient read failure of the relationship store
a relationship that is pending evidence, which validation (REL-91) owns

nodes.does: Record the entity as ORPHANED, naming which relationship is missing. This is an explicit state rather than a null field - null is unqueryable and unescalatable, and an entity with no owner has to be findable as an entity with no owner. Inherited deadlines and obligations keep running throughout; being orphaned is our problem and does not pause what was already owed

nodes.asks: Is there a deterministic replacement relationship?

branches.label: Exactly one valid replacement
branches.when: the rules resolve to a single valid counterpart

branches.label: Several possible
branches.when: more than one counterpart could be valid and nothing decides between them

branches.label: None available
branches.when: no valid counterpart currently exists

nodes.on: an orphan with several possible replacements and no rule between them
carries: the candidates and what each would imply
the explicit fact that no guess was made - a wrong parent inferred from weak evidence is worse than an unresolved state, because it looks resolved

nodes.asks: Is there a safe temporary holding scope for this entity?

branches.label: Holding scope exists
branches.when: an explicit unresolved queue or state can hold it without work proceeding against a missing relationship

branches.label: None
branches.when: nothing can safely hold it while active work continues against it

nodes.does: Hold the entity in the explicit unresolved queue, with its inherited deadlines and obligations intact and visible. Held is a state someone can query and escalate; a null relationship is neither

after.rule: The resolution SLA for this entity type.

timeout.reason: an orphan is carrying live obligations with nobody attached to them, so an unresolved one escalates rather than waiting quietly

nodes.recheck: the the entity missing its required relationship re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.does: Establish the replacement relationship, preserving the entity's inherited deadlines and obligations exactly as they stood. Reassignment changes who is connected, never what is owed or by when

Revalidate the entity's current state against the restored relationship before resuming. The relationship changed, so what the entity is entitled to or responsible for under the new one may differ from what it held under the old

nodes.state: relationship restored; entity revalidated and resumed
nodes.reEntry: a further missing relationship opens its own orphan state

nodes.asks: The resolution SLA passed with the entity still orphaned - what does policy do?

branches.label: Escalate
branches.when: the entity carries obligations that make an owner necessary rather than desirable

branches.label: Terminal handling
branches.when: policy defines an end state for entities that cannot be reconnected

nodes.on: an orphaned entity that could not be reconnected
carries: the missing relationship and what has been tried
the inherited obligations and their unchanged deadlines, which are the reason this is urgent

nodes.state: orphaned entity handled under its policy end state
nodes.reEntry: a valid relationship becoming available later re-opens this; the entity was never silently discarded

guardrails: A missing relationship never silently becomes a null field while active work continues.
A parent or owner is not guessed from weak evidence. Several candidates route to a person.
Inherited deadlines and obligations stay intact while the entity is orphaned.
journeys.reusableRule: When a required relationship disappears, the entity should enter an explicit unresolved state until a valid relationship is restored.

journeys.name: Relationship invitation → counterparty acceptance → active or expired
journeys.purpose: Put a proposed link in front of the party who has to accept it, on terms they can see before they answer, and close the question one way or the other before the invitation goes stale.

entity.scope: the invitation, plus the two parties and the scope of the link it proposes, in the direction it was issued
entity.note: The invitation is the subject, not the parties. A second invitation between the same two parties, for a different scope or the other direction, is its own instance.

distinctFrom.because: REL-91 decides whether a link has an authoritative basis and records it active or rejected. This journey exists only in the case where the missing basis is the counterparty's own acceptance, and it establishes nothing itself - it asks.
SUB-161 owns a continuing agreement with a term, effective dates and renewal. Acceptance here creates a link and no term, and an agreement later attached to that link is not this.

journeys.objective: Put a proposed link in front of the party who has to accept it, on terms they can see before they answer, and close the question one way or the other before the invitation goes stale.
eligibility: an invitation recorded by a party holding the authority to extend it
a named counterparty, the scope of the proposed link and its direction
an expiry on the invitation
no instance of this journey is already open for the the invitation
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: An invitation is not a relationship. Nothing is linked, and nothing is shown to either side as linked, until the counterparty accepts.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Acceptance links two records and merges none. Both parties keep their own identity, history and lifecycle.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Scope and direction are stated in the invitation itself, not discovered after acceptance.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: One reminder, never two. The expiry is the pressure; repetition is not.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Every invitation expires. A pending claim on somebody who never agreed to it does not sit open indefinitely.

value.rule: Every touch runs against a budget fixed when the instance opened; the budget is the plan's own length, and no touch is repeated because nothing could tell whether it arrived.

default.applicableWhen: GLB-24; an invitation, one reminder and a confirmation

cooldown.rule: This journey is per the invitation; a later instance concerns a different the invitation and no cooldown applies between them.

default.applicableWhen: the entity note: one instance per entity

roles.when: the message has to be kept and survive until the person can act on it
the person is active in the product and the action is taken there

touches.purpose: Name who is inviting them, exactly what the link would let that party do, and what it would not change about their own record.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

mustNotClaim: that accepting transfers anything they hold

touches.purpose: State who is inviting them and into what, and say plainly that accepting creates a link rather than a transfer of anything they hold.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

mustNotClaim: that accepting transfers anything they hold

touches.purpose: Confirm to both sides that the link is active, naming its scope and its direction and what each side can now see or do.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Send one reminder naming who is waiting and the date the invitation expires.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

guardrails: complaint
message_after_success
unsubscribe

useCases: a proposed link put to the party who has to accept it, on visible terms
one reminder before the invitation expires, then a closed question

requires: an invitation recorded by a party holding the authority to extend it
a named counterparty, the scope of the proposed link and its direction
an expiry on the invitation
insufficientAlone: a shared attribute between two records - an address, a name, a device
an intention to invite that has not been recorded as an invitation

nodes.asks: Does the counterparty already exist here in their own right?

branches.label: Existing holder
branches.when: the counterparty already holds a record and a session of their own, and the invitation would attach to it

branches.label: New to us
branches.when: the counterparty has no record here and knows the inviting party but not us

nodes.does: Name who is inviting them, exactly what the link would let that party do, and what it would not change about their own record. An existing holder's first question is what accepting costs them, not what it gives the inviter

State who is inviting them and into what, and say plainly that accepting creates a link rather than a transfer of anything they hold. Somebody with no prior relationship reads an unexplained invitation as a claim already made on them

after.rule: The point at which one reminder would still leave time to act before expiry.

timeout.reason: a reminder that arrives after the invitation is dead is worse than no reminder, because it asks for something that can no longer be given

nodes.recheck: the the invitation re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.asks: How was the invitation answered?

branches.label: Accepted
branches.when: the counterparty's acceptance is authoritatively recorded and the link is created

branches.label: Declined or withdrawn
branches.when: the counterparty declined, or the inviting party withdrew the invitation before it was answered

nodes.does: Confirm to both sides that the link is active, naming its scope and its direction and what each side can now see or do. An unstated scope is assumed to be total by whoever has less to gain from it

nodes.state: link active, both identities intact
nodes.reEntry: a further invitation between the same parties, for a different scope, is a new instance

nodes.state: invitation declined or withdrawn
nodes.reEntry: the inviting party may issue a fresh invitation, which is a new instance; a declined one is never revived

nodes.asks: Is a reminder still worth sending?

branches.label: Time remains
branches.when: the invitation has a meaningful period left and no reminder has been sent for it

branches.label: Window closed
branches.when: the invitation has reached or passed its expiry unanswered

nodes.does: Send one reminder naming who is waiting and the date the invitation expires. There is no second one - a counterparty who has not answered twice has answered

after.rule: After the one reminder the instance waits until the invitation's own expiry; there is no second reminder.

timeout.reason: an invitation with no expiry is a standing claim on somebody who never agreed to anything

nodes.recheck: the the invitation re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.state: expired unanswered
nodes.reEntry: a fresh invitation from the same party starts a new window

guardrails: An invitation is not a relationship. Nothing is linked, and nothing is shown to either side as linked, until the counterparty accepts.
Acceptance links two records and merges none. Both parties keep their own identity, history and lifecycle.
Scope and direction are stated in the invitation itself, not discovered after acceptance.
One reminder, never two. The expiry is the pressure; repetition is not.
Every invitation expires. A pending claim on somebody who never agreed to it does not sit open indefinitely.
journeys.reusableRule: An invitation is a question put to somebody who owes no answer, so it names its scope, names its expiry, and asks at most once more.

journeys.name: Identity or entity merge → reconcile → consolidate → verify
journeys.purpose: Consolidate records that represent one entity, after every dependent state has been reconciled under its own authority rule.

entity.scope: the source entities, the canonical target, and the merge operation itself as an auditable record
entity.note: The merge operation is its own entity. Its record of conflict decisions and provenance is what makes the consolidated result reviewable, and often what makes it reversible.

distinctFrom.because: Account consolidation unifies business structure and leaves the people distinct. This consolidates the representations of one entity, which is a decision about identity and carries a far higher evidence bar.

requires: an explicit merge authorization following a duplicate assessment, naming the sources, the target and the authority that authorised it
insufficientAlone: a duplicate detection, which produces a candidate rather than a decision
a high match score
an assessment concluding the records are probably the same, without an authorisation to act on it

nodes.does: Create the auditable merge operation: source entity IDs, the canonical target, the basis, the authority that authorised it, the time, and every conflict decision as it is made. Provenance is what makes the result reviewable - without it the consolidated record cannot say where any part of itself came from

Inventory the dependent state before anything is touched: identity attributes, consent, preferences, contact points, entitlements, purchases, subscriptions, support cases, opportunities, credentials, active journeys, open obligations and relationships. Each of these answers to a different authority, and a merge that reads them as one list applies one rule to all of them

nodes.asks: Is this merge reversible?

branches.label: Reversible
branches.when: the architecture can separate the records again if the decision turns out to be wrong

branches.label: Irreversible
branches.when: consolidation cannot be undone once applied

nodes.asks: Does the evidence and authority meet the higher bar an irreversible merge requires?

branches.label: Sufficient
branches.when: verified identifiers or authoritative external IDs establish it, at the standard an unrecoverable decision demands

branches.label: Not sufficient
branches.when: the evidence would justify a reversible merge and not this one

nodes.state: not merged; evidence sized for a reversible operation
nodes.reEntry: stronger evidence, or an architecture that makes the merge reversible, re-opens this. Leaving two records separate is recoverable and this is not

nodes.asks: Does conflicting state exist across the sources?

branches.label: Conflicts present
branches.when: two sources hold incompatible values for state that matters

branches.label: No conflicts
branches.when: every state type reconciles without contradiction

nodes.on: conflicting state discovered during merge
carries: the merge operation, the inventory and exactly which state conflicts
the fact that nothing has been consolidated yet, so the conflict is decided before rather than after

nodes.does: Consolidate each state type under its own authority rule. There is no newest-value-wins applied across the board: a newer contact point may supersede an older one, a newer consent does not supersede an older withdrawal, an entitlement is reconciled rather than either kept or duplicated, and a financial obligation is never added to itself
Repoint dependent relationships and active processes onto the canonical entity, so nothing continues to run against a representation that has been superseded

Invalidate the actions still queued against the superseded representations. A downstream synchronisation running on its own schedule will otherwise restore what was just consolidated, which undoes the merge while reporting success

Verify the merge did what it was for and nothing more: no critical obligation lost, no permission more permissive than any source held, no entitlement duplicated, no duplicate active journey still running, and the source history still traceable

nodes.asks: Did verification pass?

branches.label: Passed
branches.when: every check holds

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: a check found a lost obligation, a widened permission, a duplicated entitlement or a surviving duplicate journey

nodes.state: merged into the canonical entity, with provenance and source history intact
nodes.reEntry: a further duplicate candidate involving this entity is assessed on its own evidence, with this merge in the record

guardrails: A merge never duplicates a financial obligation.
An opt-out never disappears because another profile was opted in.
Provenance is preserved - the consolidated record can say where each part of it came from.
An irreversible merge requires stronger evidence and authority than a reversible one.
journeys.reusableRule: Entity merge consolidates representations only after dependent state has been reconciled according to the authority rules of each state type.

journeys.name: Merge conflict → safe state → resolve → continue or abort
journeys.purpose: Fail safe wherever consolidating would require inventing an authority the system does not have.

entity.scope: the merge operation and the specific state in conflict
entity.note: The conflict attaches to particular state, not to the whole merge. Some conflicts stop everything and most do not, and telling them apart is the journey's main work.

requires: state that two sources hold incompatibly: contradictory identity attributes, a permission conflict, different ownership claims, incompatible account states, duplicate active obligations, or a credential or security conflict

nodes.does: Classify the conflict by domain. The domain decides which authority rule applies, and there is no rule that applies across identity, permission, ownership, obligation and credentials at once

nodes.asks: Does a deterministic authority rule exist for this domain?

branches.label: Rule exists
branches.when: policy states which source wins for this kind of state, and why

branches.label: No rule
branches.when: nothing states how this conflict resolves

nodes.does: Apply the rule and record the basis. A conflict resolved in order to make the merge succeed is not resolved - it has been decided by the only party with an interest in the answer, which is whoever wanted the merge

Record the affected state as MERGE_CONFLICT. The most permissive consent or access value is never selected by default - defaulting that way resolves every ambiguity in the direction that cannot be undone, and it is the direction a merge is already biased toward

nodes.asks: Is this an ambiguous identity conflict?

branches.label: Identity itself is in doubt
branches.when: the conflict suggests these may not be one entity at all

branches.label: Identity is established
branches.when: the conflict is about state held by an entity we are confident is one

nodes.asks: Can the merge safely continue on the portions that carry no conflict?

branches.label: Independent portions exist
branches.when: some state can be consolidated without depending on anything in conflict

branches.label: Everything is entangled
branches.when: the conflicted state is load-bearing for the rest

nodes.does: Hold the entire merge. Where identity itself is in doubt, consolidating anything assumes the thing the merge was supposed to establish
Consolidate only the portions carrying no conflict and no dependency on conflicted state, leaving the rest explicitly unmerged rather than quietly merged with a chosen value

until: an authoritative or manual resolution is recorded

timeout.reason: a merge held in conflict leaves two records in a half-consolidated state, which is worse than either outcome and worth escalating rather than waiting out
