nodes.on: a merge conflict outliving its resolution SLA
carries: the conflict, its domain and what has been consolidated so far
the fact that the records are currently in a partially reconciled state, which is nobody's intended end state

nodes.asks: How was it settled?

branches.label: Resolved
branches.when: an authority determined the answer and the merge may complete

branches.label: Aborted
branches.when: the merge should not proceed

branches.label: Partially reconciled, remainder unresolvable
branches.when: the independent portions consolidated and the conflicted state stays separate

nodes.state: RESOLVED; the merge may complete
nodes.reEntry: a further conflict in the same merge opens its own instance

nodes.does: Abort the merge, unwinding whatever was partially consolidated where that is possible, and recording precisely what could not be unwound. The sources remain separate and the attempt remains in the record

nodes.state: ABORTED; sources remain separate
nodes.reEntry: a new merge requires new evidence. That an earlier attempt was aborted is part of what the next one is judged against

nodes.state: PARTIALLY_RECONCILED; conflicted state left separate and marked
nodes.reEntry: what remains unmerged is named rather than left as a vague inconsistency, so it can be resolved later on its own evidence

guardrails: A conflict is never resolved merely to make the merge succeed.
The most permissive consent or access state is never chosen by default.
An ambiguous identity conflict stops the entire merge rather than part of it.
What could not be unwound after an abort is recorded rather than assumed away.
journeys.reusableRule: Merge conflicts should fail safe whenever consolidation would require inventing authority that the system does not possess.

journeys.name: Account consolidation → dependency reconciliation → unified relationship
journeys.purpose: Unify business structure across accounts while every person involved stays a separate person.

entity.scope: the accounts being consolidated and the canonical structure that results
entity.note: Accounts consolidate; people do not. The members of the consolidated account remain distinct identities with distinct consent and distinct history.

requires: an authorized consolidation naming the accounts and the canonical target
insufficientAlone: two accounts sharing a domain, a billing address or an administrator

nodes.does: Determine the canonical account structure - which account survives and what the consolidated shape actually is
Inventory across every account being consolidated: members, roles, contracts, subscriptions, resources, entitlements, billing relationships, open cases, ownership and active obligations

nodes.asks: Does any part of this require treating two people as one?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: the consolidation only works if two member records are the same person

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: every member remains a distinct identity in the consolidated structure

nodes.state: consolidation stopped; it requires an identity merge
nodes.reEntry: consolidating two people into one identity is a different decision with a far higher evidence bar, assessed and authorised separately. A consolidation that needs it has exceeded what it was authorised to do

nodes.asks: Are the resources transferable to the canonical account?

branches.label: Transferable
branches.when: policy and the resource itself allow it to move

branches.label: Not transferable
branches.when: a contract, a licence or the resource's own nature keeps it where it is

nodes.does: Transfer the resources according to policy, keeping their history with them
Retain the resource under its original relationship, referenced from the canonical account rather than moved into it. A reference keeps it reachable without pretending it changed hands

nodes.asks: Do the accounts carry conflicting obligations?

branches.label: Conflicting
branches.when: two accounts hold obligations that cannot both stand in one structure

branches.label: Compatible
branches.when: the obligations coexist in the consolidated structure

nodes.on: obligations that cannot both survive the consolidated structure
carries: each obligation, its source account and what makes them incompatible
the explicit fact that nothing has been cancelled by the consolidation

nodes.does: Recalculate account-level roles, access, entitlements, routing and aggregate states from what the consolidated account actually holds. Permissions are recalculated rather than unioned - a union grants everyone the highest access anyone previously had, which turns a structural tidy-up into privilege escalation
Verify that no entitlement was duplicated, no obligation lost, no access became broader than any source account granted, and no resource left orphaned

nodes.asks: Did verification pass?

branches.label: Passed
branches.when: every check holds

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: a duplicated entitlement, a lost obligation, widened access or an orphaned resource was found

nodes.state: accounts consolidated; identities untouched
nodes.reEntry: a further consolidation is assessed against the canonical structure this produced

nodes.on: a consolidation whose verification failed
carries: which check failed and on what
the consolidated structure as it currently stands, which is not the intended end state

guardrails: Account consolidation is not person identity merge.
Members of consolidated accounts do not become the same identity.
Account-level permissions are recalculated rather than unioned.
A resource that cannot transfer is referenced rather than moved.
journeys.reusableRule: Account consolidation unifies business structure while preserving independent identities and reconciling account-level obligations explicitly.

journeys.name: Primary relationship transfer → validate new primary → transfer dependencies
journeys.purpose: Move a dependent entity to a new primary, carrying only what the primary relationship actually governs.

entity.scope: the dependent entity, its outgoing primary and its incoming one
entity.note: The dependent's own permissions and consent are not part of the transfer. They belong to the dependent and stay with it.

distinctFrom.because: Changing which primary a dependent hangs from moves a relationship. It consolidates nothing and neither party's identity changes.

requires: an authorized transfer naming the dependent entity, the outgoing primary and the incoming one

nodes.asks: Is the proposed new primary relationship valid?

branches.label: Valid
branches.when: the incoming primary can hold this relationship and is entitled to

branches.label: Not valid
branches.when: the incoming primary is ineligible, or the relationship is not permitted between these types

nodes.state: transfer rejected; the existing primary relationship stands
nodes.reEntry: a different incoming primary is validated on its own terms. The dependent is never left between two primaries while the question is open

nodes.does: Identify what the primary relationship actually governs: rights, notifications, responsibilities, billing, access, ownership and open obligations. Anything the dependent holds on its own basis is deliberately not on this list

Transfer only the dependencies the primary relationship governs, preserving the historical primary relationship and the period it covered. Existing obligations move with their deadlines unchanged rather than disappearing in the handover

nodes.asks: Does the dependent hold permission or consent on its own basis?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: the dependent gave or withheld something itself, rather than inheriting it

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: everything it held came through the primary relationship

nodes.does: Preserve it independently. It does not transfer, and the incoming primary's state is not inherited over it - a dependent who opted out does not become opted in because their primary is
Verify the dependent now holds exactly one valid required primary relationship - not zero, and not two

nodes.asks: Did verification pass?

branches.label: Exactly one valid primary
branches.when: the transfer landed cleanly

branches.label: None, or more than one
branches.when: the dependent is left without a required primary, or holding two

nodes.state: primary relationship transferred; independent state preserved
nodes.reEntry: a further transfer is validated against the current primary

nodes.on: a dependent left without exactly one valid required primary
carries: the dependent, what was transferred and what it now lacks
its inherited obligations and their unchanged deadlines

guardrails: A primary relationship transfer is not an identity merge.
The historical primary relationship and its period are preserved.
Existing obligations do not disappear during a transfer, and their deadlines do not reset.
The dependent's own permission and consent are never overwritten by the incoming primary's.
journeys.reusableRule: Changing a primary relationship transfers only the dependencies governed by that relationship, not every state associated with either party.

journeys.name: Role or responsibility handover → effective-time transfer → continue
journeys.purpose: Move a role between two people at a defined moment, without changing anything before it or rewriting anything behind it.

entity.scope: the role or responsibility, its outgoing holder and its incoming one
entity.note: A handover has an effective time, and that time is load-bearing. Authorising it today does not move authority today.

distinctFrom.because: OWN-54 moves ownership of one work item now. This moves a role and everything it carries at a future effective point, which is why both actors are revalidated when that point arrives rather than when it was scheduled.
REL-94 changes one person's role. This moves a role from one person to another, which means two actors to validate and a set of open work that has to travel intact.

journeys.objective: Move a role between two people at a defined moment, without changing anything before it or rewriting anything behind it.
eligibility: an authorized handover naming the outgoing actor, the incoming actor, the scope and the effective time
no instance of this journey is already open for the the role or responsibility
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A future handover is not an immediate authority change.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Historical decisions by the outgoing actor remain historical facts.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Inherited deadlines do not reset at the handover.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Both actors are revalidated at the effective time, not at the time of authorisation.

guardrails: state_written_on_stale_entity

useCases: a role moved between two people at a defined moment
a handover whose assumptions are re-checked at the effective time

requires: an authorized handover naming the outgoing actor, the incoming actor, the scope and the effective time
insufficientAlone: a role change with no named incoming actor
a handover discussed but not authorised
an actor leaving with no handover recorded, which orphan handling owns

nodes.does: Define the outgoing actor, the incoming actor, the scope, the effective time and the reason. A handover scheduled for a future date is not an authority change now - until the effective time the outgoing actor still holds the role and everything in it
Inventory what travels with the role: open work, deadlines, approvals, scheduled actions, commitments and the context needed to continue any of them

nodes.asks: Is the incoming actor eligible and authorized for this role?

branches.label: Eligible
branches.when: they hold the authority the role requires and nothing disqualifies them

branches.label: Not eligible
branches.when: they cannot hold the role, or their authority does not cover its scope

nodes.on: a handover into an actor who cannot hold the role
carries: the role, both actors and what makes the incoming one ineligible
the open work still with the outgoing actor, which has not moved

nodes.does: Prepare the transfer without activating it. Nothing about the outgoing actor's authority changes yet, and nothing about the incoming actor's does either

after.rule: The handover waits until its own effective time; nothing changes before it, and both actors and the target are revalidated at it.

timeout.reason: reaching the effective moment is the ordinary path; the wait watches for the handover being withdrawn before it gets there

nodes.recheck: the the role or responsibility re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.state: handover cancelled or superseded before its effective time
nodes.reEntry: the outgoing actor retained the role throughout, so nothing has to be undone - which is the point of not moving authority at the moment of authorisation

nodes.does: At the effective time, revalidate both actors and the target entity. Weeks can pass between authorising a handover and it taking effect, and either actor may have left, changed role or lost the authority the handover assumed

nodes.asks: Are both actors and the target still valid at the effective time?

branches.label: Still valid
branches.when: nothing that the handover assumed has changed

branches.label: Something moved
branches.when: an actor has left, lost authority, or the target no longer exists as scoped

nodes.on: a handover whose assumptions did not survive to its effective time
carries: what changed between authorisation and the effective moment
the open work, which is still with the outgoing actor and still running against its original deadlines

nodes.does: Activate the new responsibility from the effective time, with the inherited deadlines and obligations exactly as they stood. The handover changes who is answerable, never what is owed or by when

Invalidate the outgoing actor's future scheduled actions where their authority has now ended. Decisions they made while holding the role remain historical facts and are not touched - what changes is what they may do next

nodes.state: responsibility handed over at its effective time
nodes.reEntry: a further handover is scheduled and validated on its own terms

guardrails: A future handover is not an immediate authority change.
Historical decisions by the outgoing actor remain historical facts.
Inherited deadlines do not reset at the handover.
Both actors are revalidated at the effective time, not at the time of authorisation.
journeys.reusableRule: Responsibility handover changes future authority at a defined effective point while preserving the history and obligations of the role.

journeys.name: Account closure request → validate → resolve blockers → close
journeys.purpose: End an account relationship once the obligations that legitimately block it are resolved, and end nothing else.

entity.scope: the account and this closure request
entity.note: Closing the account ends the account relationship. It cancels no subscription and deletes no data, and neither of those happens as a side effect of it.

distinctFrom.because: RET-29 completes a subscription cancellation - a commercial relationship ending. An account can be closed with subscriptions running, and a subscription can be cancelled with the account intact.

journeys.objective: End an account relationship once the obligations that legitimately block it are resolved, and end nothing else.
eligibility: a closure request against an identified account
no instance of this journey is already open for the the account and this closure request
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Account closure is not data deletion.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Account closure is not subscription cancellation unless a contract explicitly couples them.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Closure does not silently erase audit or history.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A blocker is named specifically. An unexplained refusal is not a blocker, it is a support case.

value.rule: Every touch in this plan is the closure process itself and is mandatory; nothing discretionary exists to cap.

default.applicableWhen: GLB-24; the graph's own touch count

cooldown.rule: This journey is per the account and this closure request; a later instance concerns a different the account and this closure request and no cooldown applies between them.

default.applicableWhen: the entity note: one instance per entity

roles.when: the message has to be kept and survive until the person can act on it
the person is active in the product and the action is taken there

touches.purpose: Tell the requester that no closure took place and why this request cannot perform it, without disclosing account state they are not entitled to.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Name the state that prevents closure, without inventing a route around it.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Confirm the account relationship is closed and state plainly what closure is not - it is not subscription cancellation and it is not data deletion, both of which have their own lifecycles and their own evidence.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Surface the exact blocker.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

mustNotClaim: a route around the blocker that does not exist

guardrails: complaint
message_after_success
unsubscribe

useCases: a closure request checked for authority and blockers before anything ends
a blocker named specifically so the requester knows what to resolve

requires: a closure request against an identified account
insufficientAlone: a cancelled subscription, which ends a commercial relationship rather than the account
a data deletion request, which is a different lifecycle with a different authority
a long period of inactivity

nodes.does: Record CLOSURE_REQUESTED, and determine who requested it, whether they hold the authority to, the account's current state, its open blockers and its dependent relationships

nodes.asks: Does the requester hold authority to close this account?

branches.label: Authorised
branches.when: they own the account or hold the role that may close it

branches.label: Not authorised
branches.when: the request comes from someone who cannot make it

nodes.does: Tell the requester that no closure took place and why this request cannot perform it, without disclosing account state they are not entitled to. A closure request that disappears leaves the requester believing an account is closed when it is not

Name the state that prevents closure, without inventing a route around it. Where nothing the requester can do would change it, saying so is the answer - an unresolvable block reported as silence reads as a request still being processed

Confirm the account relationship is closed and state plainly what closure is not - it is not subscription cancellation and it is not data deletion, both of which have their own lifecycles and their own evidence. Sent only after closure is verified, never on the request

nodes.state: closure not requested by an authorised party; account unchanged
nodes.reEntry: a request from an authorised party is assessed on its own terms

nodes.asks: Is closure permitted now?

branches.label: Permitted
branches.when: no blocker stands in the way

branches.label: Blocked, recoverable
branches.when: an active financial obligation, an open transaction, a required return, a security review, a dependent entity or an administrative process stands in the way and can be resolved

branches.label: Blocked, not recoverable
branches.when: something prevents closure that the account holder cannot resolve

nodes.does: Surface the exact blocker. Telling someone they cannot close their account without saying why produces a support case rather than a closure, and it reads as an obstacle rather than a requirement

after.rule: The closure request's validity window.

timeout.reason: a closure request held open indefinitely against an unresolved blocker is neither a closure nor a refusal, and the account holder cannot tell which they have

nodes.recheck: the the account and this closure request re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.asks: With that blocker resolved, is anything else in the way?

branches.label: All clear
branches.when: no blocker remains

branches.label: Further blockers
branches.when: resolving one revealed or left others

nodes.state: one blocker cleared, others remain and are surfaced
nodes.reEntry: each remaining blocker is named and resolved on its own, and closure is requested again - stacking them into one message tells the account holder nothing they can act on

nodes.state: closure request lapsed with blockers outstanding
nodes.reEntry: a fresh request re-enters against whatever blockers still stand

nodes.state: closure not permitted
nodes.reEntry: the preventing condition changing re-opens this. The account stays open and the reason is on record rather than left as an unexplained refusal

nodes.does: Execute the account closure. This ends the account relationship and does nothing else - it cancels no subscription unless a contract explicitly couples them, and it deletes no data. The audit and history are untouched
Verify the account is no longer active for the operations closure prohibits

nodes.asks: Did the closure take effect?

branches.label: Closed
branches.when: the account no longer permits prohibited operations

branches.label: Not fully applied
branches.when: the account remains active somewhere

nodes.on: a closure that has taken effect on the account itself
carries: the closed account and the dependent relationships identified at request time
the explicit fact that no external or commercial dependency has been terminated by this

nodes.on: a closure that did not fully apply
carries: where the account remains active
the closure request and its authority

guardrails: Account closure is not data deletion.
Account closure is not subscription cancellation unless a contract explicitly couples them.
Closure does not silently erase audit or history.
A blocker is named specifically. An unexplained refusal is not a blocker, it is a support case.
journeys.reusableRule: Account closure ends an account relationship only after obligations that legitimately block closure have been resolved.

journeys.name: Account closure → reconcile external and commercial dependencies → finalize
journeys.purpose: Make sure nothing that lives outside the account is assumed to have ended because the account did.

entity.scope: the closing account plus each external or commercial dependency, individually
entity.note: Each dependency is its own relationship with its own end state. None of them ends because our account record changed.

journeys.objective: Make sure nothing that lives outside the account is assumed to have ended because the account did.
eligibility: an account closure that has taken effect on the account itself
no instance of this journey is already open for the the closing account plus each external or commercial dependency
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Closing an application account is never assumed to cancel an externally billed subscription.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: An external provider's reported success is verified rather than trusted.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A failure to terminate one dependency is not hidden behind an account marked CLOSED.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Each dependency's final state is recorded independently of the account's.

guardrails: state_written_on_stale_entity

useCases: external subscriptions and providers reconciled one by one when an account closes
a dependency that did not terminate, surfaced rather than hidden

requires: an account closure that has taken effect on the account itself
insufficientAlone: a closure requested but not yet applied to the account
a subscription cancellation, which ends a commercial relationship rather than the account

nodes.does: Inventory the external and dependent state: subscriptions, external billing agreements, third-party services, active entitlements, pending invoices, external reservations and linked contracts. Each is a relationship in its own right, and closing an application account has never cancelled a subscription billed by someone else

nodes.asks: Does an authoritative contract or system state that this dependency terminates with the account?

branches.label: Explicitly coupled
branches.when: a contract or the provider's own system says closing the account ends it

branches.label: Independent
branches.when: nothing authoritative couples them - the ordinary case

nodes.does: Verify the termination actually happened rather than assuming it. A provider reporting success is a statement about their API, and a coupling written into a contract is not the same as a coupling implemented in a system
Record that this dependency requires its own termination and raise it as such. It does not end because our account did, and the person is told which relationships they still hold

after.rule: The closure policy's window for dependency resolution.

timeout.reason: a dependency left unresolved is someone continuing to be charged or committed after they believed they had finished, and it does not become resolved by the account looking closed

nodes.recheck: the the closing account plus each external or commercial dependency re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.asks: Did every required dependency reach its terminal state?

branches.label: All resolved
branches.when: each dependency reached a recorded end state

branches.label: Some did not
branches.when: at least one dependency failed to terminate

nodes.does: Record each dependency's final state independently of the account's. They are separate relationships and their endings are separate facts, recorded as such

Record which dependencies did not terminate, visibly and by name. A failure to end one dependency is never hidden behind an account marked CLOSED - that is exactly how someone keeps being charged by a provider they believe they have left

nodes.asks: Does the closure policy permit the account to close while this dependency remains?

branches.label: Permitted
branches.when: policy allows the account to close with the dependency tracked separately

branches.label: Not permitted
branches.when: the dependency must resolve before closure finalises

nodes.does: Record the remaining dependency independently, with its own state and its own owner, so it stays visible and attributable after the account is gone

nodes.on: a dependency that did not terminate and cannot be left outstanding
carries: which dependency, with which provider, and what was attempted
the fact that the account holder may still be committed or billed, which is what makes this urgent

nodes.state: dependencies reconciled and recorded independently of the account
nodes.reEntry: a dependency discovered later is reconciled on its own, against the closed account's record

guardrails: Closing an application account is never assumed to cancel an externally billed subscription.
An external provider's reported success is verified rather than trusted.
A failure to terminate one dependency is not hidden behind an account marked CLOSED.
Each dependency's final state is recorded independently of the account's.
journeys.reusableRule: Account closure and commercial termination are independent state transitions unless an authoritative dependency explicitly couples them.

journeys.name: Closure completed → wind-down → former or terminal account state
journeys.purpose: Stop normal account activity while letting the obligations that outlive closure actually finish.

entity.scope: the closed account and the obligations still outstanding against it
entity.note: The wind-down capability is enumerated rather than left as a general exception, so a closed account cannot quietly keep behaving like an open one.

journeys.objective: Stop normal account activity while letting the obligations that outlive closure actually finish.
eligibility: a closure that has been executed and verified
no instance of this journey is already open for the the closed account and the obligations still outstanding against it
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A closed account does not reactivate through a stale login or a queued onboarding event.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: The wind-down capability is explicitly scoped and enumerated.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: A terminal relationship state does not mean the historical record is deleted.

guardrails: state_written_on_stale_entity

useCases: normal activity stopped while obligations that outlive closure finish
a wind-down outliving its horizon, escalated to ownership

requires: a closure that has been executed and verified
insufficientAlone: a closure requested, executing or not yet verified
a suspension, which is designed to be reversed

nodes.does: Suppress new acquisition, normal usage, engagement journeys that are now obsolete, and every account action incompatible with closure - including anything already queued. A closed account receiving an onboarding email is the clearest possible evidence that the closure did not reach everything

Guard against reactivation. A stale login, a queued onboarding step or a delayed synchronisation must not bring a closed account back - closure is a state that later events are checked against, never one they can silently overwrite

nodes.asks: Do obligations remain outstanding against this account?

branches.label: Obligations remain
branches.when: a final invoice, a refund, a data export, a return, an open support case, a regulatory retention or an external dependency is still outstanding

branches.label: Nothing outstanding
branches.when: the account owes nothing and is owed nothing

nodes.does: Allow only the scoped processes those obligations need, enumerated individually. A wind-down left as a general exception is an open account with a different label on it

after.rule: The wind-down horizon.

timeout.reason: an account held open in wind-down indefinitely is neither closed nor operating, and nobody is left watching which obligation is holding it there

nodes.recheck: the the closed account and the obligations still outstanding against it re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.on: a wind-down outliving its horizon
carries: which obligations are still outstanding and how long they have been
the account's state, which is closed but not finished

nodes.state: FORMER; the relationship is over and the historical record is intact
nodes.reEntry: a returning customer opens a new relationship rather than reviving this one. A terminal relationship state does not mean the records never existed - deleting them is a separate lifecycle with its own request, its own scope and its own authority

guardrails: A closed account does not reactivate through a stale login or a queued onboarding event.
The wind-down capability is explicitly scoped and enumerated.
A terminal relationship state does not mean the historical record is deleted.
journeys.reusableRule: Closure ends normal account activity while allowing explicitly required wind-down obligations to finish.

journeys.name: Data deletion request → validate scope → hold, delete or retain required data
journeys.purpose: Decide what a deletion request actually covers, and keep only what an authoritative retention obligation genuinely requires.

entity.scope: the data subject, this deletion request, and the data scope it names
entity.note: The request is bounded by what it asks for and by what governing policy covers. It is not a licence to delete everything we hold, nor a reason to keep everything we would rather not lose.

distinctFrom.because: Closing an account ends a relationship and requests nothing about data. A deletion request concerns data and says nothing about whether the relationship continues. Either can happen without the other.

requires: a deletion request naming a data subject and a scope
insufficientAlone: an account closure, which ends a relationship and requests nothing about data
a subscription cancellation
an unsubscribe, which withdraws permission to contact rather than requesting removal

nodes.asks: Is the requester's identity and authority established for this scope?

branches.label: Established
branches.when: the requester is verified as the data subject or as authorised to act for them

branches.label: Not established
branches.when: identity or authority has not been verified to the level this request requires

nodes.on: a deletion request whose requester is not yet verified
carries: the request and the verification it is blocked on
the request's own deadline, which the verification does not reset

nodes.does: Validate the scope, the jurisdiction and policy context, and which systems and data classes are actually in scope. A deletion request is bounded by what it asks for and by what the governing policy covers - not by everything we happen to hold about the person
Inventory the data in scope and classify each item as DELETABLE, RETAIN_REQUIRED, DEPENDENCY_BLOCKED, ALREADY_DELETED or MANUAL_REVIEW

nodes.asks: Does an authoritative retention obligation cover any of it?

branches.label: Retention required
branches.when: a legal or business obligation names data that must be kept

branches.label: Nothing retained
branches.when: no obligation covers anything in scope

nodes.does: Retain only what an authoritative obligation actually requires, recording which obligation and why. No retention rule is invented - where policy is silent the data is not kept on a guess, because retaining on a guess keeps what should have gone just as surely as deleting on one destroys what had to stay

nodes.asks: What remains, and can it be deleted?

branches.label: Deletable and clear
branches.when: data remains in scope, is eligible, and no dependency blocks it

branches.label: Blocked by a dependency
branches.when: something in scope cannot be removed until a dependency clears

branches.label: Needs manual review
branches.when: the classification could not be settled automatically

branches.label: Nothing left
branches.when: everything in scope is already absent or retained under an obligation

timeout.reason: a deletion request usually carries a legal deadline, and a dependency that has not cleared inside it needs a person rather than more waiting

nodes.on: data approved for deletion or anonymization
carries: the exact scope approved, per system and data class
what is being retained and under which obligation, so execution does not remove it

nodes.on: a classification or dependency the automated path could not settle
carries: the request, its deadline and what specifically is unresolved
the retention obligations already identified

nodes.state: nothing in scope to delete; retained items recorded with their obligations
nodes.reEntry: this is recorded as what it is rather than reported as a deletion. Data arriving later within the same scope is assessed against this request where the policy allows

guardrails: Account closure is not a deletion request.
A deletion request is not immediate physical deletion of every record.
No retention rule is invented. Where the governing policy is silent, data is not retained on a guess.
Audit evidence may need retaining without retaining the operational data alongside it.
journeys.reusableRule: Data deletion removes data according to defined scope while preserving only information that an authoritative retention obligation requires.

journeys.name: Data deletion execution → propagate → verify or reconcile failure
journeys.purpose: Carry a deletion through every system it has to reach, and keep any part that did not arrive visible.

entity.scope: the deletion job and each affected system's operation individually
entity.note: Each system's operation has its own type and its own terminal state. A single overall status hides the one that failed, which is the only one that matters.

requires: an approved deletion scope, per system and data class, from a validated request

nodes.does: Generate the scoped operation for each affected system - delete, anonymize, detach, restrict or place under retention hold - according to what the governing requirement for that system actually is. One operation type applied everywhere either destroys what had to be kept or keeps what had to go

Execute idempotently, keyed so a redelivered job does not repeat an operation, and so that nothing propagates back through downstream synchronisation to recreate what was just removed. A sync job running on its own schedule will otherwise restore a profile deleted an hour earlier, undoing the work while reporting success

timeout.reason: silence from a system is not confirmation, and a deletion whose SLA passes with systems unheard from is a partial failure that has not reported itself

nodes.asks: How did the operations end?

branches.label: All confirmed
branches.when: every required system reported its operation complete

branches.label: Some failed
branches.when: at least one system reported failure or did not confirm

nodes.asks: Was a further copy of the data discovered while the request was running?

branches.label: In scope
branches.when: a copy was found that the approved scope covers

branches.label: Out of scope
branches.when: a copy was found that the approved scope does not cover

branches.label: Nothing further
branches.when: no new copy surfaced

nodes.does: Generate and execute the operation for the newly discovered copy, within the same job and the same scope

Record the discovered copy as out of scope, naming why. It is not deleted on this request and it is not left unrecorded either - an unrecorded copy is one nobody knows to assess against the next request

Verify that no required target remains unintentionally active or searchable, to whatever guarantee each system actually offers. The deletion audit records what was removed and when, without keeping a copy of the personal data it removed - an audit that preserves the record has recreated the thing the deletion was for

nodes.asks: Did verification confirm every required terminal state?

branches.label: Verified
branches.when: every in-scope target reached its required state

branches.label: Something remains
branches.when: a target is still present where it should not be

nodes.state: VERIFIED_COMPLETE; every in-scope obligation reached its terminal state
nodes.reEntry: a later request covering different scope is its own job. Deletion succeeding in the primary store was never the same as deletion everywhere, and this state records that everywhere was checked

nodes.does: Record PARTIAL_DELETION_FAILURE, naming which systems did not reach their required terminal state. This is never represented as complete - a deletion reported as done while a downstream copy survives is the most consequential false report in this library, because it ends the investigation that would have found the copy

nodes.asks: Is a retry available within the policy budget?

branches.label: Retry
branches.when: the failure is transient and the budget fixed at the first failure has room

branches.label: Escalate
branches.when: the failure is not clearing, or the budget is spent

nodes.does: Retry the outstanding operations only, idempotently, so a partially completed deletion is completed rather than restarted

nodes.on: a deletion that could not reach its required terminal state everywhere
carries: which systems remain outstanding and what was attempted
the request's deadline, which is often a legal one and does not move because a system did not respond
suppresses: any representation of this deletion as complete while a target remains

guardrails: Deletion succeeding in the primary store is not deletion everywhere.
A failed downstream deletion is never represented as fully complete.
Deletion jobs do not recreate profiles through downstream synchronisation.
The deletion audit does not itself preserve the personal data that was deleted.
journeys.reusableRule: Distributed deletion is complete only when all in-scope deletion obligations have reached their required terminal state or an explicit retained exception is recorded.

journeys.name: Deletion request → verify requester → confirm scope and retention → closed
journeys.purpose: Give the person who asked for their data to be removed a durable record of what went, what stayed, under which obligation, and the date the request closed - because a deletion nobody can point to is indistinguishable from one that never happened.

entity.scope: the data subject and the single deletion request they raised, bounded by the scope that request names
entity.note: One request, one record. A later request from the same person is a separate instance and inherits neither this one's verification nor its window.

distinctFrom.because: TRM-109 decides what the request covers, what an authoritative obligation requires keeping, and executes the removal. This journey is only what the requester is told, and it states nothing TRM-109 has not resolved.

journeys.objective: Give the person who asked for their data to be removed a durable record of what went, what stayed, under which obligation, and the date the request closed - because a deletion nobody can point to is indistinguishable from one that never happened.
eligibility: a deletion request recorded against a named data subject
the scope the request itself names
the response window the governing obligation sets
no instance of this journey is already open for the the data subject and the single deletion request they raised
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Nothing is deleted on an unverified request, and nothing is asked for beyond the proof of control the obligation actually requires.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Ending the relationship is not a deletion request and is never answered as one.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: No retention is described that an authoritative obligation does not require. Where the policy is silent, nothing is claimed.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: The response window belongs to the obligation, not to the work. It is answered inside it or escalated at it.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: The closing message is a record: scope, outcome, obligation, date - readable a year later by somebody who was not there.

value.rule: Every touch in this plan is the request's own record and is mandatory; nothing discretionary exists to cap.

default.applicableWhen: GLB-24; the graph's own touch count

cooldown.rule: This journey is per the data subject and the single deletion request they raised; a later instance concerns a different the data subject and the single deletion request they raised and no cooldown applies between them.

default.applicableWhen: the entity note: one instance per entity

roles.when: the message has to be kept and survive until the person can act on it

touches.purpose: Acknowledge the request, state the date by which the obligation requires an answer, and say that establishing who is asking comes first.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Ask for exactly the proof of control the obligation requires and nothing beyond it.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

mustNotClaim: a need for identifying data beyond what the obligation requires

touches.purpose: Close the request as unverified, saying plainly that nothing was deleted, why, and that a fresh request can be raised at any time.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Confirm what was deleted, the scope it covered and the date the request closed.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: State what was deleted, what is retained, which obligation requires it and when that obligation ends.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

guardrails: complaint
message_after_success
unsubscribe

useCases: a deletion request acknowledged, verified and closed on the record inside the mandated window
a partial deletion that names what is retained and under which obligation

requires: a deletion request recorded against a named data subject
the scope the request itself names
the response window the governing obligation sets
insufficientAlone: a closure of the relationship
a request to stop receiving messages
a support conversation that mentions deletion

nodes.does: Acknowledge the request, state the date by which the obligation requires an answer, and say that establishing who is asking comes first. An unacknowledged request leaves the person unable to tell a mandated wait from being ignored

nodes.asks: Is the requester's control of the named scope already established?

branches.label: Already established
branches.when: control of the account or authority over the named scope meets the standard the obligation requires

branches.label: Not yet established
branches.when: the request arrived without sufficient proof that the requester controls what they are asking to erase

nodes.does: Ask for exactly the proof of control the obligation requires and nothing beyond it. Collecting extra identifying data in order to honour a deletion request is the contradiction the request exists to end

after.rule: The verification period held inside the mandated response window.

timeout.reason: the response window runs whether or not the requester replies, so an unverifiable request has to be closed inside it rather than left open

nodes.recheck: the the data subject and the single deletion request they raised re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.does: Close the request as unverified, saying plainly that nothing was deleted, why, and that a fresh request can be raised at any time. A silent close reads as a deletion that happened

nodes.state: closed unverified, nothing deleted
nodes.reEntry: a fresh request from the same person is a new instance with its own window and its own verification

after.rule: The resolution is waited for until the response deadline the governing obligation sets; reaching it unanswered escalates to data-protection ownership.

timeout.reason: the window belongs to the obligation rather than to how long the work takes, and passing it in silence is itself the failure

nodes.recheck: the the data subject and the single deletion request they raised re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.on: a deletion request that reaches its mandated response window with no authoritative outcome to state
carries: the request, its scope, its window and what the requester has already been told
which part of the scope remains unresolved and who holds it

nodes.asks: What does the resolved outcome actually say?

branches.label: Deleted in full
branches.when: everything in the named scope was deleted and no retention obligation covers any of it

branches.label: Partly retained
branches.when: an authoritative retention obligation covers part of the named scope

nodes.does: Confirm what was deleted, the scope it covered and the date the request closed. This message is the record the requester keeps, so it states the outcome rather than thanking them for their patience
State what was deleted, what is retained, which obligation requires it and when that obligation ends. Naming the obligation is what makes retention a rule rather than a preference

nodes.state: answered and closed on the record
nodes.reEntry: a later deletion request from the same person is a new instance, verified again from the start

guardrails: Nothing is deleted on an unverified request, and nothing is asked for beyond the proof of control the obligation actually requires.
Ending the relationship is not a deletion request and is never answered as one.
No retention is described that an authoritative obligation does not require. Where the policy is silent, nothing is claimed.
The response window belongs to the obligation, not to the work. It is answered inside it or escalated at it.
The closing message is a record: scope, outcome, obligation, date - readable a year later by somebody who was not there.
journeys.reusableRule: A deletion is only honoured if the person who asked can be told exactly what went, what stayed, and under whose rule it stayed.

journeys.name: Integration connection → authenticate → validate → activate
journeys.purpose: Make an integration active only once it has been proven to do the thing it exists for, rather than once a credential has been saved.

entity.scope: the individual integration connection, with its own credentials, scopes and validated capabilities
entity.note: One connection per configured integration. A second connection to the same provider is a separate one with its own scopes, and neither inherits the other's validation.

distinctFrom.because: This establishes that an integration works at all. INT-113 handles one that worked and has started to stop, which is a question about evidence over a window rather than about setup.

requires: a request to establish an integration connection with an identified provider
insufficientAlone: a credential saved in a settings screen, which stores a secret and connects nothing
a provider selected from a list

nodes.does: Collect and configure the connection parameters this provider requires

nodes.asks: Does authentication succeed?

branches.label: Authenticated
branches.when: the provider accepts the credentials

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the provider rejects them

nodes.state: AUTH_FAILED; not connected
nodes.reEntry: corrected credentials re-enter from the start. Nothing partial is left active, because a half-configured integration is one that fails on its first real operation rather than during setup

nodes.does: Validate the minimum capabilities and scopes this integration actually needs. Authentication proves the provider will talk to us; it says nothing about whether we are permitted to do the things we intend to do

nodes.asks: Is the required access available?

branches.label: Sufficient
branches.when: every capability the integration needs is within the granted scope

branches.label: Insufficient
branches.when: a required capability is outside what was granted

nodes.state: INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE; configuration required
nodes.reEntry: the missing scope is named rather than reported as a generic connection failure - the two produce entirely different remediation and only one of them is actionable

nodes.does: Perform a safe connectivity and capability validation - a read, a dry run, a no-op probe. Validation must not have destructive side effects: proving we can delete something by deleting it is not a test

nodes.asks: Did validation succeed?

branches.label: Validated
branches.when: the probe confirmed the capability works

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the probe did not confirm it

nodes.state: FAILED; authenticated and scoped, not operational
nodes.reEntry: remediation re-enters at validation. This state exists because authenticated and working are different, and reporting the first as the second is the failure this journey is built around

nodes.does: Record the connection as ACTIVE, with the capabilities that were actually validated rather than the ones that were configured

nodes.state: ACTIVE; authenticated, scoped and validated
nodes.reEntry: authorization changes go to INT-112 and health changes to INT-113

guardrails: A saved credential is not a connection.
Authentication success is not sufficient authorization scope.
Connection validation avoids destructive side effects.
A missing scope is named specifically rather than reported as a generic failure.
journeys.reusableRule: An integration becomes active only after authentication, required scope and minimum operational capability have been validated.

journeys.name: Integration credential or authorization change → revalidate → continue or degrade
journeys.purpose: Recheck what an integration can still do whenever its authorization changes, rather than assuming valid credentials mean unchanged access.

entity.scope: the integration connection and the authorization that changed
entity.note: Scope reduction affects the capabilities that depended on the removed scope. Everything else keeps working, and treating the whole connection as broken is its own outage.

requires: a material change to the connection's authorization: a token refreshed, a credential rotated, a scope reduced, an authorization revoked, or a service account changed

nodes.does: Invalidate the cached authorization. A queued retry holding a credential that has since been rotated away must not succeed on it - an old credential coming back through a retry is the specific failure this step exists to prevent

Revalidate the required capabilities against the new authorization. A token refreshing successfully means the provider will talk to us; it says nothing about whether the scope we had is the scope we still have

nodes.asks: What does revalidation show?

branches.label: Fully functional
branches.when: every capability the integration uses is still available

branches.label: Partially functional
branches.when: some capabilities are no longer within the granted scope and others are

branches.label: No longer usable
branches.when: authorization was revoked, or nothing the integration needs remains available

nodes.state: ACTIVE; authorization changed and capability unchanged
nodes.reEntry: the next authorization change revalidates again

nodes.does: Mark the affected capabilities DEGRADED and name exactly which. A reduced scope disables what depended on it, not the integration
Suppress the operations incompatible with the reduced authorization, leaving everything else running

nodes.state: DEGRADED; affected capabilities named, the rest operating
nodes.reEntry: restored scope revalidates and lifts the degradation for the capabilities it covers

nodes.on: authorization leaving the integration unusable
carries: what was revoked and when
any external operations already submitted and still unresolved, which the authorization change does not resolve

guardrails: A successful token refresh does not mean the integration is fully healthy.
A reduced scope affects only the capabilities that depended on it.
Old credentials do not become active again through a stale retry.
journeys.reusableRule: Integration authorization changes require capability revalidation because valid credentials do not guarantee unchanged operational access.

journeys.name: Integration health degradation → diagnose → recover, degrade or escalate
journeys.purpose: Scope a deteriorating integration to what is actually failing, and let recovery be established by evidence rather than by a metric returning to normal.

entity.scope: the integration connection, assessed per capability rather than as a whole
entity.note: Health is measured over a window. A single error is an event; a pattern across a window is evidence, and only the second one means anything.

requires: a meaningful health threshold crossed over a defined window: an elevated error rate, repeated timeouts, a partial endpoint failure, unexpected latency, authentication instability, or a declared provider degradation
insufficientAlone: one transient error
a single timeout
one slow response

nodes.does: Classify the affected scope - which endpoints, which capabilities, which operations. One endpoint failing does not make the integration unhealthy, and disabling everything because of it is a self-inflicted outage larger than the provider's

nodes.asks: What is the nature of the degradation?

branches.label: Transient
branches.when: the pattern is expected to clear and the affected operations are safe to retry

branches.label: Capability-specific
branches.when: particular capabilities are failing while others are unaffected

branches.label: Whole integration unusable
branches.when: the degradation reaches everything the integration does

nodes.does: Retry with backoff, only for operations where retrying is safe. Operations with external side effects are not retried on a health signal - their safety depends on an idempotency key and a known outcome, neither of which a health metric provides
Mark only the affected capabilities DEGRADED, preserving everything unaffected

until: the degradation worsens past the failure threshold

timeout.after: the operational SLA for this integration
timeout.reason: a degradation that neither clears nor worsens within its SLA is a steady state nobody chose, and it is worth escalating rather than watching indefinitely

nodes.asks: Which way did it move?

branches.label: Recovered
branches.when: the health evidence returned to normal across the window

branches.label: Worsened
branches.when: the degradation crossed the failure threshold

nodes.does: Revalidate the degraded capabilities before restoring them. A metric returning to normal is evidence to check rather than a conclusion to act on - the underlying cause may have been a scope change or a provider deprecation that a health graph cannot see

nodes.state: health restored; capabilities revalidated before being re-enabled
nodes.reEntry: a further threshold crossing is assessed against its own window

nodes.on: degradation reaching the failure threshold
carries: the affected scope and the evidence that established it
which capabilities were still working, so the failure stays scoped to what actually failed

nodes.on: a degradation persisting past its operational SLA
carries: the affected capabilities and how long they have been degraded

guardrails: One transient error is not a degraded integration.
Health is judged on evidence across a defined window.
Healthy capabilities are not disabled because an unrelated endpoint failed.
Operations with external side effects are not retried on a health signal alone.
journeys.reusableRule: Integration degradation should be scoped to the capabilities actually affected while recovery remains evidence-driven.

journeys.name: External request → pending outcome → confirm, fail or unknown
journeys.purpose: Keep submitting an external operation and completing one as separate states, and let an unknown outcome stay unknown.

entity.scope: the individual external operation, keyed by its own correlation and idempotency identifiers
entity.note: The identifiers are recorded before submission, because they are what makes any later retry safe or any later outcome attributable - generating them after a failure is too late to help with that failure.

distinctFrom.because: This owns the operation from submission until an outcome exists. INT-115 owns what happens to local state once one does, and most operations pass through both.

requires: an operation submitted to an external provider on behalf of a business action

nodes.does: Persist the operation id, the provider's request id, the action requested, the target entity, the submission time and the idempotency key, and record the state as PENDING_EXTERNAL_OUTCOME. Submitted is not completed, and nothing downstream may report the business action as done on the strength of this

nodes.asks: What did the provider actually return?

branches.label: An authoritative final outcome
branches.when: the response states the business operation's result, not merely that the request arrived

branches.label: Accepted, not completed
branches.when: the response acknowledges receipt - a 200 that means the request is queued is not the operation completing, and treating it as one is the most common error in this journey

until: a callback or webhook delivers the outcome
a poll returns a final result
the provider confirms out of band

timeout.reason: the window ending means we stopped hearing, which is a fact about our visibility rather than about the provider's work

nodes.does: Record the outcome as UNKNOWN, not as failed. A timeout says our side of the conversation ended; it says nothing about whether the provider completed the operation, and the distance between those two statements is a duplicate charge

nodes.on: an operation whose outcome window closed without an authoritative result
carries: the operation and provider request identifiers needed to ask the provider what actually happened
the idempotency key, so that whatever is established can be acted on without re-submitting
the explicit fact that the outcome is unknown rather than failed
suppresses: any retry of this operation until its true state is established

nodes.on: an authoritative outcome existing for this operation
carries: the outcome and the correlation identifiers it arrived with
what local state expected, so the reconciliation can tell agreement from conflict

guardrails: An HTTP 200 may mean the request was accepted, not that the business operation completed.
A timeout is not a failure.
A blind retry may duplicate an external side effect, so nothing is retried while the outcome is unknown.
Correlation and idempotency identifiers are recorded before submission.
journeys.reusableRule: External submission and external business completion are separate states; ambiguous outcomes require reconciliation before retry.

journeys.name: External outcome → local state reconciliation → apply or investigate
journeys.purpose: Apply an external outcome to local state only after establishing that it belongs here, has not already been applied, and still describes what is true.

entity.scope: the external operation the outcome refers to, and the local entity it would change
entity.note: Correlation comes first. An outcome applied to the wrong entity is a worse failure than one that arrives late, and it is much harder to find afterwards.

requires: an authoritative outcome received from or discovered at a provider
insufficientAlone: an acknowledgement of receipt
a status that the provider describes as intermediate

nodes.does: Match the outcome to the operation and entity it belongs to, using the identifiers recorded at submission

nodes.asks: Could the outcome be correlated to a known operation?

branches.label: Correlated
branches.when: it matches a recorded operation and entity

branches.label: Uncorrelated
branches.when: no recorded operation matches it

nodes.on: a provider event that cannot be matched to a known operation
carries: the event as received, unmodified
the explicit fact that it has not been applied to a best-guess entity

nodes.asks: What does local state say about this outcome?

branches.label: Expected
branches.when: local state is waiting for exactly this outcome on this operation

branches.label: Already applied
branches.when: local state already reflects this same outcome

branches.label: Conflicts
branches.when: local state holds something incompatible with the outcome

branches.label: Belongs to a superseded operation or version
branches.when: the outcome refers to something local state has since moved past

nodes.state: already applied; no duplicate side effect
nodes.reEntry: a redelivered webhook resolves here and does nothing, which is the property that makes provider redelivery survivable rather than dangerous

nodes.on: an external outcome incompatible with local state
carries: both values, their timestamps, their versions and their provenance
the fact that neither has been chosen, because the provider being external does not automatically make it authoritative for this field

nodes.asks: Does the outcome still describe the current business state?

branches.label: Still current
branches.when: nothing has superseded what the outcome reports

branches.label: Superseded
branches.when: local state has moved past it - a later operation, a newer version, a subsequent decision

nodes.does: Record the outcome as history without mutating current state. A late response can be a valid record of what happened without being a valid instruction about what is true now, and applying it would overwrite a newer decision with an older one

nodes.state: recorded as history; current state unchanged
nodes.reEntry: the operation's own history is now complete even though it changed nothing

nodes.does: Apply the outcome idempotently, so that the same outcome arriving again produces no second effect

nodes.state: outcome applied to local state
nodes.reEntry: a further outcome on the same operation is correlated and assessed on its own

guardrails: A late external response can be valid history without being a valid current-state mutation.
A provider event is correlated to the correct entity and operation before anything is applied.
A duplicate webhook is harmless.
An uncorrelated event is never applied to a best-guess entity.
journeys.reusableRule: External outcomes should update local state only after correlation, idempotency and current-state validity are established.

journeys.name: Integration failure → stop unsafe operations → diagnose → restore
journeys.purpose: Stop sending into an integration that cannot work, while keeping enough state to recover without repeating anything the provider may already have done.

entity.scope: the failed integration or capability, and the operations that depend on it
entity.note: Failure is scoped. Unrelated integrations, and unrelated capabilities within this one, are untouched.

distinctFrom.because: Degradation is an integration working badly and still working. This is one that cannot be relied on to work at all, which changes what is safe to send rather than how much.

requires: a defined failure condition: authentication permanently failed, the provider unavailable beyond tolerance, a required capability unavailable, the connection invalid, or persistent operational failure

nodes.does: Mark the affected integration or capability FAILED or DISCONNECTED, scoped to what actually failed. Unrelated integrations, and unrelated capabilities within this one, stay as they were

Stop the operations whose safe execution depends on this integration. Continuing to send into a known-failed integration produces a second population of failures that then has to be told apart from the first

nodes.asks: Are there external operations already submitted and still unresolved?

branches.label: Unresolved operations exist
branches.when: operations were submitted before the failure and never reached an authoritative outcome

branches.label: Nothing outstanding
branches.when: every submitted operation reached an outcome

nodes.does: Preserve those operations as unresolved, with their correlation and idempotency context intact. They are neither retried nor marked failed - we do not know what the provider did with them, and a connection failing is not evidence about an operation it already received
Determine the failure cause, since what recovery looks like depends entirely on it

nodes.asks: Is the failure recoverable?

branches.label: Recoverable
branches.when: reconnection, re-authorisation or provider recovery would restore it

branches.label: Not recoverable
branches.when: the capability is gone, the provider is ending it, or the configuration cannot be made valid

timeout.reason: an integration that has been failed for longer than the business can tolerate is an operational decision rather than a technical one, and it stops being something to wait out

nodes.on: a failed integration becoming operational again
carries: the outage window, which is what the backfill needs to size the gap
the operations preserved as unresolved, which reconnection does not resolve

nodes.on: a failure that reconnection cannot fix
carries: the cause and the capabilities now permanently unavailable
the unresolved operations, which still need an answer regardless of the integration's future

nodes.on: a failure outliving the business's tolerance for it
carries: how long the integration has been failed and what depends on it

guardrails: Failure does not erase queued or pending operation history.
Nothing is sent into a known unsafe failure state.
Healthy unrelated integrations are unaffected.
Submitted operations with unknown outcomes are preserved rather than retried or marked failed.
journeys.reusableRule: Integration failure should stop unsafe dependent operations while preserving enough state to recover without duplicating external effects.

journeys.name: Integration failure → queue or hold work → recover → controlled resume
journeys.purpose: Keep work that a failed integration blocked, but only where it can later be revalidated and safely resumed.

entity.scope: the failed integration and the individual work items blocked on it
entity.note: Each item is classified separately. A queue that treats every blocked item the same either holds something that needed an alternative or discards something that could have waited.

distinctFrom.because: This applies only where the integration has genuinely failed. An integration that is merely slow or backlogged is still working, and queueing more against it adds to the backlog that is already the problem - that case is a separate canonical problem and is deliberately not handled here.

requires: an integration in a FAILED or DISCONNECTED state, and valid dependent work that cannot proceed without it
insufficientAlone: an integration that is slow, lagging or backlogged while still working - a different problem, where queueing more work makes the backlog worse rather than protecting anything
an elevated error rate that has not crossed a failure condition

nodes.does: Classify each blocked item as SAFE_TO_QUEUE, TIME_SENSITIVE, REQUIRES_REVALIDATION or CANNOT_DELAY. Treating the whole queue as one class either holds something that needed an alternative route, or discards something that could safely have waited

nodes.asks: How does each class resolve?

branches.label: Safe to queue
branches.when: the work keeps its meaning after a delay and can be revalidated before it is sent

branches.label: Cannot delay
branches.when: the work loses its meaning or breaks a commitment if it waits

nodes.on: blocked work that cannot safely wait for the integration
carries: the work, its deadline and what it was blocked on
the fact that it has not been queued, so nobody assumes it will go out on recovery

nodes.does: Hold the work with its original context, entity version and idempotency key, and its original deadline. The deadline does not restart because we could not send it - the commitment was made to someone who is not waiting on our integration

until: the held work expires or becomes obsolete

timeout.reason: a queue with no horizon is an infinite retry loop with a friendlier name, and the work in it grows stale silently

nodes.asks: Which happened first?

branches.label: Integration restored
branches.when: the connection is operational again

branches.label: Work became obsolete
branches.when: the held work no longer describes anything current

nodes.does: Revalidate each held item against current state before anything is sent. The world moved while the integration was down, and a queued instruction written against the old world is not automatically still correct

nodes.asks: Is the held work still valid?

branches.label: Still valid
branches.when: it still describes something that should happen

branches.label: No longer valid
branches.when: the state it was written against has moved

nodes.does: Drain in a controlled manner rather than releasing the whole backlog at once. An integration that has just come back, met with everything it missed in one burst, goes down again - and the second outage looks like a new fault rather than our own doing

nodes.state: held work revalidated and drained
nodes.reEntry: a further failure holds its own work with its own classification

nodes.does: Discard or cancel the work as stale, recording the reason. Silently dropping it and silently sending it are both worse than saying which happened and why

nodes.state: held work discarded as stale, with an audited reason
nodes.reEntry: whatever the work was for may be requested again on current state, which is a new item rather than this one revived

guardrails: A queue is not an infinite retry loop. It has a horizon and the items in it expire.
Queued work preserves its entity, version and idempotency context.
Recovery does not release the entire backlog simultaneously.
This applies to real integration failure only. Slowness and backlog are a different problem and are not handled by queueing against them.
journeys.reusableRule: Work blocked by integration failure should be preserved only when it can later be safely revalidated and resumed.

journeys.name: Integration reconnect → backfill → deduplicate → reconcile
journeys.purpose: Close the gap an outage left in what we know, without recreating everything that would have happened if the events had arrived on time.

entity.scope: the integration connection and the specific synchronization window the outage created
entity.note: The window is the unit of work. Without a measured gap the backfill either misses events or refetches everything, and neither can be verified.

requires: a previously unavailable integration becoming operational
insufficientAlone: the connection being restored, which is not the same as being synchronized - reconnected and up to date are different states, and marking the integration healthy at reconnection hides the missing window entirely

nodes.does: Determine the outage window - from when to when we were not receiving. Without it the backfill either misses events or refetches everything, and neither outcome can be verified afterwards
Fetch the state and events covering the gap
Deduplicate against what was already processed, using the correlation identifiers. A duplicate arriving through backfill has to be exactly as harmless as one arriving through a webhook

nodes.asks: Does each historical event still represent a currently actionable state?

branches.label: Still actionable
branches.when: the state the event describes is still the state now

branches.label: Superseded
branches.when: current state has moved past what the event describes

nodes.does: Process it according to current-state rules rather than the rules that applied when it was emitted

Record it as history without acting on it. Backfill repairs what we know; it does not recreate every action that would have fired had the events arrived on time - a week of held onboarding messages delivered at once is exactly the failure this branch prevents, and current state takes priority over a stale historical action
Reconcile the final state against the authoritative source, rather than assuming the backfilled events add up to it. Events can be missed in ways the event stream itself cannot reveal
Verify that no known synchronization gap remains

nodes.asks: What does verification show?

branches.label: No gap
branches.when: the window is closed and local state matches the authoritative source

branches.label: Values disagree
branches.when: the gap is closed and the two systems hold different values

branches.label: Gap cannot be closed
branches.when: part of the window is unrecoverable from the provider

nodes.state: backfilled, deduplicated and reconciled; no known gap
nodes.reEntry: a further outage opens its own window

nodes.on: backfill completing with the two systems disagreeing
carries: both values with their timestamps, versions and provenance
the outage window, which is context for which side is more likely to be stale

nodes.on: a synchronization gap that cannot be closed from the provider
carries: the window that remains unrecoverable and what it may contain
the explicit fact that the integration is operational but not synchronized

guardrails: Backfill is not a replay of every historical journey trigger.
A historical event does not trigger obsolete customer communication.
Duplicate events are idempotent.
Current state takes priority over a stale historical action.
journeys.reusableRule: Backfill repairs missing history and state; it must not recreate every action that would have occurred if events had arrived in real time.

journeys.name: Synchronization conflict → determine authority → reconcile or hold
journeys.purpose: Settle a cross-system disagreement using an explicit authority rule, and hold rather than guess where none exists.

entity.scope: the synchronized entity and the specific fields in disagreement
entity.note: Authority can be per field. The billing system may own the plan while the identity system owns the email, and neither is authoritative for the other.

distinctFrom.because: CON-40 is a permission conflict and fails closed by suppressing communication. This is a general data conflict, where the safe state is holding the mutation rather than stopping outbound messaging.

requires: two or more systems holding materially different values for the same business field or state
insufficientAlone: a system that has not yet received a change still propagating within its expected window

nodes.does: Collect each system's value, its timestamp, its version, the provenance of the change and the authority rules that apply. A timestamp alone is not authority - clocks disagree, and write order is not the order decisions were made

nodes.asks: What determines authority here?

branches.label: A single authoritative system
branches.when: one system is defined as the source of truth for this entity

branches.label: Authority is per field
branches.when: different fields on this entity have different sources of truth

branches.label: Cannot be determined safely
branches.when: no rule states which value is right, and the evidence does not settle it

nodes.does: Reconcile toward the authoritative system's value, recording that the rule rather than the recency decided it

Apply the domain-specific authority rule for each field separately. Different fields have different sources of truth - the billing system owns the plan, the identity system owns the email, and applying one rule across both is right for one of them by accident
Record SYNC_CONFLICT and hold the affected mutations. Choosing a value to make the sync succeed is choosing whichever system wrote last, which is the rule this journey exists instead of

timeout.reason: held mutations mean a business process is stopped somewhere, so an unresolved conflict is escalated rather than left to sit

nodes.on: a conflict no authority rule could settle within its SLA
carries: every value with its source, version and provenance
which mutations are being held, and what that is blocking

nodes.does: Propagate the resolved state idempotently, carrying origin and version so the correction is not read as a new change by the system receiving it. Without that, two systems correct each other indefinitely and the conflict becomes traffic

nodes.state: conflict resolved by rule and propagated idempotently
nodes.reEntry: a fresh divergence on the same entity is assessed on its own, with this resolution in the record

guardrails: The newest timestamp is not automatically correct.
Propagation carries origin and version so reconciliation cannot become ping-pong between two systems.
Different fields may have different sources of truth.
Where authority cannot be determined, the mutation is held rather than guessed.
