Record READY_FOR_CHANGE. Eligible is not technically ready, and ready is not applied - what has been established is that this target may take the change, not that it can yet

nodes.on: an eligible target, prepared or with named outstanding prerequisites
carries: the target, the change version and its eligibility basis
any outstanding prerequisites by name, so preparation resolves specific blockers rather than running a generic checklist

guardrails: Available is not eligible.
Eligible is not technically ready.
Compatibility is never inferred from the generic entity type alone.
Excluded targets are named rather than absent from the count.
journeys.reusableRule: A change should reach only targets whose current state satisfies the prerequisites required for safe application.

journeys.name: Change preparation → resolve dependencies → ready or hold
journeys.purpose: Get an eligible target into a state where the change can actually be applied to it.

entity.scope: the target and the preparation the change requires of it
entity.note: What is required comes from the change and this target. A standard checklist applied to everything delays a rollout for reasons nobody can defend.

requires: a target established as eligible for an identified change

nodes.does: Identify the preparation this change actually requires for this target - a backup, resource capacity, a required configuration, a pre-download, a dependency upgrade, a maintenance window, user or administrator readiness, a required approval. What is required comes from the change and the target rather than from a standard checklist, and forcing unnecessary prerequisites stalls a rollout for reasons nobody can defend

nodes.asks: Are all critical dependencies ready?

branches.label: All ready
branches.when: everything the change requires is in place on this target

branches.label: Some outstanding
branches.when: at least one critical dependency is missing

nodes.does: Hold the target and record the named blockers. A hold with an unnamed blocker is a rollout that has stopped for a reason nobody can look up, and it stays stopped until somebody investigates by hand

until: the change becomes obsolete or is superseded

timeout.after: the schedule window this change allows for preparation
timeout.reason: a target held indefinitely against a change that has moved on is neither in the rollout nor excluded from it, and it will be counted as neither

nodes.asks: How did the wait resolve?

branches.label: Blockers cleared
branches.when: every critical dependency is now in place

branches.label: The change became obsolete
branches.when: a newer version supersedes the one this target was being prepared for

nodes.does: Record the preparation as abandoned because the change it prepared for was superseded. The target returns to eligibility evaluation for whatever the current change is, rather than proceeding with the old one

nodes.state: preparation abandoned; the change it was for no longer applies
nodes.reEntry: the current change evaluates this target's eligibility on its own terms. Preparation done for the superseded version may or may not still count, and that is the new evaluation's question

nodes.does: Record the preparation window as expired with the blockers still outstanding. The target is not failed - it was never applied to - and it stays visible as an unprepared member of the population

nodes.state: preparation window expired; target eligible and not ready
nodes.reEntry: the blockers clearing makes the target preparable again for this change or the next one

nodes.does: Record CHANGE_READY. Preparation complete is not the change applied - nothing about the target has changed yet, and this readiness will be revalidated before anything does

nodes.on: a target prepared for the change
carries: the target, the change version and the dependency state as it stands now
the explicit fact that this readiness is a snapshot, to be revalidated at the moment of execution

guardrails: Preparation complete is not the change applied.
Unnecessary prerequisites are not forced onto a target.
Current state is revalidated before execution rather than assumed from readiness.
journeys.reusableRule: Change preparation resolves the dependencies required for execution without confusing readiness with the change itself.

journeys.name: Change scheduled → wait → revalidate → execute or cancel
journeys.purpose: Check, at the moment of execution, that the change scheduled earlier is still the right one for this target.

entity.scope: the scheduled change and the target it is scheduled against
entity.note: The schedule stores assumptions. They are kept so the execution can see what has moved, never so it can proceed on them.

requires: a prepared target with a scheduled execution time or window

nodes.does: Record the target, the change version, the scheduled time or window, the expected current state and the dependency assumptions. What is stored is a set of assumptions, kept so the execution can see what has moved rather than so it can proceed on them

until: the change is cancelled for this target
a newer version supersedes this change
the target is removed or becomes ineligible

timeout.reason: reaching the window is what the wait exists for. It is the normal outcome and the point at which every assumption is checked again

nodes.asks: What happened before the window?

branches.label: Cancelled, removed or made ineligible
branches.when: the target should no longer receive this change

branches.label: Superseded
branches.when: a newer version of the change now exists

nodes.does: Record the schedule cancelled and stand down the job. A cancelled target revived by a stale change job receives a change nobody authorized, and on a device fleet that is discovered by the devices

nodes.state: scheduled change cancelled; the target is untouched
nodes.reEntry: the target re-entering eligibility for this or a later change is a new evaluation rather than a revival of this schedule

nodes.does: Stand down this schedule because a newer version exists. Applying the old one after the new one is available installs a regression on purpose, and the job that did it reports success

nodes.state: schedule stood down; a newer change version applies to this target
nodes.reEntry: the current version evaluates this target's eligibility and schedules on its own terms

nodes.does: At the execution moment, revalidate the target's eligibility, its version and state, its dependencies, whether the change is still current, any required approval, and whether an incident or change hold is in force. What is checked is now - the stored assumptions are used only to see what moved

nodes.asks: Is the change still valid for this target?

branches.label: Still valid
branches.when: every assumption the schedule made still holds

branches.label: No longer valid
branches.when: eligibility, state, dependencies, currency or authorization has moved

nodes.does: Suppress the stale change, naming exactly what changed since it was scheduled. A scheduled change is an intention rather than a guarantee, and executing on assumptions that have expired is how a target under an incident hold receives a deployment

nodes.state: stale scheduled change suppressed; the target is untouched
nodes.reEntry: the target is re-evaluated for the current change against its current state, which is a fresh eligibility question

nodes.on: a scheduled change revalidated at its execution moment
carries: the target, the change version and the state it was revalidated against
the explicit fact that nothing has been applied - the revalidation authorizes the attempt rather than performing it

guardrails: Scheduled is not guaranteed execution.
A superseded version invalidates the old schedule.
A cancelled target is never revived by a stale change job.
journeys.reusableRule: Scheduled changes are execution intentions whose assumptions must be revalidated at the moment the change is applied.

journeys.name: Change execution → apply → verify, fail or unknown
journeys.purpose: Establish that the target actually ended up in the state the change intended, rather than that a command was accepted.

entity.scope: the change execution against one target
entity.note: The operation carries a stable identity, so a retry re-applies the same change rather than a second one.

distinctFrom.because: RLT-243 decides whether to proceed. This performs the change and establishes what state the target actually reached, which is where the accepted-applied-verified distinction lives.

requires: a revalidated target authorized to receive an identified change version

nodes.does: Record APPLYING with the change version and a stable operation identity for this target, so a retry re-applies the same change rather than performing a second one. Retries are normal here, and a second application is how a target ends up double-migrated
Execute the change idempotently against the target, through the canonical async and reliability primitives rather than a bespoke retry loop

until: the target reports the change applied
the target reports an authoritative failure

timeout.after: the execution timeout for this change and target class
timeout.reason: a target that reports nothing is unknown rather than failed, and the difference decides whether retrying is safe

nodes.does: Record CHANGE_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN and hold any retry. A timeout is not a failure - the change may well have applied, and retrying blindly applies it twice, which for firmware and schema changes is not idempotent in practice however idempotent the command is

nodes.on: a change whose outcome could not be established
carries: the target, the change version, the operation identity and everything last known
the explicit instruction that no retry is attempted until the target's actual state is established
suppresses: any retry of this change against this target while its outcome is unknown

nodes.asks: What did the target report?

branches.label: Applied
branches.when: the target accepted and completed the change

branches.label: Confirmed failure
branches.when: the target authoritatively rejected or failed the change

nodes.does: Record CHANGE_FAILED with exactly what the target reported. The target is on its previous version and functioning - a failed application is not a broken target

nodes.on: a change that failed or left the target in an unintended state
carries: the target, what it reported and the state it is actually in
the explicit fact that this is one target's outcome - whether it is systemic is a separate question with separate evidence

nodes.does: Record VERIFYING. The command being accepted is not the change being applied, and the change being applied is not the target being in the intended state - three states, and the middle one is where most deployment tooling stops looking

Verify the target actually reached the intended new state - the version it now reports, the configuration it now holds, the behaviour it now exhibits. What is checked is the target's state rather than the command's return code

nodes.asks: Is the target in the intended state?

branches.label: Verified
branches.when: the target reports the intended version, configuration and behaviour

branches.label: Applied, but not in the intended state
branches.when: the change went through and the target is somewhere else

branches.label: Cannot be verified
branches.when: the verification could not run against this target

nodes.does: Record that the change applied and the target is not where it should be. This is worse than a clean failure, because the target is now in a state nobody designed and nothing reports it as broken
Record that verification could not run. Unverifiable is not verified, and counting it as success is how a rollout reports a population it has never actually observed

Record CHANGE_APPLIED_VERIFIED with the state the target now reports. Applied and verified is still not healthy - whether the population running this change is well is a rollout-level question observed over time

nodes.state: CHANGE_APPLIED_VERIFIED; the target is in the intended state
nodes.reEntry: the target's health under the change is observed at rollout scope. A later regression on this target is a health signal rather than an execution failure

guardrails: A command accepted is not a change applied.
Applied is not healthy.
A timeout is not a failure.
A retry never applies the same change twice.
journeys.reusableRule: A change is complete only after the target's intended new state has been authoritatively verified.

journeys.name: Staged rollout → pilot cohort → health gate → expand or hold
journeys.purpose: Widen a change only when the targets that already took it show it is safe to widen.

entity.scope: the rollout, its target population and the cohorts it progresses through
entity.note: The cohort list is finite and explicit. Progression is bounded by it, and each step through it needs its own evidence.

distinctFrom.because: This is population progression - whether the next cohort may begin. RLT-249 is one target that could not take the change while the rollout is otherwise fine. Merging them turns every unreachable device into a reason to stop, or every real regression into a target exception.

requires: a change approved for progressive application to a defined population

nodes.asks: Are the cohort rules explicit?

branches.label: Explicit
branches.when: the cohorts, their order and the gate each must pass are defined

branches.label: Not explicit
branches.when: who is in which cohort, or what a gate requires, is not written down

nodes.on: a staged rollout with implicit cohort or gate rules
carries: the change, the population and what is and is not defined about progression
the explicit fact that implicit cohorts mean nobody can say who is next or why, and an implicit gate is a judgment made under pressure by whoever is watching

nodes.does: Define the cohorts and the rollout order according to policy, and the health gate each cohort must pass before the next begins. The gate is written before the first cohort deploys, because a gate written afterwards is written knowing the result
Deploy the current cohort. Progression is bounded by the finite cohort list - each pass through this step consumes one, so the rollout terminates rather than cycling

until: sufficient health evidence accumulates for this cohort
a critical regression appears in the changed population

timeout.after: the maximum observation window for this cohort
timeout.reason: the window bounds how long a cohort may be watched, and reaching it raises the real question - whether enough was actually observed rather than merely enough time

nodes.asks: Was there enough evidence by the end of the window?

branches.label: Enough
branches.when: the changed cohort produced the volume and variety of activity the gate needs to judge

branches.label: Not enough
branches.when: the cohort was quiet, or the relevant paths never ran

nodes.does: Record HOLD. Elapsed time is not evidence - a cohort that produced no traffic produced no information, and expanding because nothing alerted is expanding on the absence of a signal rather than the presence of one

nodes.state: HOLD; the cohort did not produce enough evidence to judge the gate
nodes.reEntry: evidence accumulating, or the gate being redefined for a low-traffic population, resumes progression. Nothing was reverted and nothing expanded

nodes.asks: Does the health gate pass for this cohort?

branches.label: It passes
branches.when: failure rate, regressions, performance and business outcome are all within the gate

branches.label: It fails
branches.when: the changed population shows a problem the gate is there to catch

nodes.on: a health gate failing for a deployed cohort
carries: which gate dimension failed, on what evidence, and across which cohort
the changed and unchanged populations as they currently stand

nodes.asks: Are there cohorts left?

branches.label: More remain
branches.when: the cohort list has entries that have not deployed

branches.label: None
branches.when: every cohort in the list has deployed and passed its gate

nodes.does: Record the planned population as having reached the intended changed state, with the exception population named alongside it

nodes.on: a rollout reaching its planned population
carries: the changed population, the exception targets and the gates each cohort passed
the explicit fact that reaching the population is not stability - the regressions that matter tend to surface later

guardrails: Elapsed time alone is not sufficient rollout evidence.
A rollout never expands merely because no alert fired.
Cohort rules and health gates are explicit and written before deployment.
journeys.reusableRule: A staged rollout expands only when previously changed targets provide sufficient evidence that the change is safe to broaden.

journeys.name: Rollout pause → freeze expansion → diagnose → resume, roll back or end
journeys.purpose: Stop the change spreading while the question of what to do about it is still open.

entity.scope: the rollout, and the changed and unchanged populations at the moment it paused
entity.note: Both populations are preserved exactly. A pause that loses track of who has the change can neither resume nor roll back.

requires: a pause threshold reached, or an authorized pause of an active rollout

nodes.does: Record PAUSED and stop new cohort expansion. Paused is not failed - the targets already changed are still running, most of them fine, and treating a pause as a failure reverts a population that had no problem at all

Preserve the current changed and unchanged populations exactly as they are, and record which is which. A pause that loses track of who has the change can neither resume from where it stopped nor roll back what it applied

Diagnose the issue against the changed population rather than against the change in the abstract. What matters is whether the targets holding this change are safe, which is a different question from whether the change is good

nodes.asks: What does the diagnosis support?

branches.label: Resolved without rollback
branches.when: the cause was external, transient or fixed forward, and the changed targets are fine

branches.label: The already-changed targets are unsafe
branches.when: the population holding the change is at risk where it stands

branches.label: The rollout is abandoned
branches.when: the change will not proceed, whether or not what is applied stays

nodes.does: Revalidate health against current state before resuming. The population has moved during the pause, and resuming on the health reading that preceded it expands on evidence that is now old

nodes.asks: Is the changed population healthy now?

branches.label: Healthy
branches.when: current evidence clears the gate the pause was raised against

branches.label: Still not healthy
branches.when: the problem persists in the current population

nodes.on: a pause resolved with the changed population healthy
carries: the current health evidence and the cohort the rollout stopped at
the explicit fact that progression resumes from the preserved position rather than restarting

nodes.on: a paused rollout whose changed population is unsafe
carries: the affected scope, the failure evidence and the changed population as preserved
the explicit fact that a rollback decision has not been made - whether reverting is the right recovery is the next question

nodes.does: Terminate future expansion and preserve the already-applied state according to policy. Abandoning a rollout is not reverting it - a population that took the change successfully may well stay on it, and forcing everyone back costs more than the change did

nodes.state: rollout abandoned; the changed population preserved as policy defines
nodes.reEntry: the population is now split across versions deliberately, and that split is visible. A later change evaluates each target's eligibility from where it actually is

guardrails: Paused is not failed.
A pause never automatically reverts healthy targets.
Resumption requires current-state revalidation rather than the reading that preceded the pause.
journeys.reusableRule: Rollout pause freezes future expansion while leaving room to determine whether the valid next step is resume, remediation or rollback.

journeys.name: Change failure threshold → rollback decision → execute or forward recover
journeys.purpose: Decide whether going back is actually safer than going on, before anyone starts going back.

entity.scope: the failing rollout or change and the targets it affects
entity.note: Rollback is one strategy among several. Whether it is available at all depends on what the change has already made irreversible.

distinctFrom.because: This chooses the recovery. RLT-248 performs a rollback and verifies it. Choosing wrong here is irreversible in the other direction - a rollback across a migrated schema cannot be undone by rolling forward again.

requires: a defined failure threshold reached across the changed population
insufficientAlone: a single target failing, which is a target-scope problem until the evidence says otherwise

nodes.does: Stop further rollout where the threshold requires it, before deciding anything about what is already applied
Determine the known-good prior state, the rollback capability, the irreversible side effects, the data and schema compatibility, the forward-recovery option and the affected scope

nodes.asks: Has the change crossed an irreversible boundary?

branches.label: It has not
branches.when: the previous state is genuinely reachable from where the targets are

branches.label: It has
branches.when: a schema migration, a data transformation or an external commitment has made the previous state unreachable

nodes.does: Record that rollback is not available, naming the boundary that was crossed. Rolling back across an irreversible boundary produces old code running against new data, which fails differently and worse - and the second failure is harder to diagnose because it looks like the first one returning

nodes.asks: Is rollback safe and supported for the affected scope?

branches.label: Safe for everything affected
branches.when: the whole affected population can return to the known-good state

branches.label: Safe for a subset only
branches.when: part of the affected scope can revert and part cannot, or the failure is confined

branches.label: Not safe or not possible
branches.when: reverting would break dependencies, data or commitments

nodes.does: Scope the rollback to the affected subset where scoped rollback is supported. Reverting a whole population for a failure confined to one cohort takes a working change away from everybody who had no problem, and each of those reverts can fail on its own

nodes.on: a rollback chosen as the safer recovery
carries: the known-good state, the exact scope to revert and the boundary the rollback must not cross
the explicit fact that the rollback must be verified - a successful command is not a restored system

nodes.on: a failure where rolling back is unsafe, impossible or worse than going on
carries: the failure, the affected scope and the boundary that makes rollback unavailable
the explicit fact that the failed change stays in place and its history is preserved, so forward remediation works from a known position

guardrails: Failure does not automatically imply rollback.
A rollback is never taken across an irreversible boundary blindly.
Rollback policy accounts for changed data, schema and state.
journeys.reusableRule: Rollback is one recovery strategy and should be chosen only when returning to the previous state is safer and technically valid.

journeys.name: Rollback execution → restore → verify stability
journeys.purpose: Return the affected targets to a known-good state and prove that they actually work there.

entity.scope: the rollback operation and the targets it is reverting
entity.note: The failed change stays in the record throughout. A rollback restores state and does not erase that the change happened.

requires: an authorized rollback with a known-good state and a defined scope

nodes.does: Apply the known-good state or version to the targets in scope, with stable operation identity so a retried rollback reverts once rather than twice

until: the targets report the rollback applied
the rollback reports an authoritative failure

timeout.reason: a rollback whose outcome is unknown leaves a population that may be on either version, and every subsequent decision depends on knowing which

nodes.does: Record the rollback outcome as unknown and hold further action. A population split across two versions with nobody able to say which is where is worse than either version alone

nodes.on: a rollback whose outcome could not be established
carries: the scope, the known-good state and what each target last reported
the explicit instruction that nothing further is applied until the population's actual version distribution is known

nodes.asks: Did the rollback apply?

branches.label: Applied
branches.when: the targets in scope report the known-good state

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the rollback itself did not complete

nodes.does: Record the rollback as failed, with the population left where it is. A failed rollback is a worse position than the failure that prompted it, and it needs a person rather than another automated attempt

Verify the target state, the service or functionality, dependency compatibility, the critical health metrics, and any artifacts the change left behind that the rollback did not remove. A rollback command succeeding says the old version is installed and nothing about whether the system works - and rollbacks fail on exactly the dependency and data-shape problems that made them necessary

nodes.asks: Is the rolled-back population stable?

branches.label: Stable
branches.when: the targets are on the known-good state and functioning

branches.label: Partially rolled back
branches.when: some targets reverted and some did not

branches.label: The previous state is no longer fully recoverable
branches.when: data, commitments or side effects created under the change cannot coexist with the old version

nodes.does: Record which targets reverted and which did not. A partially rolled-back population is a split fleet, and it needs to be visible as one rather than reported as a rollback that completed

Record that some part of the prior state cannot be restored - data created under the new version, external commitments made, irreversible side effects. Restoring the old version over legitimate new data destroys it, and that is a larger loss than the failure being recovered from

nodes.on: a rollback that cannot fully restore the prior state
carries: what was restored, what cannot be, and the legitimate data or commitments that must not be overwritten
the explicit fact that forward remediation is now the path and the failed change remains in the history

nodes.on: a rollback that failed or completed only in part
carries: the exact version distribution across the affected population
the explicit fact that no further automated attempt is being made against a population in an unknown or split state

nodes.does: Record ROLLED_BACK_VERIFIED, preserving the failed change in the history. Rollback complete is not the deployment never having happened - the change ran, it affected things, and its record is what explains everything anybody noticed while it was live

nodes.state: ROLLED_BACK_VERIFIED; population restored and the failed change preserved as history
nodes.reEntry: a corrected change is a new rollout with its own eligibility, and this failure is part of what its gates are set against

guardrails: Rollback complete is not the original deployment never having occurred.
The failed change's history is preserved.
Restoring an old version never overwrites legitimate irreversible data created after the change.
A rollback is verified rather than assumed from a successful command.
journeys.reusableRule: Rollback restores current operational state while preserving the failed change as historical truth and requiring post-rollback verification.

journeys.name: Individual target change failure → retry, isolate or remediate
journeys.purpose: Recover one target that could not take the change, and notice when it stops being one target.

entity.scope: the individual target and its failed change attempt
entity.note: Target scope by default. Promotion to rollout scope happens on evidence of a pattern rather than on the count of failures.

distinctFrom.because: RLT-245 governs whether the population progresses. This governs one target that fell out of it. One unreachable device is not a broken release, and treating it as one stops a rollout that was working.

requires: a specific target failing to take the change, or ending in an unintended state

nodes.does: Diagnose the target-specific cause - compatibility, being offline or unreachable, local configuration, a resource shortage, corrupt state, a dependency mismatch. What is being established is whether this target is unusual or whether the change is

nodes.asks: Does this failure match a pattern across other targets?

branches.label: It matches a pattern
branches.when: the same signature, cause or class appears across targets that should have differed

branches.label: It looks target-specific
branches.when: the cause is local to this target's state or environment

nodes.does: Promote it from a target problem to a rollout problem. A failure signature appearing on forty targets is not forty individual problems, and handling them one at a time means nobody ever sees the shape of it

nodes.on: a target failure whose pattern makes it systemic
carries: the shared failure signature and the targets exhibiting it
the explicit fact that this reached rollout scope through evidence of a pattern rather than through a count of failures

nodes.asks: Is a retry safe and likely to help?

branches.label: It is
branches.when: the cause was transient - unreachable, momentarily short of resource, a temporary lock

branches.label: It is not
branches.when: the cause is structural to this target and retrying will reproduce it

nodes.does: Retry against this target only, within a bounded budget and using the same operation identity so a change that actually applied is not applied twice

nodes.asks: Does retry budget remain?

branches.label: Budget remains
branches.when: this target has attempts left

branches.label: Exhausted
branches.when: the attempts this target allows have been used

nodes.state: retrying against this target only; the rollout is unaffected
nodes.reEntry: each attempt reports its own outcome and returns here with the budget one lower. Retrying is bounded rather than continuous

nodes.asks: Can this target safely remain on the previous version?

branches.label: It can
branches.when: the previous version is supported, secure and compatible for this target

branches.label: It cannot
branches.when: staying behind leaves the target unsupported, insecure or incompatible

nodes.does: Record TARGET_EXCEPTION. The exception population stays explicitly visible - a rollout reporting complete while quietly leaving targets behind produces a version distribution nobody can account for, and the forgotten targets are the ones that break in six months with nobody remembering why they are different

nodes.state: TARGET_EXCEPTION; on the previous version, visible and countable
nodes.reEntry: the blocking cause clearing makes the target eligible again, and it is picked up by this change or the next one rather than staying behind permanently

nodes.does: Record that this target cannot stay behind and cannot proceed unattended, with what is blocking it. Leaving it as an exception when it cannot safely be one is how a target ends up unsupported without anybody deciding that it should be

nodes.on: a target that must take the change and cannot
carries: the target, its diagnosis and why remaining on the previous version is not acceptable
the explicit fact that automated attempts are exhausted and the rollout itself is unaffected

guardrails: One target failure is not a rollout failure.
Retries are bounded rather than indefinite.
The exception population remains observable and countable.
Promotion to systemic happens on pattern evidence rather than on failure count.
journeys.reusableRule: Individual change failures should be recovered at target scope until evidence shows that the problem is systemic.

journeys.name: Change completed → observe → close, reopen or deprecate previous version
journeys.purpose: Wait long enough to know the change held, and keep what a recovery would need until it clearly does not.

entity.scope: the completed rollout, the changed population and the exception targets
entity.note: Completion and stability are different claims. The previous version stays available until both the recovery and the audit requirements are satisfied.

requires: the planned target population having reached the intended changed state
insufficientAlone: a rollout dashboard reporting complete, which reports coverage rather than health

nodes.asks: Does this change require post-change observation?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: the change touches behaviour, data or paths whose problems surface over time

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: the change is fully exercised at application and nothing further can emerge

nodes.does: Record the change as applied and under observation. Deployment completion is not long-term stability - the regressions that matter most surface on a weekly cycle, at month-end, or the first time a rare path runs, all of them after the rollout dashboard turned green

until: a regression appears in the changed population

timeout.reason: the window is the point of the wait - reaching it without a material regression is what makes the change stable rather than merely deployed

nodes.asks: Is the regression material?

branches.label: Material
branches.when: it affects correctness, availability or a business outcome the gate was protecting

branches.label: Not material
branches.when: it is noise, or a known issue already accounted for

nodes.on: a late material regression in a completed change
carries: the regression, when it appeared and across which part of the changed population
the explicit fact that the rollout is complete, so pausing expansion is not the remedy - the question is what to do with a population that already has it

nodes.does: Record CHANGE_STABLE, and record the exception population explicitly alongside it. A change reported stable while its exceptions are invisible produces a version distribution nobody can account for, and every later change inherits that ambiguity

nodes.asks: Can the previous version now be deprecated?

branches.label: It can
branches.when: no target remains on it, and the recovery and audit retention it was held for is satisfied

branches.label: Not yet
branches.when: recovery or audit still depends on it, or exception targets are still running it

nodes.does: Retain the previous version and the state a recovery would need, with the condition that would release it. Deleting it because the rollout completed removes the only thing a late rollback could restore from, and late is exactly when rollbacks are actually needed

nodes.state: CHANGE_STABLE; previous version retained and exception targets named
nodes.reEntry: the retention condition being satisfied allows the previous version to be retired on its own terms. A later regression reopens recovery against a population that still has somewhere to go back to

nodes.on: a previous version nothing depends on any longer
carries: the version, the confirmation that no target runs it and that retention is satisfied
the change lineage, which stays auditable regardless of whether the artifact is retired

guardrails: Deployment completion is not long-term stability.
A previous version or state required for recovery or audit is not deleted immediately.
Exception targets remain explicit in the completion record.
journeys.reusableRule: Change lifecycle closes only after the applied population demonstrates sufficient stability and remaining version dependencies are resolved.

journeys.name: Upgrade blocked by a resolvable prerequisite → prompt → ready or expired
journeys.purpose: Tell the holder of a blocked target the one specific thing standing between it and the change, while there is still enough of the preparation window left for them to clear it.

entity.scope: the target, the change waiting on it, and the named prerequisite that is blocking it
entity.note: One target, one blocker, one change. A second blocker on the same target is named in the same prompt or not at all - two prompts about one target read as two problems.

distinctFrom.because: RLT-242 works out what preparation this change requires and records the blockers that hold the target. This journey is what the holder is told about a blocker, and it sends nothing until that hold exists with a named cause.
RLT-241 decides whether the target is in scope for the change at all. Here scope is already settled and the only open question is a prerequisite.

journeys.objective: Tell the holder of a blocked target the one specific thing standing between it and the change, while there is still enough of the preparation window left for them to clear it.
eligibility: a target authoritatively held for a planned change
the specific prerequisite that is blocking it, named rather than described
a preparation window with time still in it
no instance of this journey is already open for the the target
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: The prompt names the specific blocker. A notice that an update is available, sent to somebody who cannot take it, is the failure this journey exists to stop.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Nothing is asked of a holder who cannot clear the prerequisite.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Two prompts at most, and both name the same blocker and the same date.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Not ready is not failed. A target that was never touched is recorded as unprepared, not as a failed change.

value.rule: Every touch runs against a budget fixed when the instance opened; the budget is the plan's own length, and no touch is repeated because nothing could tell whether it arrived.

default.applicableWhen: the corpus rule: two prompts at most, both naming the same blocker

cooldown.rule: This journey is per the target; a later instance concerns a different the target and no cooldown applies between them.

default.applicableWhen: the entity note: one instance per entity

roles.when: the person is active in the product and the action is taken there
the message has to be kept and survive until the person can act on it

touches.purpose: Say that the change is held and why, with nothing asked of the holder - because there is nothing they can do.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Name the one prerequisite, what clearing it involves, and the date after which the change can no longer be applied in this window.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

touches.purpose: Send one further prompt naming the same prerequisite and the date it stops mattering.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

guardrails: complaint
message_after_success
unsubscribe

useCases: the one prerequisite standing between a target and a planned change, named while there is time
a hold the holder cannot clear, stated with nothing asked

requires: a target authoritatively held for a planned change
the specific prerequisite that is blocking it, named rather than described
a preparation window with time still in it
insufficientAlone: a change that is available but not yet scoped to this target
a hold whose cause has not been identified

nodes.asks: Can the holder clear this blocker themselves?

branches.label: Theirs to clear
branches.when: the prerequisite is something the holder controls - capacity to free, a version to move off, a dependency to accept, a confirmation to give

branches.label: Not theirs
branches.when: the prerequisite depends on a supplier, an internal approval, or a fixed period elapsing

nodes.does: Say that the change is held and why, with nothing asked of the holder - because there is nothing they can do. A prompt to act where acting is impossible reads as blame and produces a support contact instead of a cleared blocker

nodes.state: held on a blocker the holder cannot clear
nodes.reEntry: if the blocker later becomes theirs to clear, the target qualifies again on the resolvable path

nodes.does: Name the one prerequisite, what clearing it involves, and the date after which the change can no longer be applied in this window. A generic notice that something is available leaves the holder to discover the blocker themselves, which is the whole reason the target is stuck

after.rule: The point in the preparation window past which a target still blocked cannot be made ready in time.

timeout.reason: a prompt that arrives with no time left to act on it is worse than no prompt - it names a deadline that has already gone

nodes.recheck: the the target re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.asks: What ended the wait?

branches.label: Blocker cleared
branches.when: the prerequisite is authoritatively satisfied on the target

branches.label: Change withdrawn
branches.when: the change was superseded or withdrawn before the prerequisite cleared

nodes.on: a named prerequisite cleared by the holder inside the preparation window
carries: which blocker cleared and when
what the holder was told, so readiness is not announced to them twice

nodes.state: change withdrawn before the blocker was cleared
nodes.reEntry: the next change with the same prerequisite scopes this target again

nodes.asks: Is a second prompt still worth sending?

branches.label: Time remains
branches.when: the preparation window has a period left in which clearing the blocker would still make the target ready

branches.label: Window closed
branches.when: no remaining action could make the target ready in this window

nodes.does: Send one further prompt naming the same prerequisite and the date it stops mattering. There is no third - a blocker nobody has cleared twice is a decision, not an oversight

after.rule: After the last call the instance waits until the preparation window itself closes; there is no third prompt.

timeout.reason: the window is what separates a target that is not ready from one that has failed, and the two must not be recorded together

nodes.recheck: the the target re-read from the system of record before acting on the timeout

nodes.state: preparation window closed with the blocker outstanding
nodes.reEntry: the target stays an unprepared member of the population and is prompted again by the next change that needs the same prerequisite

guardrails: The prompt names the specific blocker. A notice that an update is available, sent to somebody who cannot take it, is the failure this journey exists to stop.
Nothing is asked of a holder who cannot clear the prerequisite.
Two prompts at most, and both name the same blocker and the same date.
Not ready is not failed. A target that was never touched is recorded as unprepared, not as a failed change.
journeys.reusableRule: A blocked change is worth telling somebody about only when the blocker is theirs to clear and the window is still open enough for clearing it to matter.

journeys.name: Correlated failure detection → incident candidate → confirm or reject
journeys.purpose: Establish whether several failures actually share a cause, before treating them as one thing.

entity.scope: the incident candidate and every individual failure correlated into it
entity.note: Each affected entity keeps its own case and its own link. The incident is a layer above them rather than a replacement for them.

distinctFrom.because: RSK-192 assesses risk evidence about one actor or transaction. This asks whether failures across many unrelated entities plausibly share an operational cause - a question about the system rather than about anybody using it.

requires: multiple failures or anomalies across entities, exceeding a meaningful correlation threshold
insufficientAlone: a spike in alert volume, which is a count rather than a correlation
several failures happening at once, which is often several failures happening at once

nodes.does: Correlate by time, service or dependency, region, version, provider, resource cohort, failure signature and shared infrastructure. What is being tested is whether these failures plausibly share a cause, rather than whether there are a lot of them

Preserve the link from the candidate to each individual affected entity, and keep each entity's own case open. A correlation that absorbs its members leaves every affected customer without a case of their own, and when the incident closes they have nothing left to point at

nodes.asks: What does the correlating evidence support?

branches.label: A shared cause
branches.when: the failures share a dependency, cohort, signature or infrastructure in a way that explains them together

branches.label: Independent failures
branches.when: the correlation is coincidental and each failure has its own explanation

branches.label: Insufficient evidence
branches.when: a shared cause is plausible and unestablished

nodes.does: Retain the individual cases as independent, and record why they were not merged. Several failures at once is often several failures at once - merging them for operational convenience gives each customer a generic status page instead of an answer to their specific problem

nodes.state: no incident; the individual cases continue independently
nodes.reEntry: further correlated evidence reopens the question. Not merging now does not prevent an incident being confirmed later on better evidence

nodes.does: Record INCIDENT_CANDIDATE and investigate. Candidate is a real state - it starts a look without asserting a shared cause to anybody, and it is what stops a hunch from becoming a status-page announcement

until: evidence rules a shared cause out

timeout.reason: a candidate held open indefinitely is neither an incident anybody is responding to nor a set of cases anybody is working, and both populations wait

nodes.does: Record INCIDENT_CONFIRMED with the correlating evidence that supports it. What is asserted is a shared cause - not that it is known, but that these failures belong together

nodes.on: an incident confirmed on correlating evidence
carries: the correlating evidence and every individual affected entity, still linked and still holding its own case
the explicit fact that a shared cause is asserted and not yet known

guardrails: Multiple failures are not automatically one incident.
Unrelated customer cases are never merged for operational convenience.
Correlation preserves the linkage to each individual affected entity.
journeys.reusableRule: An incident should be created only when evidence shows multiple failures plausibly share a common operational cause.

journeys.name: Incident confirmed → determine severity and blast radius → assign command
journeys.purpose: Establish what is actually affected, how badly, and who is running the response.

entity.scope: the confirmed incident, its blast radius and its operational ownership
entity.note: The incident owner runs the systemic response. The owners of the individual cases keep owing their customers an answer, and neither absorbs the other.

requires: a confirmed incident with its correlating evidence and affected entities
insufficientAlone: an alert that has fired and not been confirmed as an incident
a single failed request with no impact established

nodes.does: Determine the affected systems, capabilities, regions, customers and accounts, dependencies, the start time, the current impact and the business criticality

Set the severity from the actual operational impact. A high event count is not a severity - a retry storm generates a hundred thousand events and affects nobody, and a single failing payment path generates twelve and affects everything downstream of it

Assign incident ownership and command according to the operating model, and record it separately from the owners of the individual cases. The incident owner runs the systemic response; the case owners still owe their customers an answer, and one absorbing the other means whichever survives stops doing the other job
Record ACTIVE_INCIDENT with the scope, the severity and the command as established

nodes.asks: Has the affected scope grown since the incident was confirmed?

branches.label: It has
branches.when: a new cohort, region, dependency or capability is found affected

branches.label: It has not
branches.when: the blast radius as established still holds

nodes.does: Expand the blast radius and re-derive the severity from it. A blast radius fixed at confirmation time understates every incident that spreads, which is most of them - and the response level set against the original scope is then wrong for the whole rest of the incident

nodes.asks: What does the response need first?

branches.label: Immediate containment
branches.when: the impact is ongoing and reducing it does not have to wait for a cause

branches.label: Investigation first
branches.when: the impact is bounded or already stopped, and acting without understanding risks making it worse

branches.label: The impact resolved before the response began
branches.when: the condition passed on its own before anything was done

nodes.on: an active incident needing immediate impact reduction
carries: the blast radius, the severity and the capabilities currently affected
the incident ownership, and the separate case ownerships that continue alongside it

nodes.on: an active incident where understanding comes before acting
carries: the correlating evidence, the timeline and the affected cohort
the explicit fact that no mitigation has been applied, so the system is in its failed state rather than a modified one

nodes.does: Record that the impact ended before the response engaged, preserving the incident and its evidence. A self-resolving incident is still an incident that happened, and it is usually the first occurrence of something that will recur

nodes.state: impact ended before response; the incident and its evidence are preserved
nodes.reEntry: recurrence is assessed against this record. An incident that resolved itself once and returns is a pattern rather than two coincidences

guardrails: Severity reflects actual impact rather than event volume.
A high event count is not a severity.
The incident owner and the individual case owners remain separate.
Blast radius is re-derived as scope grows rather than fixed at confirmation.
journeys.reusableRule: Incident response begins by establishing the affected scope, severity and accountable operational ownership.

journeys.name: Incident → contain and mitigate → preserve critical operations
journeys.purpose: Reduce the damage now, without pretending the cause has been dealt with.

entity.scope: the incident and the mitigations applied against its impact
entity.note: Each mitigation is recorded as temporary with the condition that would remove it. Nothing here touches the cause.

distinctFrom.because: Mitigation reduces impact while the cause remains. INC-256 acts on the cause and asks whether the service actually came back. A system can be fully mitigated and entirely unfixed, and reporting the first as the second stops the second happening.

requires: an active incident with ongoing impact that could be reduced

nodes.does: Identify the mitigations actually available - disabling a failing feature, shifting traffic, increasing capacity, moving to an alternate provider, rate limiting, a manual fallback, a degraded mode, pausing unsafe operations. Each rejected option is struck from the list, so the search through them terminates

nodes.asks: Is the candidate mitigation safe to apply?

branches.label: Safe
branches.when: its secondary effects are understood and acceptable

branches.label: Unacceptable secondary risk
branches.when: applying it could produce a larger failure than the one it addresses

branches.label: No safe option remains
branches.when: every candidate has been considered and rejected

nodes.does: Reject this option, strike it from the list and consider the next. A workaround that creates a larger failure than the one it addresses is the most expensive kind of response, and it is usually applied under pressure with nobody checking what else it touches

Record that no safe mitigation is available, and say so rather than applying an unsafe one. An incident with no safe containment goes straight to recovery with its full impact visible, which is honest and is what the response should be working from

Apply the mitigation, scoped to what it actually needs to touch, and record it as temporary with the condition that would remove it. A workaround with no stated end becomes permanent by nobody's decision, and is found years later by somebody wondering why a feature is disabled

Record MITIGATED and explicitly not RESOLVED. The impact is smaller and the cause is untouched - reporting mitigation as resolution stops the investigation that would have found the cause, and the incident returns

nodes.asks: Does the mitigation materially change what affected users should do?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: a workaround is now available, or a capability is now degraded rather than absent

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: the user-visible position is unchanged

nodes.on: a mitigation that changes user guidance
carries: what is now available, what is still affected, and any safe workaround
the explicit fact that the state is mitigated rather than resolved, so the message does not claim a fix

nodes.asks: Does the mitigation reduce impact enough to stand down the emergency?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: the remaining impact is tolerable while the cause is investigated on a normal footing

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: impact remains severe and the cause has to be acted on now

nodes.state: MITIGATED; impact contained, cause untouched, incident still open
nodes.reEntry: the mitigation failing, or the impact growing past it, brings the incident back here. The mitigation stays recorded as temporary and its removal condition stays stated

nodes.on: an incident whose impact cannot be adequately contained
carries: the mitigations attempted, what each achieved and what remains affected
the explicit fact that containment is insufficient, so the corrective action is now the only path to reducing impact

guardrails: Mitigated is not resolved.
A workaround never creates a larger failure than the one it addresses.
A temporary workaround remains explicitly temporary, with the condition that would remove it.
journeys.reusableRule: Incident mitigation reduces current impact while preserving the distinction between temporary containment and permanent resolution.

journeys.name: Incident communication → identify affected cohort → inform, update or close
journeys.purpose: Tell the people actually affected something true and useful, through the mechanism that already owns delivery.

entity.scope: the incident, the affected recipient cohort and the communication obligation it creates
entity.note: This decides what should be said and to whom. Channels, permissions, delivery and retries belong to the communication lifecycle.

journeys.objective: Tell the people actually affected something true and useful, through the mechanism that already owns delivery.
eligibility: an incident state change that could change what an affected party should do or expect
no instance of this journey is already open for the the incident
hard gates (GLB-31) allow communication for this purpose

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: No root cause or resolution is claimed before it is confirmed.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: No promotional content appears in incident communication.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: Uncertain technical detail is never communicated as fact.

suppressions.label: CANONICAL_RULE
suppressions.text: The affected cohort is identified as precisely as the evidence allows.

value.rule: Every touch runs against a budget fixed when the instance opened; the budget is the plan's own length, and no touch is repeated because nothing could tell whether it arrived.

default.applicableWhen: GLB-24; the graph's own touch count

cooldown.rule: This journey is per the incident; a later instance concerns a different the incident and no cooldown applies between them.

default.applicableWhen: the entity note: one instance per entity

roles.when: the message has to be kept and survive until the person can act on it
the person is active in the product and the action is taken there

touches.purpose: Raise the communication through the canonical communication mechanism, which owns the obligation, the recipient resolution, the channels, the permissions and the delivery evidence.
touches.label: CANONICAL_RULE

guardrails: complaint
message_after_success
unsubscribe

useCases: the people actually affected told something true and useful when the incident state changes
no update sent when nothing material changed

requires: an incident state change that could change what an affected party should do or expect
insufficientAlone: time having passed since the last update, which is not itself information

nodes.does: Determine who is materially affected, what is known, what is not known, what action the user needs to take, any safe workaround, and the condition under which the next meaningful update would happen. Saying what is not yet known is information; leaving it out and stating the rest as certainty is not

nodes.asks: Can the affected cohort be identified with reasonable precision?

branches.label: It can
branches.when: the affected population is identifiable by account, region, capability or cohort

branches.label: It cannot yet
branches.when: the boundary of the impact is genuinely unclear

nodes.does: Scope the communication to the affected population. Telling everybody about an incident affecting one region trains the whole base to ignore incident notices, and the next one will be one that matters to them

Broaden only as far as necessary, and say explicitly that the scope is still being established. Uncertainty stated is information; uncertainty implied as precision is a claim that will have to be corrected

nodes.asks: Is what would be said actually confirmed?

branches.label: Confirmed
branches.when: every claim in it is established rather than believed

branches.label: Not confirmed
branches.when: the cause, the fix or the timing is still a hypothesis

nodes.does: Say what is known and what is not, and claim nothing about cause or resolution that has not been established. A root cause announced and then retracted costs more credibility than a slow update, and technical detail stated as fact while still uncertain is the most common source of that retraction

nodes.asks: Does this materially change the guidance the recipient already has?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: what they should do, expect or avoid has changed

branches.label: It does not, and no commitment requires an update
branches.when: nothing has changed for them since the last message

branches.label: It does not, but a commitment requires an update
branches.when: a status-page cadence, a contract or a regulatory obligation requires one regardless

nodes.does: Send nothing, and record why. Sending because time has passed produces noise, and noise is what makes the eventual resolution notice go unread by the people who were waiting for it

nodes.state: no update sent; nothing material had changed
nodes.reEntry: the next material change, or the next point a commitment requires an update, brings this back

nodes.does: Raise the communication through the canonical communication mechanism, which owns the obligation, the recipient resolution, the channels, the permissions and the delivery evidence. Incident communication does not build its own delivery path, and the message carries no promotional content

nodes.asks: Is this the resolution notice for this recipient scope?

branches.label: It is
branches.when: the incident is resolved for the population this message goes to

branches.label: It is not
branches.when: the incident continues for them

nodes.state: update issued; the next update is bound to a stated condition rather than to a clock
nodes.reEntry: the stated condition occurring, or a material change, produces the next update

nodes.state: resolution communicated to this recipient scope
nodes.reEntry: a relapse is communicated as a relapse rather than as a new incident, because the recipients were told it was over

guardrails: No root cause or resolution is claimed before it is confirmed.
No promotional content appears in incident communication.
Uncertain technical detail is never communicated as fact.
The affected cohort is identified as precisely as the evidence allows.
journeys.reusableRule: Incident communication should provide verified, actionable information to the population actually affected by the incident.

journeys.name: Root cause investigation → hypothesis → confirm or reject → corrective action
journeys.purpose: Find the thing that actually explains the incident, rather than the thing that was nearest to it.

entity.scope: the incident and the investigation into what caused it
entity.note: Hypotheses are a finite list, tested one at a time. Rejections are recorded so the next investigator does not retest them.

requires: a confirmed incident whose cause is not established
insufficientAlone: the incident having a trigger, which is what set it off rather than what made it possible

nodes.does: Collect the timeline, the logs and evidence, the change history, the dependency state, the affected cohort, the failure signatures and the effects the mitigations had. What a mitigation did or did not fix is itself evidence about the cause

Form hypotheses that would explain the whole incident rather than its first symptom. The change that shipped just before an incident is the most available explanation and is frequently not the cause - often it is what made a latent problem visible, and fixing it leaves the problem in place

Test the current hypothesis against the evidence, including the parts of the evidence it does not explain. A hypothesis that accounts for most of an incident and not its timing, or not its cohort, has not been confirmed

nodes.asks: Does the evidence support this hypothesis?

branches.label: Supported and it explains the incident
branches.when: it accounts for the failure, its timing, its cohort and its behaviour under mitigation

branches.label: Not supported
branches.when: the evidence contradicts it or leaves it unexplained

branches.label: Correlated but unexplained
branches.when: the condition was present and nothing connects it to the failure

nodes.does: Reject the hypothesis and record why, so the next investigator does not retest it. Correlation is not causation, and a condition present during an incident that nothing connects to the failure is a coincidence that will be treated as an answer unless it is rejected explicitly

nodes.asks: Are hypotheses left to test?

branches.label: Some remain
branches.when: the list has untested candidates

branches.label: None explains it
branches.when: every candidate within the investigation's bounds has been tested and rejected

nodes.does: Record the incident as unexplained rather than attributing it to the most plausible remaining candidate. An unexplained incident is a known gap somebody can work on; a wrongly attributed one is a closed question that will reopen as the same incident with everybody convinced it was fixed

nodes.on: an incident no available hypothesis explains
carries: every hypothesis tested and why each was rejected
the explicit fact that no cause was assigned - the incident is recorded as unexplained rather than closed against a guess

nodes.does: Record ROOT_CAUSE_CONFIRMED with the evidence supporting it and exactly what it explains. Service may already have been restored - restoration and understanding proceed independently, and holding one for the other extends an outage for the sake of tidiness

Define the corrective action the confirmed cause implies, separately from whatever mitigation is currently holding the impact down. The mitigation is a workaround; this is the thing that makes the workaround unnecessary

nodes.on: a confirmed cause with a defined corrective action
carries: the confirmed cause, the evidence for it and the corrective action it implies
the mitigations currently in place, which the corrective action may make removable

guardrails: The first plausible explanation is not the root cause.
Correlation is not causation.
The root cause remains evidence-based rather than assigned by elimination.
Service may be restored before the root cause is known.
journeys.reusableRule: Root cause is established through evidence that explains the incident, not merely through the first condition correlated with failure.

journeys.name: Recovery action → restore service → verify or continue
journeys.purpose: Act on the cause and then check the affected population, not the command's return code.

entity.scope: the incident, the recovery action and the capability it is meant to restore
entity.note: The recovery actions available are a finite list defined by the response. Attempts progress through it rather than repeating indefinitely.

requires: an authorized corrective or recovery action against an active incident

nodes.does: Execute the corrective action against the affected scope, through the canonical execution and reliability primitives rather than a bespoke path built during the incident

timeout.reason: an action whose outcome is unknown may or may not have changed the system, and the next decision depends entirely on which

nodes.does: Record the action's outcome as unknown and hold further attempts. Applying a second recovery action on top of one that may have landed is how an incident gets a second cause

nodes.on: a recovery action whose outcome could not be established
carries: the action, the scope it targeted and everything last known about its effect
the explicit instruction that no further recovery action is applied until this one's effect is known
suppresses: any further recovery action while this one's outcome is unknown

nodes.asks: Did the action apply?

branches.label: Applied
branches.when: the corrective action completed against the affected scope

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the action itself did not complete

nodes.does: Verify from the affected population rather than from the action's own success - service availability, error rates, critical transactions, business functions, dependency health, and the recovery of the cohort that was actually affected. A recovery command succeeding says the command ran, and one successful synthetic check says one path works for one caller

nodes.asks: Is service restored across the affected population?

branches.label: Restored
branches.when: the affected cohort's real traffic succeeds and the critical functions work

branches.label: Partially restored
branches.when: some of the affected population works and some does not

branches.label: Not restored
branches.when: the action applied and the impact continues

nodes.does: Keep the incident active and name the unresolved scope explicitly. A partial restoration reported as recovery leaves the remaining population inside an incident everybody has stopped watching, which is how a long tail of affected customers goes unnoticed for days

nodes.asks: Is another recovery action available?

branches.label: One remains
branches.when: the response defines a further corrective action that has not been attempted

branches.label: None
branches.when: the defined actions are exhausted

nodes.does: Take the next action from the response's defined list. The list is finite, so attempts progress through it and terminate rather than cycling on the same action with different hopes

nodes.on: an incident whose defined recovery actions are exhausted
carries: every action attempted, what each achieved and the scope still affected
the explicit fact that the incident remains active and any partial restoration is named rather than counted as recovery

nodes.does: Record RECOVERY_OBSERVED. What has been established is that the affected population works now - not that it will still be working in an hour, which is the next question and a different one

nodes.on: service observed restored across the affected population
carries: what was verified, across which cohort and against which functions
the explicit fact that this is a first good signal rather than a stable recovery

guardrails: A recovery command succeeding is not service restored.
One successful synthetic check does not prove population recovery.
Partial restoration stays explicit and keeps the incident active.
journeys.reusableRule: Incident recovery becomes meaningful only when the affected service and user population demonstrate restored operation.

journeys.name: Service restored → observation window → stable or relapse
journeys.purpose: Hold the incident open long enough to know the recovery held.

entity.scope: the incident and the recovered service under observation
entity.note: The window is set from the incident's own character rather than from a standard duration.

distinctFrom.because: RET-27 buffers one relationship's recovery signal before concluding the relationship is healthy. This applies the same principle to a shared operational failure - same discipline, different entity, and here a relapse returns a population to an incident rather than a person to a risk state.

requires: verified restoration across the affected population
insufficientAlone: a recovery action completing, which is what produced the signal rather than the signal itself

nodes.does: Record RECOVERY_OBSERVATION. The incident is not resolved - recoveries that hold for ten minutes and fail again are common, and closing on the first good signal means reopening in front of the same customers who were just told it was over

Set the observation window from the incident's own character - how long the failure took to manifest, how often the affected path runs, and whether the fix addressed a cause or a symptom. A fixed window applied to every incident is either too long for a trivial one or far too short for one on a rare path

timeout.after: the observation window set for this incident
timeout.reason: reaching the window without recurrence is what makes the recovery stable. Holding it open longer without need keeps a response engaged on something that has finished

nodes.asks: What appeared during observation?

branches.label: The same failure returned
branches.when: the incident's own signature recurs in the affected population

branches.label: New cases, a different failure
branches.when: something else is failing during the window

nodes.does: Return the incident to ACTIVE. What resumes is this incident rather than a new one - the recurrence is evidence about the recovery, and opening a fresh incident hides that the fix did not hold and makes the pattern invisible

nodes.on: a recovery that did not hold
carries: the recovery that was applied, how long it held and the signature of the relapse
the explicit fact that this is the same incident recurring, which is evidence the confirmed cause was incomplete

nodes.does: Assess it separately rather than absorbing it into this incident. Attaching every failure that occurs during an observation window to the incident makes the incident unfalsifiable - it can never be shown to have ended

nodes.state: an unrelated failure raised separately; this observation continues on its own terms
nodes.reEntry: if the separate assessment shows the two do share a cause, they are correlated on that evidence rather than on having overlapped in time

nodes.does: Record STABLE_RECOVERY with what was observed and for how long. The observation is part of the record, because the next similar incident's window is set against it

nodes.on: a recovery that held through its observation window
carries: what was observed, over what window and across which cohort
the mitigations still in place, which the resolution has to remove or formalize rather than leave running

guardrails: Service restored once is not the incident resolved.
The observation duration and evidence reflect the incident's type rather than a standard.
Observation is not kept artificially long without need.
journeys.reusableRule: Initial restoration should enter an observation state until sufficient evidence shows the recovery is stable.

journeys.name: Incident resolution → close operational response → preserve residual cases
journeys.purpose: Close the shared failure without closing the individual problems it caused.

entity.scope: the incident and the individual cases and obligations linked to it
entity.note: The incident's resolution is a statement about the shared cause. Every linked case reaches its own resolution on its own terms.

requires: a stable recovery and the incident's own resolution criteria met
insufficientAlone: service being restored, which is one of the criteria rather than all of them

nodes.does: Mark the systemic incident RESOLVED, preserving its timeline, its mitigations and every decision taken during it. The record is what the review works from and what any later recurrence is compared against - an incident that keeps only its outcome teaches nothing
Stop the incident-specific emergency operations - the elevated monitoring, the standing bridge, the suspended changes. These have their own cost and they end with the incident rather than drifting on

nodes.asks: What happens to the temporary mitigations?

branches.label: Safe to remove
branches.when: the corrective action makes them unnecessary

branches.label: They should become permanent
branches.when: the mitigation turned out to be the right long-term behaviour

nodes.does: Remove them and verify the service holds without them. A mitigation left in place because removing it is frightening becomes permanent by nobody's decision, and it joins the set of quietly permanent emergency controls that is the least-understood part of most systems
Formalize it explicitly as a change with an owner and a rationale, rather than leaving a temporary control quietly running forever. Every one of those was meant to last an afternoon

nodes.asks: Do individual affected cases remain unresolved?

branches.label: Some remain
branches.when: linked entity-level problems are still outstanding

branches.label: None
branches.when: every linked case has independently reached resolution

nodes.does: Detach them and let each continue on its own recovery. The systemic cause is fixed and the customer whose order failed still has a failed order - closing their case because the incident closed tells them the problem is solved at exactly the moment they discover it is not

nodes.asks: Do financial or remedy obligations remain from the incident?

branches.label: Some remain
branches.when: refunds, credits, compensation or unmet service obligations were created by the incident

branches.label: None
branches.when: nothing is owed as a result of it

nodes.on: obligations surviving an incident's closure
carries: the obligations, their affected scope and what created them
the explicit fact that the incident is resolved and these are not - they run on their own lifecycle at their own pace

nodes.asks: Does this incident qualify for a post-incident review?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: its severity, novelty or recurrence meets the threshold for review

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: it falls below the review threshold and nothing about it was novel

nodes.on: a resolved incident qualifying for review
carries: the timeline, the mitigations, the decisions and the root cause where one was confirmed
the detached cases and surviving obligations, which are part of the incident's real cost

nodes.state: RESOLVED; the shared failure closed and its record preserved
nodes.reEntry: a recurrence is correlated against this record rather than assessed from nothing, which is what makes a pattern visible across incidents

guardrails: An incident resolved is not every individual case resolved.
Temporary mitigations do not silently become permanent.
Incident closure preserves the timeline and the decisions taken.
journeys.reusableRule: Incident resolution closes the shared systemic failure while leaving entity-specific obligations open until they independently reach resolution.

journeys.name: Post-incident review → learn → corrective work → verify
journeys.purpose: Turn what the incident showed into work somebody owns and somebody checks.

entity.scope: the resolved incident and the corrective work its review produces
entity.note: The review's output is owned work with deadlines. A published document is not a control and is not the deliverable.

requires: a resolved incident meeting the threshold for post-incident review
insufficientAlone: an incident resolved without meeting the review threshold policy defines
a review requested by an individual for an incident the policy does not select

nodes.does: Review the timeline, the detection, the response, the root cause, the blast radius, the mitigations, the communication, the recovery, the control failures and the near misses. What is examined is the system and the response rather than the people - a review that finds a person found the wrong thing, because the person will move on and the condition will not

Identify the corrective and preventive actions the evidence actually supports. An action nobody can trace to something the incident revealed is a good idea rather than a finding, and mixing the two makes the real findings harder to prioritise

nodes.asks: Does the review produce corrective work?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: the evidence supports specific preventive or corrective actions

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: the response worked, the controls held, and nothing the incident revealed needs changing

nodes.does: Record explicitly that the review found no corrective work required, with the reasoning. That is a legitimate outcome and it needs to be a stated one rather than an empty section that reads as an unfinished review

nodes.state: reviewed; no outstanding corrective work
nodes.reEntry: a recurrence reopens the question of whether the conclusion that nothing needed changing was right

nodes.does: Assign owners and deadlines to each corrective action. An action item with no owner is a sentence in a document, and a document is not a control - the whole value of the review is what somebody is now accountable for delivering

until: the required corrective actions are claimed complete
corrective actions are abandoned or superseded

timeout.after: the deadlines assigned to the corrective actions
timeout.reason: prevention work that slips past its deadline unremarked is how the same incident recurs, and by then nobody remembers the action existed

nodes.on: corrective work outliving its assigned deadline
carries: the outstanding actions, their owners and the incident they came from
the explicit fact that the risk the incident revealed is still present
