nodes.asks: What happened to the corrective work?

branches.label: Claimed complete
branches.when: the owners report the actions done

branches.label: Abandoned or superseded
branches.when: the actions were dropped or replaced

nodes.does: Record which actions were dropped and on whose authority. Silently abandoned prevention work is the reason the same incident recurs, and without this record nobody can point to the moment it was dropped or ask why

Verify the corrective work where verification is required. An action item created is not a risk reduced, and a document published is not a prevention - what is checked is whether the condition that produced the incident can still produce it

nodes.asks: Did the corrective work actually reduce the risk?

branches.label: Verified
branches.when: the condition the incident exposed can no longer produce it

branches.label: Not effective
branches.when: the work completed and the condition remains reachable

nodes.does: Return the action to its owner with what the verification found. Work completed that did not reduce the risk means the action was aimed at the wrong thing, and repeating it produces the same result
Record the corrective work as complete and verified, with what the verification established

nodes.state: review closed with verified corrective work
nodes.reEntry: a recurrence despite verified prevention is strong evidence the diagnosis was wrong, and is assessed at pattern level rather than as a fresh incident

guardrails: A postmortem is not a blame exercise.
An action item created is not a risk reduced.
Prevention is never marked complete solely because a document was published.
journeys.reusableRule: Post-incident review converts incident evidence into owned, verifiable improvements rather than treating documentation itself as remediation.

journeys.name: Incident pattern recurrence → detect systemic weakness → escalate prevention
journeys.purpose: Notice when the same weakness keeps producing incidents, and stop treating each one as new.

entity.scope: the family of materially similar incidents and the weakness they may share
entity.note: Similarity is established by comparing causes rather than by counting occurrences or matching alert names.

distinctFrom.because: INC-251 correlates failures happening now into one incident. This compares incidents across time to ask whether the same systemic weakness keeps producing them - a question about the prevention strategy rather than about any one response.

requires: multiple incidents across a defined window or context that appear materially similar
insufficientAlone: the same alert firing repeatedly, which is a repeated alert name and nothing more
a raised incident count, which measures how often something was declared rather than why

nodes.does: Compare the root causes, the affected systems, the failure modes, the mitigations, the recovery actions, the corrective actions and any prevention work that was never finished. What is compared is the causes rather than the symptoms - two incidents that both presented as elevated latency can have nothing else in common

nodes.asks: Do these incidents share a systemic weakness?

branches.label: The same weakness recurring
branches.when: the confirmed causes point to one underlying condition that keeps producing failures

branches.label: Superficially similar, different causes
branches.when: they looked alike and their causes are unrelated

branches.label: Not determinable from the evidence
branches.when: the incidents lack confirmed causes, or the comparison is inconclusive

nodes.on: a recurrence pattern the evidence cannot establish
carries: the incidents compared, their causes where confirmed and where they were not
the explicit fact that no shared root cause was inferred from the count - inferring one from repetition is exactly the mistake this journey exists to prevent

nodes.does: Keep them separate and record why the apparent similarity does not hold. Grouping incidents by how they looked produces a pattern that is an artifact of the monitoring rather than of the system, and prevention work aimed at it fixes nothing

nodes.state: incidents kept separate; the apparent pattern was superficial
nodes.reEntry: further incidents with confirmed causes may still establish a genuine pattern. This comparison is recorded so it is not repeated identically

nodes.does: Elevate the prevention priority and create or strengthen the long-term corrective programme. Repeated recovery without prevention is an operational risk, and it should be visible as a risk rather than as a series of incidents that were each handled well

nodes.asks: Was remediation previously attempted for this weakness?

branches.label: It was
branches.when: corrective work from an earlier incident targeted this same condition

branches.label: It was not
branches.when: this weakness has not previously been worked on

nodes.does: Reopen the previous remediation's assumptions. A fix that was applied and did not hold means the diagnosis was wrong rather than the execution, and repeating the same remediation produces the same incident at greater cost and with less credibility

nodes.on: remediation that was applied and did not prevent recurrence
carries: the previous corrective work, what it assumed and what the recurrence shows about that assumption
the explicit fact that increasing customer messaging is not the response to recurrence - the prevention strategy is what has to change

nodes.state: systemic weakness identified; prevention elevated as a standing risk
nodes.reEntry: further recurrence is measured against the elevated programme rather than raising the priority again, so the escalation means something the first time

guardrails: A repeated alert name is not the same root cause.
Customer messaging is not increased simply because incidents recur.
Repeated recovery without prevention stays visible as operational risk.
A shared root cause is never inferred from a count of occurrences.
journeys.reusableRule: Recurring incidents should change the prevention strategy when evidence shows the same systemic weakness continues to produce failures.

rules.rule: Anonymous identity, known identity, permission, qualification and conversion are five separate states, and reaching one never implies another.
rules.because: Every collapse between two of them produces a specific, familiar failure: merging strangers on a shared device, mailing someone who only filled in a support form, treating a lead as a pipeline number, treating a click as revenue.

rules.rule: An intent signal carries both a strength and a freshness, and neither alone qualifies it. A single weak signal cannot escalate anyone, and a strong signal stops counting once it is stale.
rules.because: Intent that is recorded without decay turns one pricing visit two years ago into a permanent high-intent flag, and everything downstream inherits that lie.

rules.rule: A higher-priority lifecycle state suppresses lower-priority acquisition messaging, and the suppression has to reach sends that are already queued.
rules.because: A handoff that only stops future scheduling still delivers the superseded journey's next message, which is the one moment the person notices the seam.

rules.rule: A commercial destination is reached when the system of record says so. Engagement with a message about the destination is not the destination.
rules.because: Clicks and landing-page visits are the cheapest signals to instrument and the easiest to mistake for outcomes, so the substitution happens by default unless it is forbidden by default.

rules.rule: Entity scope is preserved: an outcome on one order, application or opportunity resolves only the journeys about that entity.
rules.because: Person-scoped success closes journeys that were never about the thing that happened - a second order is not recovery of a cancelled first one.

rules.rule: Qualification and disqualification reasons are appended, never overwritten. The current state is readable together with how it got there.
rules.because: Routing in this category depends on why a state changed, so a state without its reason history cannot be routed on at all - and 'not now' silently becomes 'never'.

rules.rule: Acquisition and nurture journeys are bounded. The window is fixed when someone enters it, and engagement inside the window does not extend it.
rules.because: A clock that any interaction resets makes the most engaged unconverted people the most heavily messaged, which is where perpetual nurture actually comes from.

rules.rule: Existing customer state outranks acquisition state. Where the two disagree about who someone is, the customer record wins.
rules.because: Acquisition data is fragmentary by nature; continuing to pursue someone who has already bought is the failure that reads as the company not knowing its own customers.

rules.rule: Entry, setup, activation, first value and adoption are five separate states. Reaching one never implies the next.
rules.because: Each collapse has its own failure. Treating entry as activation congratulates people who have done nothing; treating setup as value measures our own checklist; treating one use as adoption declares a habit after a single instance.

rules.rule: Activation is defined by an authoritative event in which the product produced value, and by nothing else.
rules.because: Every cheaper definition is available first - a login, a completed checklist, a clicked email - so without this rule one of them becomes the definition by default, and every downstream number inherits it.

rules.rule: Onboarding responds to progress, not to elapsed time. A fixed day-one, day-three, day-seven schedule is not onboarding.
rules.because: A calendar sequence tells someone who finished on day one to finish, and tells someone stuck on step two about step five. Both are the same bug: the message was chosen before the state was read.

rules.rule: Once activation occurs, every onboarding action still pending is invalidated, including sends already queued.
rules.because: The setup reminder that arrives after the person has already succeeded is the single most expensive message in this category - it says plainly that nothing was watching.

rules.rule: Assistance is offered on evidence of effort without progress. Activity volume alone never triggers it.
rules.because: Heavy usage with real progress looks identical to heavy usage with none if only the count is read, and the first group is exactly who should not be interrupted.

rules.rule: A declared role or use-case and a behaviourally inferred one are stored separately and stay distinguishable.
rules.because: Inference written into the field that holds declared answers cannot be told apart from something the person actually said, and the mistake is unrecoverable once it is written.

rules.rule: Adoption expectations follow the intended usage pattern of the product. Absence of use is only a signal against a pattern that predicted use.
rules.because: A tool used twice a year is not stalling in month three, and a stall model built on a daily product will report every seasonal user as failing.

rules.rule: Onboarding and adoption journeys carry explicit exits and handoffs. Neither is allowed to be open-ended.
rules.because: Without a stated end, an onboarding that never activates simply keeps running, and the person stays in a state the business has already stopped believing in.

rules.rule: Where a person or an open support case is already working the same blocker, automated rescue for that blocker is suppressed.
rules.because: Two channels chasing one problem contradict each other in front of the customer, and the automated one is always the one that does not know the current state.

rules.rule: Engagement with a message is never activation and never adoption. Opens and clicks measure the message.
rules.because: It is the same substitution ACQ-R4 forbids on the acquisition side, and it reappears here because the events that would prove real activation are the harder ones to instrument.

rules.rule: Activity, engagement, health, churn risk and churn are five separate concepts and are never used as proxies for one another.
rules.because: They are ordered by how hard each is to measure, so the cheap one always stands in for the expensive one unless that substitution is forbidden outright.

rules.rule: Inactivity is evaluated against the expected usage cadence of the relationship, never against a fixed interval.
rules.because: A universal no-login-for-N-days rule reports every episodic and seasonal customer as failing, and the resulting noise trains everyone to ignore the alert.

rules.rule: Risk scores and risk signals are evidence. They are not the business decision, and nothing is enforced on a score alone.
rules.because: A score is a compression of evidence, and acting on the compression rather than the evidence means nobody can say afterwards what actually happened.

rules.rule: A known operational problem is resolved before any promotional retention tactic is used.
rules.because: A discount offered to someone whose integration is broken answers a question they did not ask and confirms that nobody read the ticket.

rules.rule: Recovery passes through an observation state. One positive event opens it; sustained behaviour closes it.
rules.because: Declaring recovery on the first good signal is how a relapse becomes invisible - the state says recovered, so nothing is watching when it goes wrong again.

rules.rule: Cancellation intent and cancellation completion are separate states and never share an event.
rules.because: Treating intent as completion writes off customers who were still deciding; treating completion as intent keeps selling to people who have already left.

rules.rule: A completed cancellation immediately invalidates every incompatible retention action, including sends already queued.
rules.because: The save offer that arrives after the cancellation went through is the last thing the relationship produces, and it is the one that gets screenshotted.

rules.rule: Cancellation, account closure and data deletion are three independent lifecycle states with three separate triggers.
rules.because: Collapsing them destroys data someone still has a right to, or keeps data someone has asked to have removed. Both failures are irreversible and only one of them is visible.

rules.rule: Where a person or an open case is already resolving the underlying problem, duplicate automated intervention on it is suppressed.
rules.because: The automated track is always the one working from stale state, so it contradicts the human one in front of the customer at the worst possible moment.

rules.rule: Retention interventions are bounded in number and complete only on an explicit outcome.
rules.because: An intervention with no defined end repeats until someone leaves, which converts a retention programme into a reason to go.

rules.rule: A declared cancellation reason stays auditable and is never silently replaced by an inferred one.
rules.because: The declared reason is the only direct evidence of why someone left; overwriting it with a model's guess destroys the one input that could have improved the product.

rules.rule: Every risk, health and recovery state is scoped to the person, account, subscription or entity it was observed on.
rules.because: One failing subscription does not make an account unhealthy, and treating it as though it does suppresses messaging the rest of the relationship still needs.

rules.rule: Identity, permission, preference, contactability and engagement are five separate states and none of them implies another.
rules.because: They arrive together at signup and get written to one record, which is why an email address so often becomes a subscription nobody asked for.

rules.rule: Permission is modelled as purpose x channel x scope, not as a flag.
rules.because: Every question that actually gets asked - may this campaign run, does this withdrawal cover that message, which system is right - has no answer against a boolean, so the answer gets guessed, and the guess is always the permissive one.

rules.rule: Permission withdrawal is enforced immediately on affected communication, before any downstream system has confirmed anything.
rules.because: Enforcement that waits for distributed convergence is enforcement that runs at the speed of the slowest integration, and the message goes out in the meantime.

rules.rule: Preference changes shape future eligible communication. They never create permission.
rules.because: Saying how you would prefer to be contacted is not saying you want to be, and the two are captured in the same forms often enough that the distinction has to be enforced rather than assumed.

rules.rule: A contactability failure does not change permission state, and a permission change does not mark a channel undeliverable.
rules.because: Collapsing them loses a reachable customer to a mailbox that was full for a week, or keeps sending to someone who opted out through a channel that still technically works.

rules.rule: An alternative channel may be used only where it is both permitted and appropriate to the journey.
rules.because: Availability is the easiest of the three to check and the least meaningful. Falling back to SMS because email bounced is a permission decision dressed as a routing one.

rules.rule: Every suppression carries an explicit reason and an explicit scope.
rules.because: Without them nothing can tell a cooldown from a legal restriction, so either everything is released too early or nothing is ever released at all.

rules.rule: When a temporary suppression or cooldown ends, current eligibility is re-evaluated. What was held is not replayed.
rules.because: The queue describes a state that has since moved. Releasing it delivers a week of messages at once, most of them about things that are no longer true.

rules.rule: Delivery retries are bounded by a budget fixed when the first failure occurs.
rules.because: An unbounded retry is indistinguishable from a working integration until it is examined, and by then it has been hammering a dead address for months.

rules.rule: A distributed permission conflict fails safe. The more permissive state is never chosen because it is more permissive.
rules.because: Defaulting to permissive resolves every disagreement in favour of sending, which converts an integration bug into a compliance incident.

rules.rule: Communication engagement is not a business outcome. Delivered is not read, read is not agreed.
rules.because: It is the same substitution ACQ-R4 and ACT-R10 forbid, arriving here from the other direction: the delivery pipeline emits engagement events by default and outcome events only if someone builds them.

rules.rule: Permission, preference and contactability history is preserved and auditable. Nothing is overwritten in place.
rules.because: The current value cannot answer the only questions that matter under challenge - what were we authorised to do, when, and on what evidence.

rules.rule: A queued action re-validates permission and suppression state at execution, not at scheduling.
rules.because: The gap between the two is where every late-arriving message lives, and it is the one moment at which the system can still avoid sending it.

rules.rule: Enforcement precedes propagation. Withdrawal stops outbound communication locally even while downstream systems are still catching up.
rules.because: Propagation can be retried; a message that has already been sent cannot. The ordering is chosen so the recoverable failure is the one that happens.

rules.rule: Feedback requested, feedback received and feedback resolved are three separate states.
rules.because: Collapsing the first two makes non-response into a data point it is not; collapsing the last two closes loops with the person still waiting to hear back.

rules.rule: Negative feedback never automatically creates a confirmed service failure.
rules.because: A report of a bad experience and a record of something going wrong are different evidence, and treating the first as the second manufactures faults that operations then has to disprove.

rules.rule: Positive feedback never automatically creates advocacy permission.
rules.because: Telling us something went well is not agreeing to be quoted, referenced or published, and the gap between those is where most advocacy programmes lose people's trust.

rules.rule: An advocacy request requires credible positive relationship evidence and the absence of a conflicting unresolved issue.
rules.because: Asking for a review while a complaint is open reads as not knowing who you are talking to, and it costs more than the review was worth.

rules.rule: An operational obligation created by feedback carries an owner and an explicit closure condition.
rules.because: Feedback that generates work without ownership generates the appearance of responsiveness and nothing else.

rules.rule: An appeal preserves the original decision. Nothing is edited in place while a review is running.
rules.because: The original decision is the thing under review; overwriting it means the review has no subject and no record of what was actually appealed.

rules.rule: Declared data and inferred data stay distinguishable, and inference never writes into a declared field.
rules.because: The same rule as ACT-R6 and CON-R4, arriving from a third direction - the merge is cheap to perform, unrecoverable afterwards, and always happens by accident.

rules.rule: Missing critical data and progressive profiling are different mechanisms. Critical data blocks a named process; profiling improves a future decision and blocks nothing.
rules.because: Dressing profiling as a blocker teaches people that our requests are not real, which means the genuine blockers get ignored too.

rules.rule: Relationship signals stay scoped to the entity they were observed on and carry the time they occurred.
rules.because: Without scope, one bad experience colours an entire account; without time, evidence from two years ago is weighed the same as evidence from yesterday.

rules.rule: An existing issue or case suppresses duplicate recovery workflows for the same underlying problem.
rules.because: The same rule as RET-R9 and ACT-R9. It appears in three categories because three different systems can each independently decide to help.

rules.rule: Communication engagement is never substituted for relationship evidence.
rules.because: Opens and clicks are abundant and cheap, relationship evidence is scarce and expensive, and any model that accepts both will fill up with the first.

rules.rule: No advocacy contribution is publicly reused because someone submitted it. Publication and reuse permission is captured separately, as its own permission record.
rules.because: Submitting a testimonial is a gift to us; publishing it is a use of their name and words, and the second requires an authorisation the first did not give.

rules.rule: Routing, assignment, acceptance and active ownership are four separate states.
rules.because: Work that is routed but unassigned, or assigned but unaccepted, looks owned in every report and is being done by nobody.

rules.rule: An ownership change preserves open obligations, deadlines and the historical owner chain.
rules.because: The obligation was made to someone outside the organisation; who holds it internally is our concern and not a reason for it to change.

rules.rule: Transferring ownership never resets an inherited commitment or its clock.
rules.because: A deadline that restarts on reassignment converts an internal handover into an external delay, and makes reassignment the cheapest way to buy time.

rules.rule: Owner and approver are separate roles unless a policy explicitly says one person holds both.
rules.because: Collapsing them removes the review from the process while leaving its record intact, which is worse than having no approval step at all.

rules.rule: An approval request references the exact subject version reviewed.
rules.because: An approval bound to an entity rather than a version silently authorises everything that entity later becomes, and nothing in the record shows when the authorisation stopped matching what was approved.

rules.rule: Approval is not execution. Authorisation permits an action; it does not perform it or record it as done.
rules.because: Systems that mark approved work as complete report a pipeline that has been authorised rather than one that has happened.

rules.rule: A material change invalidates only the approvals whose decision basis is no longer true.
rules.because: Invalidating everything on every edit trains people to approve without reading, which is the same outcome as having no approvals.

rules.rule: Multi-party approval aggregation comes from the governing policy. Majority, unanimity, quorum and tie-breaks are never inferred.
rules.because: An invented decision rule is indistinguishable from a real one until it is challenged, and by then it has been authorising things for months.

rules.rule: A rejected request re-enters approval only through an explicit revision path, and only where policy permits one.
rules.because: Without it, rejection becomes a retry loop: the same version resubmitted until an approver stops reading.

rules.rule: Escalation and ownership transfer are different operations and are not assumed to accompany each other.
rules.because: Treating every escalation as a handover lets the original owner put a case down by raising it, which is the opposite of what escalation is for.

rules.rule: Actions queued by a former owner or approver do not execute once that authority has ended.
rules.because: The message that arrives from someone who is no longer responsible is the visible half of a stale-authority bug, and the invisible half is whatever it committed us to.

rules.rule: A missing owner or authority is an explicit state, never a null field, wherever active responsibility is required.
rules.because: Null is unqueryable and unescalatable. Work with no owner has to be findable as work with no owner.

rules.rule: Owner, approver and decision records stay auditable. Nothing in the chain is overwritten in place.
rules.because: Who was responsible, who decided, and on what version, are the only questions that get asked after something goes wrong.

rules.rule: Internal approval establishes internal authorisation only. It does not establish that a counterparty has accepted anything.
rules.because: The two are separated by an act nobody on our side controls, and treating an internal yes as a done deal is how forecasts and commitments diverge.

rules.rule: Time passing is not a business outcome unless the governing state machine explicitly defines it as one.
rules.because: A timer firing proves only that a clock advanced. Reading it as failure, expiry or consent converts an absence of information into a decision nobody made.

rules.rule: Deadline, due state, expiry, grace and temporary state are five separate concepts.
rules.because: They share a date field and nothing else. Collapsing them produces systems where a missed deadline revokes access and an expiry is treated as a reminder.

rules.rule: Expiring and expired are separate states, and nothing acts on the first as though it were the second.
rules.because: The whole value of a pre-expiry window is that the outcome can still change. A system that treats them alike has no window, only an early notification of a decision already taken.

rules.rule: Every scheduled future transition re-reads the authoritative current state at execution time.
rules.because: The schedule was written against a version of the world that no longer has to exist. Execution is the only moment at which that can be checked, and skipping it is what makes stale automation.

rules.rule: An older timer never overwrites a newer authoritative change or extension.
rules.because: Jobs fire in the order they were scheduled, not the order decisions were made, so without this the most recent decision is the one most likely to be undone.

rules.rule: A temporary state carries an explicit expiry or an explicit exit condition.
rules.because: A time-bound state with no ending is an unmanaged permanent state, and it is invisible precisely because everyone remembers granting it as temporary.

rules.rule: Grace is a degraded continuity state, not a normal active one, and it names which capabilities continue.
rules.because: A grace period that behaves identically to active has no purpose except to delay a decision, and nobody downstream can tell which one an entity is actually in.

rules.rule: A reversal restores only what is independently still valid. It does not rewind the side effects of the original transition.
rules.because: Restoring an entity wholesale resurrects withdrawn consent, revoked credentials and cancelled integrations, each of which ended for its own reason that reversal never addressed.

rules.rule: An expired entity re-enters through renewal, replacement or requalification - never by editing the expiry away.
rules.because: Moving a timestamp makes the entity active without making it valid, and it destroys the record of the period during which it was not.

rules.rule: Completing an obligation invalidates the reminders and escalations queued against it.
rules.because: The nudge that arrives after someone has already done the thing is the most reliable signal a customer gets that nothing is watching.

rules.rule: Timezone and authoritative timestamp semantics are explicit wherever they change a business outcome.
rules.because: A deadline at midnight is a different deadline in two places, and the ambiguity only surfaces in the cases where it cost someone something.

rules.rule: Timer-driven actions are idempotent. A redelivered job applies its transition once or not at all.
rules.because: Schedulers retry by design, so an action that is not idempotent is not a bug that might happen - it is one waiting for its first redelivery.

rules.rule: An extension or renewal supersedes the expiry actions scheduled under the previous validity.
rules.because: Without it the extension is granted and the old expiry still fires, which is worse than never having extended anything.

rules.rule: A scheduled action does not replay once its underlying obligation has already been resolved.
rules.because: The obligation is the thing the schedule existed to serve; once it is met the job is not early or late, it is meaningless.

rules.rule: Eligibility, entitlement, provisioning, authorization, access and credentials are six separate states.
rules.because: They are usually stored as one flag because they usually agree. The cases where they disagree are exactly the incidents nobody can diagnose.

rules.rule: Granting an entitlement does not prove the resource behind it was provisioned.
rules.because: The grant is a business record and the provisioning is a distributed operation, so the first can succeed while the second silently does not - and the customer discovers it before we do.

rules.rule: Provisioning success is verified against actual availability wherever the difference matters.
rules.because: A provisioning API returning 200 is a statement about the API. Whether the holder can reach the thing is a different question with a different answer.

rules.rule: Losing an entitlement stops future use. It does not automatically invalidate commitments created while the right was held.
rules.because: The commitment was valid when it was made, and cancelling it because a plan changed takes something away that was already paid for or already promised.

rules.rule: Authorization evaluates the actor, the action, the resource and the current state together.
rules.because: Any of the four alone produces a decision that is right most of the time, and the times it is wrong are the ones that matter.

rules.rule: Authentication and authorization stay separate. Knowing who someone is says nothing about what they may do.
rules.because: They are adjacent in every login flow and the conflation is invisible until an authenticated user reaches something they should never have seen.

rules.rule: A credential has its own validity lifecycle, independent of the entitlement it represents.
rules.because: A valid credential for a lapsed entitlement and a revoked credential for a live one are both real, and treating either as one fact loses the other.

rules.rule: Security revocation supersedes queued and in-flight access operations, including refresh and activation.
rules.because: A token invalidated at ten o'clock must not still authorise a request that was queued at one minute to, which is precisely the window an attacker is operating in.

rules.rule: Suspension and termination are separate states.
rules.because: Suspension is designed to be reversible and termination is not. Recording one as the other either destroys a recoverable relationship or leaves a terminated one looking recoverable.

rules.rule: Capability restoration is rebuilt from current valid state, never replayed from a historical snapshot.
rules.because: A snapshot restores expired credentials, withdrawn permissions and roles that no longer exist, each of which ended for a reason that restoration never addressed.

rules.rule: Entitlement changes apply as a scoped delta between the old and new rights.
rules.because: Re-applying the whole new scope reprovisions what already worked and revokes what should have survived, and both are visible to the holder as an outage.

rules.rule: Deprovisioning checks active dependencies before any destructive action.
rules.because: Shared resources do not belong to the entitlement that happened to end, and removing one takes it from everyone else still entitled to it.

rules.rule: Deprovisioning and data deletion are separate lifecycle mechanisms with separate authorisation.
rules.because: Removing a capability is reversible and removing the record of it is not. A deprovision that deletes history has performed an action nobody asked for and nobody can undo.

rules.rule: An access restriction uses the smallest scope that addresses its reason.
rules.because: A payment problem does not justify blocking a security setting, and over-broad restriction makes the restriction itself the incident.

rules.rule: Grant, revoke, provision and deprovision side effects are idempotent.
rules.because: All four are triggered by distributed events that retry, so an operation that is not idempotent is not at risk of double-applying - it is waiting to.

rules.rule: Identification, verification, authentication and authorization are four separate mechanisms and none implies the next.
rules.because: They arrive together in a login flow and diverge everywhere else. A system that stores them as one state cannot answer the only question an incident asks: which of the four actually held.

rules.rule: Verification applies to a defined claim and scope. One verified attribute does not verify the person.
rules.because: A verified email address proves control of an inbox. Read as a verified identity, it becomes the basis for decisions the evidence never supported.

rules.rule: Document submission and document validation are separate states.
rules.because: Uploading is a transfer and validating is a judgement, and the gap between them is where a process appears to be waiting on the customer while it is waiting on us.

rules.rule: Verification failure preserves its reason, and a technical failure is never recorded as an identity rejection.
rules.because: Without the reason every failure becomes the same retry, and recording our own outage against someone's verification history marks them as having failed something they never attempted.

rules.rule: Required authentication assurance follows the sensitivity of the action, not the identity of the actor.
rules.because: Assurance is a property of what is being done. Setting it per user produces both an over-challenged ordinary session and an under-challenged sensitive one.

rules.rule: Completing a step-up revalidates the original action before executing it.
rules.because: The challenge takes time, and the entitlement, the resource or the policy can move while it runs. Resuming on the state that requested the step-up executes a decision made before the check.

rules.rule: Authentication failures are signals, not proof of compromise.
rules.because: Forgetting a password is the most common event in this category, and a system that treats it as an attack locks out mostly legitimate people.

rules.rule: Account recovery never becomes a weaker bypass around normal security controls.
rules.because: It exists for the case where normal authentication has already failed, which makes it the route an attacker reaches for first.

rules.rule: An identity attribute change reconciles dependent credentials, contactability and permissions independently.
rules.because: A new email address inherits neither the old one's deliverability nor its consent. Carrying either across turns a profile edit into a permission grant nobody made.

rules.rule: A security restriction uses the smallest scope that addresses its evidence.
rules.because: Most security signals are false positives, and for those the containment is the entire customer-visible incident.

rules.rule: Suspected compromise and confirmed compromise remain separate states.
rules.because: Containment is designed to be reversible and confirmation is not. Recording the first as the second makes every false positive permanent.

rules.rule: Security restoration rebuilds valid access from current state rather than restoring a historical snapshot.
rules.because: The same rule as ACC-R10, and it matters most here: a snapshot taken before an incident restores exactly the credentials and sessions the incident was about.

rules.rule: Verification and authentication retries are bounded wherever abuse or security risk exists.
rules.because: An unbounded retry is a brute-force channel with a friendly interface, and it is indistinguishable from a persistent legitimate user until it is counted.

rules.rule: A stale verification, recovery or identity-update action never overrides newer authoritative state.
rules.because: These operations are slow and human-paced, so the world routinely moves while they run - and the late-arriving result carries the confidence of a decision made against facts that have gone.

rules.rule: Security and identity histories remain auditable. Nothing in either is erased, including cleared suspicions.
rules.because: A cleared signal is still a fact about what was seen. Deleting it makes a recurrence look like a first occurrence, which is the pattern most worth catching.

rules.rule: Person, account, organization, relationship and role are separate entities and separate concepts.
rules.because: One person can hold several accounts, one account can carry several people, and a role is a property of the link rather than of either end. Collapsing any pair produces a data model that cannot express ordinary situations.

rules.rule: A relationship change recalculates only the rights and obligations that actually depend on that relationship.
rules.because: Rebuilding everything on every change reprovisions what already worked and revokes what should have survived, and the person experiences both as a fault.

rules.rule: Ending a relationship erases neither the historical relationship nor commitments validly created while it existed.
rules.because: The relationship having existed is what made those commitments valid. Removing the record retroactively makes them look unauthorised.

rules.rule: A role change applies an authority and capability delta. It does not rebuild identity.
rules.because: Rebuilding treats the person as new, which loses their history and reprovisions what a delta would have left alone.

rules.rule: Parent and child state are never copied blindly in either direction.
rules.because: Downward it deletes children that stood on their own; upward it lets one child's failure become the parent's state. Both look like correct propagation until someone checks what was actually dependent.

rules.rule: Deriving a parent state from children requires an explicit aggregation policy. ANY, ALL, majority and thresholds are never inferred.
rules.because: The same rule as OWN-R8, arriving from the structural side. An invented aggregation rule is indistinguishable from a real one until the first case where they disagree.

rules.rule: Duplicate detection and entity merge are separate decisions with separate evidence.
rules.because: Detection asks whether two records might be the same. Merge asks whether consolidating them is safe and reversible. The first is cheap and often wrong; the second is expensive and usually permanent.

rules.rule: Linking preserves independent identities. Merging consolidates them. They are not degrees of the same operation.
rules.because: A link that quietly behaves as a merge shares consent and entitlement across two people who never agreed to be treated as one.

rules.rule: An entity split preserves the historical fact that the records were previously represented together.
rules.because: Rewriting history as though they had always been separate makes every past event unattributable, and the split itself becomes invisible to anyone investigating later.

rules.rule: Consent, entitlements, financial obligations and credentials are never blindly duplicated during a split, nor propagated during a link.
rules.because: These four do not divide by being copied. Duplicating an obligation creates one that nobody incurred; duplicating a consent creates one that nobody gave.

rules.rule: A required relationship that disappears creates an explicit orphan state, never a null field.
rules.because: Null is unqueryable and unescalatable. Work with no owner has to be findable as work with no owner, or it is simply lost while appearing normal.

rules.rule: Orphan resolution does not reset inherited deadlines or obligations.
rules.because: The obligation was made to someone outside the organisation. Losing track of who owns it internally is our problem and not a reason for their clock to restart.

rules.rule: Relationship and entity operations invalidate the stale actions that depended on the superseded structure.
rules.because: An action queued against a relationship that has since ended executes on behalf of a structure that no longer exists, and neither end of it will recognise the result.

rules.rule: Cross-entity propagation always follows an explicit dependency rule.
rules.because: Inheritance is the default assumption in every hierarchy and it is wrong often enough that assuming it is how a suspended organisation deletes an unrelated subsidiary's data.

rules.rule: Entity history stays reconstructable after any relationship change, link, split or reconciliation.
rules.because: These operations are the ones most likely to be questioned afterwards, and they are also the ones most likely to destroy the evidence needed to answer.

rules.rule: Duplicate detection, merge authorization and merge execution are three separate stages.
rules.because: Detection is cheap and frequently wrong, authorization is a judgement about consequences, and execution is usually permanent. Running them as one step means the cheapest evidence drives the least reversible action.

rules.rule: Merge is reconciliation, not field overwrite. Newest-value-wins is never applied across all state types.
rules.because: A newer contact point may supersede an older one while a newer consent does not supersede an older withdrawal. One rule across every field silently picks the wrong answer for whichever fields it was not designed for.

rules.rule: Each state type carries its own authority and conflict rule during consolidation.
rules.because: Consent, entitlement, credentials, obligations and attributes answer to different authorities, and a merge that reads them as one list applies one authority to all of them.

rules.rule: Identity merge and account consolidation are separate mechanisms.
rules.because: Consolidating business structure is routine; consolidating two people into one identity is not, and the second must never happen as a side effect of the first.

rules.rule: Account consolidation never collapses independent people into one identity.
rules.because: Members of a consolidated account remain distinct people with distinct consent and distinct history, and any consolidation that needs them not to be has exceeded what it was authorised to do.

rules.rule: Relationship and role transfer preserves historical responsibility and inherited obligations.
rules.because: Who was answerable at the time something happened is a fact about the past. Transferring the role forward does not move it, and inherited deadlines do not restart because the holder changed.

rules.rule: Account closure, subscription cancellation and data deletion are three independent state transitions.
rules.because: Coupling any pair produces one of the two worst outcomes available here: continuing to charge someone who thought they had left, or destroying records that had to be kept.

rules.rule: Closing an account inventories its external and commercial dependencies.
rules.because: A subscription billed by a third party does not end because our account record did, and the person discovers the difference on their next statement.

rules.rule: A closed account may require a scoped wind-down state, with its permitted capabilities enumerated.
rules.because: Final invoices, refunds, exports and open cases all outlive closure. Leaving that as a general exception rather than an enumerated scope is how a closed account keeps behaving like an open one.

rules.rule: A terminal relationship state does not mean the historical records never existed.
rules.because: Ending a relationship and erasing its history are different acts with different authority, and only one of them was requested.

rules.rule: Data deletion respects its explicit scope and its authoritative retention obligations. No retention rule is invented.
rules.because: Retaining on a guess keeps what should have gone; deleting on a guess destroys what had to stay. Both are unrecoverable and only one of them is visible.

rules.rule: Distributed deletion requires downstream verification.
rules.because: Deletion succeeding in the primary store says nothing about the caches, the warehouse, the backups and the third parties, and those are where the data is actually found later.

rules.rule: A partial deletion failure stays visible as an unresolved state.
rules.because: A deletion reported as complete while a downstream copy survives is the most consequential false report in this library - it ends the investigation that would have found the copy.

rules.rule: Merge, closure and deletion operations are idempotent wherever their side effects can repeat.
rules.because: These jobs are retried like any others, and a second application of a destructive operation is not a duplicate - it is a second destruction.

rules.rule: Stale jobs never recreate, reactivate or overwrite an entity after a merge, closure or deletion.
rules.because: Downstream synchronisation runs on its own schedule and will happily restore a profile that was deleted an hour earlier, which undoes the operation while reporting success.

rules.rule: Consent, credentials, entitlement and active journeys are explicitly reconciled during a merge.
rules.because: These four are the ones a naive consolidation gets wrong in the permissive direction, and an opt-out that disappears because another profile was opted in is not recoverable by noticing it later.

rules.rule: Destructive operations preserve enough auditability without unnecessarily preserving the personal data they removed.
rules.because: The audit has to show what was done and when. An audit that keeps a copy of the deleted record has recreated the thing the deletion was for.

rules.rule: Connection, authentication, authorization scope, synchronization and health are five separate states.
rules.because: An integration can be connected and unauthorised, authorised and unsynchronised, synchronised and unhealthy. One status field reports the first of those and hides the rest.

rules.rule: Submitting an external request and completing an external business operation are separate states.
rules.because: The provider's acknowledgement describes their queue, not their outcome, and the gap between the two is where every duplicate side effect is created.

rules.rule: A timeout or a lost connection is not proof that an external operation failed.
rules.because: It proves our side of the conversation ended. The provider may have completed the operation, and treating our silence as their failure is what turns one payment into two.

rules.rule: An ambiguous external outcome is reconciled before any retry.
rules.because: Retrying an unknown is how a single unknown becomes two operations, one of which nobody is looking for.

rules.rule: Processing a duplicate webhook or event is harmless.
rules.because: Providers redeliver by design. An integration that is not safe against redelivery is not broken occasionally - it is broken on a schedule set by someone else.

rules.rule: A late external event is checked against current state before it mutates anything.
rules.because: It can be a valid record of what happened without being a valid instruction about what is true now, and applying it blindly overwrites a newer decision with an older one.

rules.rule: Integration failure and integration lag are separate problems.
rules.because: One means operations cannot proceed; the other means they proceed late. Queueing work against a slow integration adds to the queue that is already the problem.

rules.rule: Reconnecting does not mean synchronization or backfill is complete.
rules.because: The connection recovering is the moment the gap becomes measurable, not the moment it closes. Marking the integration healthy there hides the missing window entirely.

rules.rule: Backfill repairs state and history without blindly replaying historical customer-facing actions.
rules.because: A week of held events replayed on reconnection delivers a week of messages at once, most of them describing states that have since moved.

rules.rule: Synchronization conflicts are resolved through explicit authority rules.
rules.because: Without one, the resolution is decided by whichever system happened to write last, which is a property of scheduling rather than of correctness.

rules.rule: Last-write-wins is never used as a universal reconciliation strategy.
rules.because: Different fields have different sources of truth. A single rule across all of them is right for the fields it was designed against and silently wrong everywhere else.

rules.rule: Integration failure affects the smallest valid capability scope.
rules.because: Disabling a whole integration because one endpoint failed converts a provider's partial outage into a total one on our side.

rules.rule: Work queued during a failure is revalidated after recovery, not simply sent.
rules.because: The world moved while the integration was down, and a queued instruction written against the old world is not automatically still correct.

rules.rule: A recovery backlog is drained in a controlled manner.
rules.because: An integration that has just come back, met with everything it missed at once, goes down again - and the second outage looks like a new fault rather than our own doing.

rules.rule: A provider outage does not convert an UNKNOWN outcome into a FAILED one without evidence.
rules.because: Marking a user's action failed because we lost sight of it is a statement about us presented as a statement about them, and it is acted on downstream as though it were confirmed.

rules.rule: Integration state changes and external side effects are auditable and idempotent.
rules.because: These operations are retried by design at every layer, and the audit is the only way to reconstruct what actually reached the provider when the two sides disagree.

rules.rule: Accepted, queued, processing, stalled and completed are five distinct operational states.
rules.because: Collapsing them lets infrastructure acknowledgement stand in for business completion, which is the failure that produces a customer waiting on something a dashboard says is finished.

rules.rule: Queue lag and external integration failure are separate problems with separate responses.
rules.because: One means we cannot keep up; the other means we cannot proceed. Queueing more work against a lagging system adds to the backlog that is already the problem.

rules.rule: Long-running work is not automatically classified as stalled.
rules.because: Duration describes the work; loss of progress describes its health. Killing legitimate long jobs on a duration threshold produces exactly the failures the threshold was meant to catch.

rules.rule: Retry eligibility requires both a transient failure and a safely repeatable operation.
rules.because: Transience alone justifies trying again; repeatability alone justifies it being harmless. Retrying on the first without the second is how one operation becomes two.

rules.rule: Retry budgets are bounded and durable across worker restarts.
rules.because: A counter held in process memory renews itself every time a worker cycles, which turns a bounded policy into an unbounded loop that looks bounded in the code.

rules.rule: An unknown side-effect state is reconciled before any replay.
rules.because: The whole risk of asynchronous work is that something may already have happened where we cannot see it, and replaying into that uncertainty is the one action that makes it worse.

rules.rule: Deduplication operates on logical business-operation identity, not payload similarity.
rules.because: A customer buying the same item twice produces two identical payloads and two legitimate operations. Collapsing them is a worse failure than executing a duplicate, because they asked for both.

rules.rule: A composite parent outcome requires an explicit aggregation policy. ALL, ANY and majority are never invented.
rules.because: The same rule as OWN-R8 and REL-R6, arriving from the processing side. A guessed aggregation rule is right for the cases it was imagined against and silently wrong for the rest.

rules.rule: Dead-letter state creates a remediation obligation. It is not disposal.
rules.because: A queue nobody reviews is indistinguishable from deletion, except that it produces a reassuring metric while the work quietly does not happen.

rules.rule: Worker failure and work failure are separate states.
rules.because: A worker dying says where the process was, not what the work did. The operation may have completed a moment before, and replaying it on that assumption repeats it.

rules.rule: Backlog recovery revalidates delayed work before executing it.
rules.because: The world moved while the queue was stuck, and an instruction written against the old world is not automatically still correct just because it was once queued.

rules.rule: A stale customer-facing action is not replayed merely because it was queued.
rules.because: Appropriateness has a shelf life. A message that was right on Tuesday arriving on Friday describes a state that has moved and reads as a system talking to itself.

rules.rule: A recovery backlog is drained according to downstream capacity and current priority, not arrival order.
rules.because: Strict arrival order makes new urgent work wait behind old obsolete work, and an unthrottled drain takes down the capacity that has just come back.

rules.rule: Technical job success and business outcome success are separate wherever the architecture requires additional confirmation.
rules.because: A job returning true reports that the code ran without raising. Whether the state it was supposed to create exists is a different question, and only one of them is what anyone actually wanted.

rules.rule: Queue, job and work transitions and retries are idempotent and auditable.
rules.because: Every layer here retries by design, so a transition that is not idempotent is not at risk of double-applying - it is scheduled to.

rules.rule: A stale job never overwrites a newer entity version.
rules.because: Jobs execute in the order workers pick them up, not the order decisions were made, so without a version check the most recent decision is the one most likely to be undone.

rules.rule: Operational recovery preserves original deadlines and business context unless a governing policy explicitly changes them.
rules.because: The commitment was made to someone who is not waiting on our queue. Our backlog is our problem, and restarting their clock to accommodate it moves the cost onto them.

rules.rule: A financial obligation and a payment attempt are separate entities.
rules.because: The obligation outlives every attempt against it. Deleting or closing it because an attempt failed loses what is owed, and treating a successful attempt as the obligation loses the balance it left behind.

rules.rule: Initiated, authorized, captured, settled and obligation-satisfied are distinct states.
rules.because: Each is a different commitment about funds, and collapsing them into a generic success grants irreversible outcomes against money that has been reserved rather than taken.

rules.rule: Payment failure and payment unknown remain separate states.
rules.because: Failure means we know nothing moved. Unknown means we do not know, and the correct response to the second is to find out rather than to try again.

rules.rule: An unknown financial outcome is reconciled before any replacement attempt.
rules.because: The original may have succeeded where we could not see it, and a replacement submitted into that uncertainty is a duplicate charge the customer will find before we do.

rules.rule: A payment failure does not terminate the commercial relationship.
rules.because: A declined card is a payment event. Cancelling the relationship on it removes something the customer was paying for because of a problem they were about to fix.

rules.rule: Financial recovery and entitlement or access consequences are separate, and hand off to each other rather than merging.
rules.because: Whether money is owed and whether access continues are governed by different policies with different timelines, and merging them makes each decision on the other's evidence.

rules.rule: A partial payment or partial refund preserves the remaining balance explicitly.
rules.because: Partial is not paid. A balance that is rounded away or implied is one nobody can collect and nobody can dispute.

rules.rule: Refund requested, refund approved and refund completed are three separate states.
rules.because: The first is an ask, the second is a decision, and the third is money that has actually arrived. Telling a customer any of the first two happened when they wanted the third is how a refund becomes a dispute.

rules.rule: A financial dispute and a generic decision appeal are separate mechanisms.
rules.because: A dispute is adjudicated by an external authority with its own deadline, its own evidence rules and its own power to move funds. An internal appeal has none of those.

rules.rule: Opening a dispute is not proof of fraud or wrongdoing by anyone.
rules.because: Most disputes are confusion, a forgotten subscription or an unrecognised descriptor. Treating the claim as a finding penalises customers for a process that exists to protect them.

rules.rule: Financial reconciliation preserves transaction history.
rules.because: The history is what any correction has to be explained against. A mismatch fixed by deleting the inconvenient record has removed the evidence of what it fixed.

rules.rule: Corrections are explicit adjustments, never silent historical rewrites.
rules.because: An adjustment can be audited, reversed and explained. An edited record cannot be distinguished from one that was always that way.

rules.rule: An external provider accepting a request does not prove funds moved.
rules.because: The acknowledgement describes their queue. Whether money reached the other side is a separate fact established separately, and it is the only one the customer experiences.

rules.rule: A late financial outcome is reconciled against the obligation's current state before it mutates anything.
rules.because: The balance moved while the outcome was in flight, and applying it against the balance it was written for creates a discrepancy rather than resolving one.

rules.rule: Duplicate payment or refund execution is prevented through idempotency and reconciliation, not through hoping.
rules.because: Every layer here retries, and a duplicate in this category is money that has to be found, returned and explained rather than a log line that has to be ignored.

rules.rule: Financial state is authoritative enough that communication activity cannot redefine it.
rules.because: A reminder being sent is not a debt existing, and a receipt being emailed is not a payment succeeding. Where the messaging layer can move financial truth, the truth follows the schedule of whatever sends.

rules.rule: Currency and amount semantics stay explicit. Monetary values are never reconciled across incompatible currency or context.
rules.because: An amount without its currency is a number, and netting two of them produces a balance that is confidently wrong in a way no later check can detect.

rules.rule: Request, acceptance, availability, allocation, fulfillment and delivery are six separate states.
rules.because: Each is a different commitment, and the ones most often collapsed - accepted with fulfillable, dispatched with delivered - are exactly the ones a customer experiences as a promise that was never real.

rules.rule: Acceptance creates an obligation only when the authoritative acceptance criteria are met.
rules.because: An obligation created from an unvalidated request is one nobody is working and nobody knows exists, and it surfaces when the customer asks where their order is.

rules.rule: Availability and allocation stay separate wherever resources can be consumed concurrently.
rules.because: Availability is a reading taken at a moment. Allocation is a claim. Treating the reading as the claim is how two orders are both promised the last unit.

rules.rule: Allocation and release operations are idempotent.
rules.because: A retried allocation that consumes twice oversells without anyone overselling anything, and a retried release returns capacity that was never held.

rules.rule: Partial fulfillment preserves both the completed scope and the remaining scope explicitly.
rules.because: Marking a partly-delivered obligation as failed destroys work that was actually done; marking it complete abandons what is still owed. Only carrying both is correct.

rules.rule: Fulfillment exception, delay and terminal failure are three different states.
rules.because: One says something went wrong, one says it will be later, and one says it will not happen. Collapsing them either cancels recoverable work or leaves failed work looking merely late.

rules.rule: A delay changes expected timing and does not mean failure.
rules.because: An obligation that is late is still owed. Treating lateness as failure releases the resources and closes the obligation the customer is still waiting on.

rules.rule: Substitution or alternative fulfillment respects the approval or choice the policy requires.
rules.because: A substitute is a different thing from what was promised. Deciding on the recipient's behalf that it is acceptable is a decision only they can make.

rules.rule: Dispatch and delivery completion are separate states.
rules.because: Handing something to a carrier transfers execution and nothing else. The obligation stays ours and stays unresolved until an authoritative outcome exists.

rules.rule: A delivery attempt and a successful delivery are separate outcomes.
rules.because: An attempt tells you a van arrived. Whether anything was handed over is a different fact, and the two are reported through the same channel by systems that blur them.

rules.rule: An unknown delivery outcome is reconciled before any unsafe re-execution.
rules.because: Re-sending against an unknown produces two of the thing, one of which nobody is expecting and nobody will pay for.

rules.rule: Delivered and accepted stay separate wherever the business semantics require it.
rules.because: Where acceptance is contractually meaningful, treating arrival as agreement closes an obligation the counterparty has not agreed is finished.

rules.rule: Cancellation stops only the remaining work and preserves the completed scope.
rules.because: Work already delivered happened. A cancellation that erases it produces a record nobody can reconcile against what the customer actually received.

rules.rule: Resource release happens when the resource is no longer required and never touches unrelated or shared allocations.
rules.because: A release scoped too widely takes capacity away from obligations that are still going ahead, and those failures appear somewhere else entirely.

rules.rule: Existing fulfillment obligations survive ownership, integration and timing changes unless explicitly resolved.
rules.because: The obligation was made to someone outside the organisation. Which team owns it, which system carries it and when it is expected are all our concerns and none of them discharge it.

rules.rule: A stale fulfillment job or event never overwrites newer cancellation, reallocation or completion state.
rules.because: Fulfillment events arrive from warehouses, carriers and field systems on their own schedules, so without a version check the most recent decision is the one most likely to be undone.

rules.rule: Every fulfillment terminal state states the remaining obligation explicitly: zero, partial, replaced, cancelled or unresolved.
rules.because: An obligation that ends without saying what is left is one nobody can finish, and the remainder is discovered by the person who was waiting for it.

rules.rule: A post-completion issue, a confirmed defect and remedy eligibility are three separate states.
rules.because: Most reports are not defects and most defects do not entitle every remedy. Collapsing them produces either a manufactured fault or a refused customer with a real problem.

rules.rule: Return requested, authorized, in transit, received and accepted are five separate states.
rules.because: Each fails independently. Authorising a return does not make it arrive, and receiving something does not mean it met the conditions it was authorised under.

rules.rule: Return and refund are separate lifecycle mechanisms with separate eligibility.
rules.because: Someone can be entitled to send something back without being entitled to their money, and entitled to money without needing to return anything.

rules.rule: A refund hands off to the financial lifecycle rather than being implemented as a generic return outcome.
rules.because: Deciding money is owed and moving it are financial acts with their own authority and their own confirmation. Bolting them onto a returns process skips both.

rules.rule: A replacement creates a new fulfillment obligation tied to the original defect.
rules.because: It is a second delivery against the same promise, not a new sale and not an edit to the first one. Treating it as a new order bills for it; treating it as a correction loses that the first was wrong.

rules.rule: Correction and reperformance preserve the original incorrect outcome as history.
rules.because: Rewriting the original as though it had always been right removes the evidence anything needed fixing, and with it the ability to see the same fault recur.

rules.rule: Remedy selection starts from the unresolved obligation, not from the complaint.
rules.because: The complaint says how someone feels; the obligation says what is owed. A remedy chosen from the first satisfies nobody when what was actually missing is still missing.

rules.rule: Remedy approval, remedy execution and verified resolution are three separate states.
rules.because: An approved refund that never arrived, a replacement dispatched to the wrong address and a correction that did not correct anything all look identical from an approval record.

rules.rule: Partial return, correction and remedy outcomes preserve the remaining scope explicitly.
rules.because: Half a remedy recorded as a whole one closes an obligation that is still live, and the customer discovers the remainder rather than being told about it.

rules.rule: Compensation and resolving the underlying problem are independent decisions.
rules.because: A credit acknowledges impact. It does not deliver the thing that was owed, and a system that treats it as the fix leaves someone holding money and the same broken outcome.

rules.rule: Compensation that requires financial or entitlement execution reuses those canonical mechanisms.
rules.because: A service credit is an entitlement and a goodwill payment is a financial movement. Implementing either inside a remedy flow skips the confirmation each of them needs.

rules.rule: Duplicate remedies and duplicate compensation are prevented.
rules.because: Two recovery cases against one obligation produce two replacements or two refunds, and the second one is found by accounting rather than by the process that issued it.

rules.rule: An existing recovery case suppresses duplicate issue and remedy creation covering the same obligation.
rules.because: The same rule as ACT-R9, RET-R9 and FBK-R10, arriving here for the fourth time. Where several channels can each open a case, several of them will.

rules.rule: Post-remedy recurrence preserves previous attempts and escalates diagnosis where appropriate.
rules.because: A remedy that did not hold usually means the diagnosis was wrong rather than the execution. Repeating it without that reassessment produces the same failure at greater cost.

rules.rule: Historical fulfillment, issue and remedy records stay auditable.
rules.because: Recovery is the area most likely to be questioned afterwards, by a customer, a regulator or an accountant, and each of them asks what was delivered, what went wrong and what was done about it.

rules.rule: A remedy is not marked successful because an internal task or external request completed technically.
rules.because: The same substitution OPS-R15 forbids for jobs, applied to recovery: a refund submitted is not a refund received, and a replacement dispatched is not one that arrived.

rules.rule: An unknown return or remedy outcome is reconciled before any irreversible downstream action.
rules.because: Issuing a second remedy against an unknown produces two of it, and in this category the second one is usually money or goods that have already gone out.

rules.rule: Every terminal recovery state says whether the original obligation is fully resolved, partially resolved, replaced, financially compensated or still outstanding.
rules.because: Recovery ends in five genuinely different places, and a state that does not say which one it reached leaves the remainder to be discovered by the person who was waiting for it.

rules.rule: Continuing relationship creation and activation are separate states.
rules.because: An agreement can exist for months before it starts, and can exist forever without ever starting if a condition it depends on is never met.

rules.rule: Future-effective activation revalidates its prerequisites at execution time.
rules.because: Everything the activation depends on can change between the schedule and the date. A job that fires on stored assumptions activates a relationship the parties no longer have.

rules.rule: An active relationship and an entitlement are related and separate.
rules.because: Active says the agreement is running. Entitled says this specific right is one it grants. Reading the first as the second is how a basic plan gets enterprise features.

rules.rule: Renewal eligibility, renewal decision and renewal execution are three separate stages.
rules.because: Each fails on its own. Eligible and undecided, decided and unpaid, and paid but not yet started are three different situations that need three different things said about them.

rules.rule: Each renewal term preserves the previous term's history.
rules.because: Overwriting the old term's dates and price with the new ones means last quarter's invoice no longer matches any terms the system knows about.

rules.rule: Renewal payment failure is not automatic relationship termination.
rules.because: A card expiring is the most common failure in this category and the least meaningful. Terminating on it ends relationships over an event the counterparty would fix in thirty seconds if told.

rules.rule: Grace and lapse semantics come from governing policy and are never invented.
rules.because: An invented grace period either cuts off someone who was entitled to continue, or keeps serving someone who was not. Both are found later, by the wrong person.

rules.rule: Plan and terms changes are effective-time aware and are applied as deltas.
rules.because: Storing the resulting terms freezes an answer computed against a relationship that will have changed by the time it lands. Storing the delta lets it be recomputed against what is actually there.

rules.rule: Scheduled changes are version-aware and suppress stale execution.
rules.because: The same discipline INT-R7 and OPS-R11 apply to queued work, arriving here where the stale action changes what someone pays and what they can use.

rules.rule: Cancellation request, scheduled cancellation and effective relationship end are separate states.
rules.because: The gap between them is often months, and during it the relationship is fully active. Collapsing them cuts service off at the moment someone asks about stopping.

rules.rule: End-of-term cancellation preserves current-term validity until the effective end.
rules.because: The term was paid for. Ending access early bills someone for a period they cannot use, which converts a clean exit into a refund claim.

rules.rule: Suspension and cancellation are separate lifecycle mechanisms.
rules.because: Suspension is reversible and the relationship survives it. Treating one as the other either ends something recoverable or leaves something ended still counting toward renewal.

rules.rule: Restoration from suspension rebuilds current valid capability rather than replaying a stored snapshot.
rules.because: The same restore-from-snapshot ban ACC-R13 and IDN-R12 state, and here the snapshot is usually months old and describes a plan the relationship no longer has.

rules.rule: Relationship end, account closure and data deletion are three independent lifecycle events.
rules.because: A former customer usually keeps an account, and almost always keeps records that have to be retained. Chaining these treats leaving a plan as asking to be erased.

rules.rule: Relationship end hands off entitlement loss and deprovisioning rather than reimplementing them.
rules.because: Which rights survive an ending is a property of the entitlements. A relationship record deciding it locally will disagree with the entitlement lifecycle, and one of them will be wrong.

rules.rule: Financial, fulfillment, dispute and remedy obligations can survive relationship termination.
rules.because: An order placed while it was active is still owed, a refund still due is still due, and a dispute still open is still open. Ending stops future rights, not existing commitments.

rules.rule: Historical terms, renewals, suspensions and cancellation decisions stay auditable.
rules.because: This is the category where someone eventually asks what they agreed to and when. A record that only holds the current terms cannot answer it.

rules.rule: Late payments and stale scheduled events are reconciled against the current relationship version before they change state.
rules.because: A payment arriving after a lapse does not retroactively renew a term that never started, and a cancellation firing after a resubscription ends the wrong relationship.

rules.rule: Availability, hold and confirmed reservation are three separate states.
rules.because: They protect different amounts of nothing. Availability protects none of it, a hold protects it briefly, and only a confirmation is something either party can rely on.

rules.rule: An availability query guarantees no future capacity.
rules.because: What is returned is true at the instant it is computed. Under contention it can be false before the page finishes rendering, which is why the reservation re-reads rather than trusting it.

rules.rule: Temporary holds expire and release deterministically.
rules.because: A hold that outlives its window silently removes capacity nobody owns and nobody can book, and the resource looks full while standing empty.

rules.rule: A reservation request revalidates current capacity before it confirms.
rules.because: The gap between seeing a slot and requesting it is exactly where two people end up holding one appointment, and only one of them will find out at the door.

rules.rule: A confirmed reservation creates an explicit time-bound commitment on both sides.
rules.because: It is the point at which the customer arranges their day around it and the provider stops selling the slot. Everything before it is provisional and has to say so.

rules.rule: Preparation dependencies never redefine the reservation's truth.
rules.because: A missing form is a reason to chase, escalate or contact. Moving or voiding a confirmed time because a prerequisite is late is a booking decision, and belongs to the booking lifecycle.

rules.rule: Rescheduling preserves the original reservation until replacement capacity is secured.
rules.because: Releasing first leaves the customer with nothing when the replacement does not materialise, and the slot they had is gone by the time anyone notices.

rules.rule: Reschedule history stays auditable.
rules.because: A reservation that only ever shows its current time cannot answer how many times it moved, which is the first question anyone investigating a service problem asks.

rules.rule: Cancellation, no-show and provider cancellation are three distinct states.
rules.because: They differ in who failed, what is owed and what the customer is told. Collapsing them charges a fee to someone whose appointment we could not keep.

rules.rule: Reservation cancellation and refund or fee decisions are separate lifecycle mechanisms.
rules.because: Whether the booking ends and whether money moves are decided by different rules, and a cancellation flow that settles both will get one of them wrong quietly.

rules.rule: Scheduled-time jobs are version-aware so cancelled or rescheduled bookings cannot be revived.
rules.because: The same discipline SUB-R9, INT-R7 and OPS-R11 apply to queued work. Here the stale job allocates a provider to an appointment nobody has and then records a no-show for it.

rules.rule: Check-in, attendance, service start and service completion can be four different states.
rules.because: Someone can check in and never be seen, be seen and receive half the service, or receive all of it and have none of that recorded. Each gap is a real operational failure.

rules.rule: Partial service preserves the remaining obligation explicitly.
rules.because: A half-delivered appointment recorded as complete closes something the customer is still owed, and they discover it rather than being told.

rules.rule: A no-show is established only after cancellation, rescheduling and provider-side failure are excluded.
